#9706. Simple Sudoku Solver in Verilog

Welcome back to another round of Simple Sudoku Solvers! If you are unfamiliar with the series, I suggest you start with the first post or by perusing the backlog. Last time, in assembly, we told the CPU exactly what to do, one instruction at a time. Today we go one level lower and build the machine directly in Verilog.

Verilog is a hardware description language. You donât write a program that will at some point run on hardware. Instead, you describe a circuit, and the compiler turns that description into gates and flip-flops. Weâll run it in a simulator, because I donât have a Sudoku chip lying around (future work), but the solver is real hardware in the sense that a synthesis tool accepts it and tells us how many gates it would take. Still counts, even with sim2real TBD.

The solver is about 145 lines, plus 40 lines of ceremony to feed it a puzzle and print the result. You can run it with iverilog -o sudoku sudoku.v && vvp sudoku, using Icarus Verilog. I didnât test it anywhere else. As always, the code is on GitHub.

Season three is about solvers, specifications, and constraints, and somehow also about hardware and the lowest of low levels. Thatâs because hardware is possibly the purest version of a specification (and, to be quite honest, because I felt like it).

I think this was the strangest episode so far, for me. I donât mean that in a bad way.

If youâve never read Verilog before, here is what you need for this post.

A module is a circuit with inputs and outputs. wire [8:0] x is a bundle of nine wires, numbered 8 down to 0. reg is a bit of a misnomer: itâs a value we assign in a procedural block, and whether it becomes an actual register is actually dependent on our usage of it.

There are two kinds of blocks we care about. always @* describes combinational logic. Its outputs are a pure function of its inputs, and they change whenever the inputs do. Think of it as a very big expression.

always @(posedge clk), on the other hand, describes sequential logic. It runs once at every rising clock edge, and the <= assignments inside it all happen together at the end of that edge. Thatâs where all our state lives.

for loops exist, but in synthesizable code they are unrolled completely. A loop over 81 cells is 81 copies of its body. Keep that in mind, it will matter. Itâs also very cool, so itâs worth keeping in mind anyway.

The board is the same 81 cells as always, but since hardware doesnât really do arrays of bytes, it is one 324-bit vector, with four bits per cell and 0 for an empty cell:

We have three input wires and output regs (remember, not necessarily registers). Thatâs the whole interface of our chip.

We put a puzzle on the puzzle wires, hold start for one cycle, and wait until done goes high (think in currents). Then, if solved is set, board has the answer. Otherwise, the board is unsolvable.

Reading a cell is a slice, which we wrap in a small function.

Slices work like in many other languages, except that the operators +: and -: encode a direction from the start index. Here, we say âstart at 4 * i and take the next 4 bitsâ.

Units are the 27 rows, columns, and boxes we always care about. We describe them with a function that tells us which cell is the k-th member of unit u:

The first 9 are the rows, then come the columns, and the icky expression at the end there is the box arithmetic with our usual set of magic numbers.

Fun fact: this looks like it does division at runtime, but it doesnât. We only ever call it with constants from unrolled loops, so the synthesis tool computes all of it ahead of time (much like an optimizing compiler would). What is left is just the wiring, and the box arithmetic decides which wires connect.

Like in many previous installments, we track digits as bitmasks. And like in our assembly episode, when itâs convenient we use the trick where digit d lives in bit d, and an empty cell lands in bit 0, which we throw away:

In hardware this is a decoder, four wires in, ten wires out, one of them lights up. Dropping bit 0 is just not connecting it. We donât need a branch, and in this case not even an instruction. These sorts of tricks are annoying the higher up the stack we go, but they come naturally to us when weâre thinking in circuits and currents.

We also need the opposite direction, from a single bit back to a digit, and a popcount:

We are back to having to write our own popcount, regretfully, but it doesnât have to be smart. Itâs a chain of adders in the end, unrolled by our magical synthesis tool again.

This is where Verilog differs from everything else weâve done!

The following block is combinational. Every clock cycle, it looks at the whole board and computes, for all 81 cells at the same time, everything the solver could want to know.

Thatâs quite a few symbols, but it almost looks familiar I think.

For each of the 27 units we or together the digits it contains into seen. While we do that, we check if a digit was already there, and if so, the unit has a clash. No other solver in the series has needed this check so far, and youâll see in a minute why we need it now. Hint: it has to do with the parallel nature of the system.

The candidates are the usual not-yet-taken numbers, and we compute them for all cells. We end up with four answers:

This reads much like the solver loop weâve written many times, but it works completely differently, because there is no loop. The circuit that is synthesized has 81 candidate calculators and a long chain of comparators for the minimum that are all settling at once.

Why the clash check? Here, because of parallelism, forced fills in every forced cell in the same cycle. If two cells in the same unit are both set to the same number, we write both of those in the same cycle and nothing checks at the end. Instead, we check the unit for duplicates at the next cycle, and treat a clash like any other unsolvable branch.

So weâve successfully parallelized our work, including our mistakes! Fun!

Since there is no recursion, the search becomes a state machine with three states:

RUN propagates and branches, BACK backtracks, and HALT is the stop condition.

For backtracking we need a stack. The entry has the board before a guess, the cell we guessed in, and the candidates we havenât tried yet:

Every guess fills at least one cell, so the search canât go deeper than 81, and 81 entries are enough to hold our search tree. Math! Logic!

Unfortunately, we have to pay for every entry in hardware, no matter if we end up using it or not.

I originally called the second array cell, but it turns out cell is a reserved word in Verilog. Itâs used for configurations, which I had never heard of before. Shows what I know. Iâm just documenting this because where is a bit of an odd name, I think, but I didnât think to pull out the thesaurus1.

Anyway, time to look at the actual states.

Side note: the first cycle is spent initializing, then we fall through to our case structure.

RUN is our whole solver as an if chain. If the board is dead, we backtrack. If there are forced cells, we fill all of them and come back next cycle to continue our work. If the board is full, weâre done and set HALT and all our stopping variables.

Otherwise we dance. pick is the candidate mask of the MRV cell:

We push the current board, the cell, and the remaining candidates, and then write the lowest candidate into the board. pick & -pick isolates the lowest set bit, and pick & (pick - 1) clears it, so together they split the mask into what to try now vs.Â what to try later. Thatâs my official favorite trick from the last episode making a second appearance as a subtractor and a row of and gates.

This is also the place that tripped me up most when I was learning Verilog for this: all of these <= assignments happen together at the clock edge. We write board into the stack and change one cell of board in the same cycle, and the stack still gets the old board, because everything on the right-hand side was read before the edge. The timing is very explicit, and my intuitions are still very much developing.

The BACK state looks at the top of the stack:

If the stack is empty, weâve tried everything, and there is no solution.

If the top entry has no candidates left, we pop it and stay in BACK, so the next cycle looks at the entry below. So we do one backtracking step per cycle, at worst 81 times. This seems wasteful at first, but itâs actually beautiful in its simplicity I find.

Otherwise we restore the saved board, try the next candidate, and go back to RUN. The entry stays on the stack with one fewer candidate, ready to come back if this oneâs a dud, too.

This, too, is the same copy-and-restore dance number from assembly, but itâs copying a board in one cycle. A register that is 324 bits wide is just 324 flip-flops that all load at the same time. If you design the board you can do whatever, it turns out.

And thatâs it! Weâve solved the board!

Our usual hard puzzle takes 7,639 cycles. The puzzles from the repository take between 5 cycles (easy) and 411 cycles (evil), and a puzzle with two 8s in the first row is rejected in 2 cycles, because the clash check catches it right away.

That number is hard to compare with the other episodes. If the circuit ran at 1 MHz, 7,639 cycles would be about 7.5 milliseconds. But I havenât placed and routed it, so I donât know how fast it could really be made2. The 81 comparator chain we built above would probably be the limit, but again, I have no intuitions on how to measure this.

The simulation, on the other hand, is slow. Icarus simulates every wire of that circuit on every cycle, and running the hard puzzle takes about 11 seconds on my machine. That makes it the slowest solver in the series by a wide margin, beating even Agda. Thatâs not a fair comparison, but I think itâs funny anyway, because we came to the land of speed and wires and ended up with the slowest simulations of the series.

As for size, I let the genie guide me and ran the solver through Yosys targeting Lattice iCE40, a family of small FPGAs that hobbyists like. It comes out at about 35,000 lookup tables and 28,000 flip-flops, almost all in the stack. That is a lot more than any iCE40 chip Iâve found has, so weâd need a bigger FPGA, or a stack in block RAM, which would cost us a cycle per access.

If you want to build this circuit, be my guest! Do send pictures and/or measurements, though, please.

We built a Sudoku solver out of (simulated) wires and flip-flops, and made the thing nicely parallel. Through our little state machine, we also added a new tool to our bag of tricks. Time will tell if we need it again.

I still think this one fits the season better than it might have seemed on paper. We really did specify Sudoku in hardware, in a way, in a very lop-sided chip.

In the next episode, we stop writing search code entirely once again: we hand the constraints to z3 and let it find the answer for us, much like in Prolog and miniKanren, but differently. See you there!

2. Synthesis turns the description into gates. Placing and routing then decide where on the chip each gate goes and how the wires run between them, and only then do you know how long a signal takes to get through the slowest path, which sets the maximum clock speed through the annoyances of physics. I didnât do that step by hand, and I donât know whether there is a tool for doing it automatically for me.

#9705. AttackIQ Research Reveals How Iranian Cyber Groups Hand Off Network Access to Enable Destructive Attacks

Analysis of 20 Iranian state-sponsored threat groups details how espionage, ransomware, and hacktivism intersect in state-backed cyber campaigns.

ANTA CLARA, Calif. — (BUSINESS WIRE) — AttackIQ, the leader in threat-informed Continuous Threat Exposure Management (CTEM), today released new research that connects previously fragmented reporting on individual Iranian cyber campaigns to map the relationships among state-sponsored operators and the institutions supporting them. The findings show Iranian espionage groups turn compromised networks into launchpads for other operators, transforming intelligence-gathering operations into destructive attacks.

Threat reporting on Iran typically covers one campaign at a time, and vendors track the same groups under different names. Helix Kitten alone appears under eight other names, including OilRig, APT34 and Scarred Manticore. AttackIQ’s Adversary Research Team consolidated that reporting into Weighing Cyber Power: Evaluating the Strategic and Operational Significance of Iran’s State-Sponsored Cyber Capability, a single map of 20 Iranian adversaries, the government institutions they are linked to and the contractors that supply their personnel, tooling and infrastructure.

Related:Africa Retakes Top Spot as Most Attacked Region, Led by Nigeria Surge

“The value of threat research is measured by the decisions it informs,” said Paul Reid, VP of Adversary Research at AttackIQ. “Understanding which Iranian groups work together, and how confident we can be in each relationship, gives defenders a clear starting point for emulation and a realistic picture of what could follow an initial compromise. It turns a single detection into a forecast of what comes next.”

The report traces how a single intrusion can pass between groups. In one documented case, Helix Kitten (Scarred Manticore), conducted prolonged intelligence collection inside a network before handing off the network access to Banished Kitten (Void Manticore), which pursued destructive objectives. In a second case, Static Kitten (Mango Sandstorm) established access and passed it to Storm-1084, a destructive operator. In a separate campaign against the Albanian government, four separately tracked groups contributed to the same operation, which spanned reconnaissance, initial access, data theft and the deployment of destructive tooling.

When the damage arrives, it is frequently disguised. The research also found Iranian groups staging destructive attacks as ransomware or hacktivism, obscuring the intent behind the attacks. Pioneer Kitten provided criminal ransomware affiliates with access to compromised networks.

The organizations hit first may be a route to other targets. Several groups can gain access to more heavily defended organizations, including in the defense industrial base, through their subsidiaries, contractors, and suppliers.

Related:Ransomware Attacks Increase Behind AI, but Payments Decline

The analysis classifies 20 Iranian adversaries into three weight classes based on their organizational significance, operational relevance, and demonstrated capabilities. The classifications underscore that even smaller, specialized groups can play critical roles in larger cyber campaigns.

Heavyweight: Established groups with sustained espionage operations, internally developed tooling and a central role in Iran’s cyber strategy.

Lightweight: Groups with more focused missions, including specialized espionage, access facilitation and destructive operations.

Featherweight: Groups with narrower or less consistently documented activity, some relying on support from more established adversaries.

“Iran isn’t as technically sophisticated as China, Russia or North Korea, but what it lacks in sophistication it makes up for in cadence,” said Francis Guibernau, Senior Adversary Research Engineer at AttackIQ. “They target anything and everything, on every operating system and in industrial environments. That volume, combined with how freely these groups share access, is what makes the ecosystem dangerous.”

Related:Chinese AI Project Scouts Spies in Taiwan Chip Industry

The research draws on more than 200 references and consolidates more than 2,600 procedures, 1,300 file indicators, and 2,300 network indicators. The analysis was also validated against threat intelligence and real-world activity observed by several Fortune 150 companies actively targeted by Iranian threat actors. The research team also received input from National Computer Incident Response Teams (CIRTs) and members of the intelligence community.

To help organizations put the research into practice, AttackIQ will be releasing adversary emulations based on the documented tactics, techniques, and procedures of Iranian threat actors over the coming weeks. These emulations will enable security teams to safely test their defenses against relevant adversary behaviors, identify gaps in detection and prevention, and prioritize improvements based on real-world threat intelligence.

For a closer look at the findings with AttackIQ’s adversary research team, join the December 10 webinar, Breaking Down Iran’s Most Dangerous Cyber Tactics.

AttackIQ is the leader in threat-informed Continuous Threat Exposure Management (CTEM), helping organizations continuously validate defenses, break attack paths, and reduce threat debt through evidence-based security operations.

Through AVA Agentic OS, AttackIQ has introduced the industry’s first agentic operating system purpose-built for CTEM, enabling organizations to execute Continuous Threat Exposure Management autonomously at enterprise scale.

By orchestrating specialized AI agents across threat intelligence, adversary exposure validation, security validation, detection engineering, control optimization, threat debt reduction, and AI security validation, AttackIQ transforms fragmented security activities into continuous cyber resilience.

Trusted by the world’s largest enterprises, government agencies, and managed security providers, AttackIQ empowers organizations to continuously discover, validate, and reduce cyber risk with confidence.

#9703. Fine-tuning a 350M Model for Better Structured Outputs in 100 GRPO Steps

This guide is a fully public, inexpensive recipe for making a small model substantially better at structured-output compliance. We fine-tune LFM2.5-350M with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) using the TRL library and evaluate it on the IFStruct benchmark. The full run takes around 500 samples and 100 training steps, small enough for a free-tier Colab or Kaggle GPU, and is available on GitHub. The results show that even a light fine-tuning procedure improves performance from 22.6% to 29.7% on the IFStruct benchmark.

Structured output is one of the most common real-world tasks for LLMs, yet most benchmarks fold it into broader reasoning or extraction scores rather than measuring it on its own. Whether a model reliably returns valid, parseable output in the requested format and shape — schema compliance — is often what decides whether it can be wired into a downstream system at all.

Note that the training pipeline described here is not the one used to train the RL model described in the IFStruct blog. This notebook doesn't aim to recreate the IFStruct benchmark score, but to show how task-specific fine-tuning of smaller models can improve performance and match that of far larger models.

This guide has two halves that run in different places:

We will need uv for the Python tooling and llama.cpp for serving. Following the Liquid AI llama.cpp deployment docs, install llama.cpp with Homebrew and verify that llama-server is available:

Before we begin, let's evaluate LFM2.5-350M on the IFStruct benchmark and see whether we can reproduce the reported score of 21.1%.

IFStruct is a benchmark for testing the validity of LLM outputs and schema adherence. The benchmark is open-source in Liquid4All/ifstruct, with the public benchmark dataset available on Hugging Face at LiquidAI/ifstruct-v1.0.

For the eval comparison, we serve the model locally on the MacBook with llama.cpp. We will use the BF16 GGUF (LiquidAI/LFM2.5-350M-GGUF).

Then we start the base-model server with the following command:

Once the server is running, we can run the full benchmark with 2000 samples:

The IFStruct release blog reports 21.1% for LFM2.5-350M. Our local llama.cpp/BF16 setup measures 22.6%, close to the 21.1% reported in the IFStruct blog. We use this local result as the baseline for the same serving stack comparison.

The full, runnable pipeline lives in the accompanying notebook. We will cover only the relevant pieces in this section.

We use nvidia/Nemotron-RL-instruction_following-structured_outputs, which pairs each prompt with a target JSON Schema and an expected field count. We use about 500 samples for training.

Because the Nemotron data distribution differs from the IFStruct evaluation, we augment the prompts to close two gaps between them:

We load LiquidAI/LFM2.5-350M and attach a LoRA adapter. Because LFM2.5 uses a hybrid attention/convolution architecture, we target the LFM-specific module names:

This trains ~6M parameters, about 1.66% of the model.

Then we define three reward functions, each on a [0, 1] scale, which score every completion on whether the extracted structure is correct:

We combine the three as a weighted sum with reward_weights=[1.0, 0.5, 2.0].

We train for 100 steps with 8 generations per prompt group, sized for a free-tier 16 GB GPU:

As you can see in the notebook, over the run, all three reward components climb, the KL from the reference model lifts off zero after warmup, and the truncated-completion fraction stays near zero.

Finally, we merge the LoRA adapter back into the base weights and save it as a single self-contained checkpoint, ready to convert to GGUF for serving:

After GRPO fine-tuning, we rerun the IFStruct evaluation. For this, we need to convert the merged model checkpoint into a BF16 GGUF. The converter script ships with the llama.cpp source, so we clone the repo once and install the converter's gguf package.

Then we serve the merged model with the following command:

Then, we will run the full IFStruct evaluation again with the fine-tuned model:

Comparing the two runs on the identical serving stack:

The gains land exactly where the training aimed: the JSON pass rate rises by nearly 14 points (18.0% → 31.9%), while YAML stays mostly the same. While this is still below the Qwen3.5-2B score of 33.15%, it shows that even light task-specific fine-tuning can bring a small model close to a larger one.

A short GRPO run with about 500 samples and 100 steps can lift a small 350M parameter model from 22.6% to 29.7% on IFStruct. The takeaway is that a cheap, task-specific reward signal can make a small model substantially more reliable about form, closing much of the gap to models several times its size.

To reproduce or extend this work, see the original IFStruct v1.0 blog post, the Liquid4All/ifstruct benchmark repo, and the LiquidAI/ifstruct-v1.0 dataset.

#9702. NeoMME: an efficient Multimodal-native and Multilingual Encoder

We introduce NeoMME, a family of 260M and 800M multilingual multimodal encoders. Unlike many generative visual language models, NeoMME does not use a separate pretrained vision tower or a causal language model. A single bidirectional Transformer processes both text tokens and raw image patches, and we train the entire model from scratch with a masked discrete-diffusion objective.

We fine-tuned NeoMME for visual document retrieval using ColPali's page-image approach. NeoMME-Retriever returns dense and late-interaction embeddings in one forward pass. Both model sizes lie on the ViDoRe v3 Pareto frontier for nDCG@10 and model size. At a matched 2048×2048 image input size on an NVIDIA L40S GPU, the 260M model encodes about 51 pages per second, or about twice ColModernVBERT's throughput. Hierarchical token pooling and asymmetric quantization reduce late-interaction index storage from roughly 1.5 MB to 6 kB per page (255× smaller) while retaining more than 95% of baseline nDCG@10.

NeoMME is available in Hugging Face Transformers. We release all model checkpoints under the Apache 2.0 license.

Many recent visual document retrievers are adapted from pretrained generative visual language models. A separately pretrained vision encoder produces visual features, which a projector maps into the language model's input space. A causal decoder then processes the combined image and text representations. Retrieval, classification, and token labeling do not generate text autoregressively, so they do not require a causal decoder or the parameter and compute overhead of this architecture.

ModernBERT brought efficient architecture and training improvements to bidirectional encoders. For visual document retrieval, ModernVBERT applied a bidirectional ModernBERT-style text encoder while retaining a separate pretrained SigLIP2 vision tower. We wanted to push this even further by designing and training a multimodal encoder without having to carry over the parameter and compute overhead of a VLM.

NeoMME (pronounced "nee-oh-me", IPA /ˈniː.oʊ.mi/) is a multilingual, multimodal foundation encoder that generates vector representations for input text and/or images using a single Transformer encoder. It is not based on an existing pretrained vision tower, text encoder, or text decoder.

Images and text use the same computational path, so NeoMME can more easily support pretraining, fine-tuning, parallelization, and serving across both modalities.

NeoMME comes in two sizes, 260M and 800M. Both variants share the same architecture:

We pretrain NeoMME from scratch as a discrete masked-diffusion text denoiser. For each text-only example, we sample a corruption rate uniformly between 0 and 1. Each eligible text token is then independently masked at that rate.

Multimodal examples use corruption rates between 0.3 and 1. The image patches remain visible while NeoMME reconstructs masked text. With light masking, the model can often recover a missing word from the surrounding text alone. For example, "cat" is a plausible completion of "The [MASK] sat on the mat," even without an image. But high masking forces the model to learn image-grounded descriptions with little to no signal from the non-masked input text tokens.

Pretraining mixes multilingual text, code, mathematics, natural images, and document images. Each model processes about 524 billion packed input tokens, including 290 billion tokens from text-only examples. This text budget is relatively small compared with ModernBERT's 2 trillion training token budget. Hence, we chose the NorMuon optimizer to improve data efficiency during training.

To get a meaningful downstream evaluation of the backbone, we fine-tune NeoMME for visual document retrieval using the page-image methodology introduced by ColPali. While traditional text-based retrieval consists of retrieving text chunks, NeoMME-Retriever ranks document page screenshots and bypasses all the preprocessing OCR steps necessary to extract text from PDFs. Treating the pages as images preserves layout, charts, tables, font type and size, and other visual clues that cannot be captured even by a perfect OCR model.

NeoMME-Retriever reuses the NeoMME backbone but adds two jointly trained heads on top of it for retrieval:

Omar Khattab, who introduced late-interaction in ColBERT, explains why the term is more precise than "multi-vector." It describes the granularity and learnability of the scoring function, not simply the number of stored vectors.

To learn more about late-interaction, we recommend reading this crash course by Amélie Chatelain.

One NeoMME-Retriever forward pass returns both representations, which gives you flexibility no matter your use case and infrastructure. We recommend using late-interaction embeddings in general since they are more powerful and can be used easily with open-source libraries like NextPlaid. However, if you have a very large corpora, you can run a single forward pass with NeoMME-Retriever to get the dense embedding, retrieve a small number of documents through an ANN index, and then use late-interaction to rerank the retrieved candidates.

We report nDCG@10 on ViDoRe v3. NeoMME-Retriever-260M reaches 0.523, the highest score among evaluated models strictly below 800M parameters. It is within 0.002 nDCG@10 of ColQwen2.5 while using about 14× fewer parameters. NeoMME-Retriever-800M reaches 0.556, within 0.009 nDCG@10 of the similarly sized Vultron Retriever Flash (0.8B). Both NeoMME-Retriever models lie on the model-size Pareto frontier.

ViDoRe v1 and v2 use nDCG@5. On both benchmarks, NeoMME-Retriever-260M outperforms ColModernVBERT and the twice-larger ColSmol-500M. NeoMME-Retriever-800M outperforms ColPali v1.3 while using 3.6 times fewer parameters.

† Scores from MTEB. ‡ Results from our own evaluations.

Late-interaction storage scales linearly with the number of vectors in the output embedding. Higher-resolution images contain more patches, so they produce larger embeddings. For example, a 2048×2048 square page produces embeddings containing 4,200 vectors with NeoMME-Retriever, or about 2.1 MB in float32. Across the ViDoRe v3 benchmark, the measured average is about 1.5 MB per document.

To reduce the storage footprint of the late-interaction index, we combine two complementary compression methods:

We tested this setup on ViDoRe v3. With a pooling factor 10 and int8 queries and documents, storage decreased from about 1.5 MB to 39 kB per page, a 39× reduction, while keeping more than 99% of the baseline nDCG@10. A more aggressive configuration uses pooling factor 8, int8 queries, and binary documents. That version uses 6 kB per page (255× smaller) and keeps more than 95% of the original retrieval quality.

Users can pick a compression setting from that frontier based on storage budget and required retrieval quality.

Before you can search a corpus, a retriever model must turn your documents into embeddings, which will be stored in a vector store like Qdrant, Weaviate, or Milvus. Faster encoding makes building and adding new documents to the index faster, thus reducing the GPU uptime and compute cost required.

So we measured image encoding speeds for NeoMME-Retriever against other multimodal document retrievers. We used preprocessed image tensors and calibrated the batch size separately for each model and image size. At a matched 2048×2048 input size on one NVIDIA L40S, NeoMME-Retriever-260M encodes about 51 pages per second, nearly twice ColModernVBERT's 26 pages per second. Both 260M and 800M NeoMME-Retriever models are also faster than the other models we compared on smaller input images.

NeoMME-Retriever (260M and 800M) returns dense and multi-vector embeddings together. The example below scores two text queries against two document-page images with MeanMaxSim late interaction and dense cosine similarity.

We provide separate dense and late-interaction checkpoints for fine-tuning with Sentence Transformers v6. Following the same pattern as text encoders such as ModernBERT, Sentence Transformers loads the backbone through NeoMMEModel rather than the dual-head NeoMMEForRetrieval class. Sentence Transformers currently supports one retrieval head per model, so each checkpoint lets you fine-tune the dense or late-interaction head independently. To train both heads together, use NeoMMEForRetrieval with a custom Trainer.

Visual document retrieval can be used as the first stage of a visual retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) system. Unlike text RAG, which retrieves extracted text chunks, visual RAG retrieves the original page images and sends them to a visual language model. The model can then use tables, plots, diagrams, and page layout that text extraction may flatten or omit. Here is how visual RAG works:

You can test visual RAG directly with NeoMME-Retriever in our HF Space: 🤗 tonywu71/neomme-retriever-demo.

NeoMME replaces separate pretrained image and text encoders with one long-context bidirectional Transformer. We train it from scratch to process both multilingual text tokens and raw 32×32 image patches.

NeoMME-Retriever is a fine-tuned version of NeoMME for visual document retrieval. One forward pass produces both dense and late-interaction representations. The 260M model outperforms all evaluated models strictly below 800M parameters and, at a matched 2048×2048 input size, encodes pages at about 2× ColModernVBERT's throughput. To reduce the large storage footprint of late-interaction embeddings for high-resolution documents, we experimented with hierarchical token pooling and asymmetric quantization and managed to reduce the late-interaction embeddings from roughly 1.5 MB to 6 kB per page, a 255× compression, while retaining more than 95% of the baseline nDCG@10.

We release all NeoMME model checkpoints and a day-zero Hugging Face Transformers implementation to allow practitioners to build efficient multimodal and multilingual representation models on top of our work.

NeoMME began as a side quest between two good friends. We worked with limited time and compute, and we decided to share the results so the community can build on them. We thank H Company for supporting the work and providing the compute used to train NeoMME.

Visual document retrieval and RAG with NeoMME-Retriever

Visual document retrieval and RAG with NeoMME-Retriever

#9701. Falsehoods Programmers Believe About ATProto

assumptions about handles, DIDs, records, and servers that will break your code

In the year 2010, Patrick McKenzie wrote and published the article “Falsehoods Programmers Believe About Names” — a list of reasonable-sounding assumptions about people's names that not only were not true, but also (if assumed) would create bugs and even break software. That article started a whole genre of Falsehoods Programmers Believe articles. This article ("Falsehoods Programmers Believe About ATProto") is one of my contributions to that genre.

Every numbered statement below is false. Each one is followed by what is actually true — and where to read more.

These are not made up for effect. Each one is backed by the specification, or by a live request to real ATProto servers (made in November 2026).

Handles can change. The account's DID is what is permanent — the accounts specification calls it (DIDs) “unique and immutable”.

My handle changed! My handle was first reiver.bsky.social, then became reiver.myatproto.social, and then later became reiver.blacksky.team. You can see that if you dig through the data at plc.directory/did:plc:scewmn2pl3oz36mxme2b6czz/log/audit. (did:plc:scewmn2pl3oz36mxme2b6czz is my DID-PLC DID.)

So, a handle is a good database key for a user.

Use the DID. Store the handle only for display (cosmetic) purposes — and re-check what each DID's handle is from time to time.

But, you need to normalize the DID before using it. DIDs are URIs, and URI schemes are case-insensitive (RFC 3986) — so DID:plc:scewmn2pl3oz36mxme2b6czz and did:plc:scewmn2pl3oz36mxme2b6czz are the same DID. ATProto requires the normalized (lowercase) form: normalize DIDs when they come from user input, store and compare only the normalized form, and reject non-normalized DIDs that arrive in protocol data.

When a user changes their handle, the first part stays the same — such as reiver.bsky.social → reiver.myatproto.social → reiver.blacksky.team.

A new handle does not have to have anything in common with the old one. joeblow.bsky.social → me.example.com → bbqlover.net → ilikeicecream.com would be fine. Changing a handle just means pointing the account at a different domain — com.atproto.identity.updateHandle takes any valid handle, and only “Verifies handle validity”.

For example, Bluesky's own account (did:plc:z72i7hdynmk6r22z27h6tvur) started out as bluesky-team.bsky.social, and then became bsky.app. You can see that in its audit log at plc.directory/did:plc:z72i7hdynmk6r22z27h6tvur/log/audit. (Another reason to key users by DID, and not by any part of their handle.)

You can trust a handle you saw five minutes ago.

A handle can change at any moment. The user can switch to a new handle. The domain's owner can point it at a different DID — or the domain can expire, and be registered by someone else. Or, its DNS record or /.well-known/atproto-did file can just disappear, and the handle stops resolving. The handle specification says “If the handle for a known DID is confirmed to no longer resolve, it should be marked as invalid.”

So, a handle → DID mapping is only as good as when you last checked it. The specification recommends caching handle resolution “up to some lifetime”, and re-resolving “periodically”. Watch the firehose for #identity events, which announce handle changes. And, never use a cached handle to decide who someone is (for example, for permissions) — use the DID.

An account might have no handle in its DID document (no at:// entry in alsoKnownAs), or a handle that no longer resolves back to it. The DID specification says “an account whose DID document does not contain a valid and confirmed handle can still participate in the atproto ecosystem. Software should be careful to either not display any handle for such account, or obviously indicate that any handle associated with it is invalid.”

In API responses, such an account's handle may show up as the special value handle.invalid — which “can not be used in most situations (search queries, API requests, etc).” And, the handle field on the firehose's #identity event is optional. So, your code needs a “no handle” case.

Any Internet domain can be a handle. And, other PDSes hand out their own — the blacksky.app PDS, for example, offers .blacksky.app, .myatproto.social, .cryptoanarchy.network, and others.

Even if a user's handle is not a .bsky.social handle now, their first handle was.

A user's first handle is whatever they got when their account was created — on whichever PDS they signed up with. com.atproto.server.createAccount just takes a “Requested handle for the account”, and each PDS offers its own domains. So, someone who signed up on blacksky.app might start out as alice.myatproto.social — and never have had a .bsky.social handle at all.

You can see this in a DID's audit log on plc.directory (https://plc.directory//log/audit) — the very first operation (the one that created the DID) shows the first handle, and the first PDS. For example, the audit log for did:plc:ub2k2k5zahuegnkkvxjk5y2w (plc.directory/did:plc:ub2k2k5zahuegnkkvxjk5y2w/log/audit) has just 1 operation — the one that created it, on November 13th, 2026. Its first handle was shadowoftruth.myatproto.social, and its first PDS was blacksky.app. It has never had a .bsky.social handle.

A handle is a third-level domain — like alice.bsky.social, alice.blacksky.app, or alice.myatproto.social.

A handle can have any number of segments, as long as there are at least 2. example.com is a valid handle — and so is apple.banana.cherry.example.com. The handle specification only says “there must be at least two segments” (so a bare top-level domain like com is not allowed), each segment can be 1 to 63 characters, and the whole handle can be at most 253 characters. Its own examples include a.co, 8.cn, and XX.LCS.MIT.EDU; and the official test vectors include john.test.bsky.app, and a valid handle with 10 segments.

With DNS (a TXT record at _atproto.) or HTTPS (/.well-known/atproto-did). You need to support both.

If a DID document lists a handle, the account owns that handle.

Anyone can put any handle in their own DID document. The handle has to resolve back to the same DID — both directions must agree. Otherwise, show handle.invalid.

com.atproto.identity.resolveHandle checks both directions for you.

Its own lexicon says it “Does not necessarily bi-directionally verify against the the DID document.” (See: How-To Resolve a Handle to a DID.)

Handles are case-sensitive — so keep the capitalization the user typed.

Handles are not case-sensitive. The handle specification says “Only normalized (lowercase) handles should be stored in records or used in outbound API calls. Applications should not preserve user-provided case information and attempt to display handles in anything other than lower-case.” Its example: “the handle input string BlueskyWeb.xyz should be normalized, stored, and displayed as blueskyweb.xyz.”

It is just decoration, for display. The handle specification says “Handles may be prefixed with the "at" symbol (like @user.example.com) in user interfaces, but this is not a valid syntax for a handle in records, APIs, and other back-end contexts.” So, strip it from user input before resolving.

On example.com's own site, it is fine to show @alice.example.com as just @alice.

The handle specification says “Handles should generally not be truncated to local context. For example, the handle @alice.example.com should not be displayed as @alice, even in the local context of an example.com service.” (It also warns that very long handles “can result in similar issues when truncated at the start or end” — for example, a handle that starts with paypal.com being shown as paypal.com….)

did:web is supported too. Your code needs to handle both.

In ATProto, “did:web is restricted in atproto to only full domains, not paths or port specification” (from the record key specification).

Whatever plc.directory returns for a DID is that DID's document.

Check that the document's id matches the DID you asked for. (See: How-To Resolve a DID to a PDS.)

A did:plc is case-insensitive — so DID:PLC:… or did:plc:Z72I7HDYNMK6R22Z27H6TVUR is fine.

The did: and the method name (plc) must be lowercase — “The URI starts with lowercase did:”, and “The method segment is one or more lowercase letters”. And, a did:plc identifier is lowercase too: “the entire identifier is lower-case (and should be normalized to lower-case)” (from the did:plc specification). The ATProto specification says “protocol implementations should reject DIDs with invalid casing.” (plc.directory answered did:plc:Z72I7HDYNMK6R22Z27H6TVUR, did:PLC:…, and DID:PLC:… with 400 “Resolution of non-PLC DIDs not supported”.)

(This is about DIDs in protocol data — records, tokens, API responses. As a URI, the did: scheme is case-insensitive, so DID: means the same thing — but ATProto requires the normalized, lowercase form there. DIDs typed in by a user may be normalized; see item 2. And, even under the general DID syntax, the method name must be lowercase, so did:PLC:… is invalid on its own.)

DIDs are case-sensitive — so did:plc:abc… and did:plc:ABC… are 2 different accounts.

For did:plc, the uppercase one is not a different DID — it is not a valid did:plc at all, since its identifier is lowercase-only base32. The ATProto specification says “the currently-supported methods are not case sensitive, and could be safely lowercased”, and that “It is permissible to attempt case normalization when receiving user-controlled input, such as when parsing public URL path components, or text input fields.” So: reject bad casing in protocol data; lowercasing what a user typed is fine.

If a DID parser accepts it, it is a valid DID.

A generic DID parser only checks the generic syntax — which allows uppercase in the identifier (the test vectors list did:method:VAL as valid). The indigo library's syntax.ParseDID accepts did:plc:Z72I7HDYNMK6R22Z27H6TVUR — but plc.directory rejects it. Generic syntax is not the same as a valid did:plc.

The DID never changes — but its DID document can. Each change is a signed operation, and the handle (alsoKnownAs), the PDS (the #atproto_pds service), the signing key (#atproto), and the rotation keys can all be changed.

For example, my DID's audit log (plc.directory/did:plc:scewmn2pl3oz36mxme2b6czz/log/audit) has 4 operations:

And, the did:plc specification has 2 more surprises. A “tombstone” operation “clears all of the data fields and permanently deactivates the DID”. And, there is a 72-hour window during which a higher-authority rotation key can “"rewrite" history”. So, do not cache a DID document forever — re-resolve it from time to time, and watch the firehose for #identity events.

“Personal” Data Server means one server per person.

“Many PDSes will host multiple users” (the glossary). Most host many.

Bluesky's accounts are spread across many PDS hosts — for example, @bsky.app is on puffball.us-east.host.bsky.network. bsky.social is where they log in.

The server a user logs in at is the server that has their data.

It might be an entryway — a separate OAuth server for many PDSes. puffball.us-east.host.bsky.network's /.well-known/oauth-protected-resource lists https://bsky.social as its authorization server. (blacksky.app, on the other hand, lists itself.)

Accounts can migrate to another PDS — that is a core design goal. Always look up the current PDS from the DID document (and do not cache it forever).

A user's PDS can show them everyone's posts.

A PDS only has its own accounts' data. For timelines, threads, and counts, it forwards the request to an AppView. (See: ATProto PDS.)

A user's PDS builds (or renders) their timeline.

The timeline (app.bsky.feed.getTimeline) is built by an AppView. The PDS just forwards the app's request to it. And, no server renders it — the AppView returns JSON, and the app (on the user's phone or computer) renders that.

(This one used to be closer to true. Bluesky's feed generator starter kit still says “In the future, the PDS will hydrate the feed with the help of an App View, but for now, the PDS handles hydration itself.” Today, the AppView does it. See: ATProto Feed Generator.)

Bluesky's PDS software is the only PDS software.

Any server that implements the right end-points is a PDS. (For example, the Blacksky team's rsky project, written in Rust, includes rsky-pds.)

Self-hosting a PDS means you have to index the entire network.

A PDS only stores its own accounts' data. Indexing the network is the job of relays and AppViews — a self-hosted PDS uses someone else's. (In Bluesky's PDS software, PDS_CRAWLERS defaults to https://bsky.network, and PDS_BSKY_APP_VIEW_URL defaults to https://api.bsky.app.)

That is why the hardware is small. The official PDS instructions recommend 1 GB of memory, 1 CPU core, and a 20 GB SSD — for 1 to 20 users. (See: ATProto PDS.)

Every record on the network is a Bluesky post.

A repository can hold records of any type — any lexicon, from any app — all mixed together in the same user's repository. Calendar events, bookmarks, blog posts, game state, workout logs, or a custom app's own schema: each is just another collection. (And, by default, a PDS accepts records whose lexicon it does not know — “optimistic validation”.)

For example, my repository (reiver.blacksky.team) has these collections, according to com.atproto.repo.describeRepo:

Only one of those 14 collections is Bluesky posts (app.bsky.feed.post). Even among Bluesky's own record types, most are not posts — likes, reposts, follows, lists, a profile. And, actor.rpg.* and equipment.rpg.item are from a different app altogether. (See: ATProto Record.)

Everything a user does on ATProto is public.

Everything in a user's repository is public — posts, likes, follows, and even blocks (see the next item). But, not everything a user does is stored as a record in their repository. For example, in Bluesky:

(The spaces proposal would add something new: records that only some people may read — see the Spaces section, below.)

In Bluesky, a mute is private — but a block is a public record. A block is an app.bsky.graph.block record in the blocker's repository, and its lexicon says so plainly: “Record declaring a 'block' relationship against another account. NOTE: blocks are public in Bluesky; see blog posts for details.”

So, anyone can list an account's blocks — for example, with com.atproto.repo.listRecords, or from the firehose — and see who blocked whom. If you build features on blocks, treat them as public information.

The author is the repository the record is in. (See: ATProto Record.)

A record key is unique within a repository.

“The tuple of (did, rkey) is not unique; the tuple (did, collection, rkey) is unique.”

TIDs (like 3n2opitxdyc2j) are the most common, but each record type's lexicon says which kind of record key it uses. The record key specification defines 4 kinds:

A tid record key tells you when the record was created.

“Record keys are "user-controlled data" and may be arbitrarily selected by hostile accounts.” Do not trust them as timestamps.

A record's createdAt is when it was created.

It is whatever the client put there. The app.bsky.feed.post lexicon describes it as a “Client-declared timestamp”. A client can set it to any time — past or future.

When a record was actually seen is tracked separately, by the services that see it:

For example, for one of @bsky.app's posts, public.api.bsky.app reported createdAt as 2026-11-19T18:33:36.813Z, and indexedAt as 2026-11-19T18:33:38.543Z — close, here, but nothing requires them to be. (Even these are each one service's view — a different AppView may have indexed it at a different time.)

It is JSON with extra rules, from the ATProto data model — the same data model that is also written as DRISL-CBOR (the successor to DAG-CBOR) for storing, signing, and hashing. The differences from regular JSON:

It is not DAG-JSON either — the data model specification says ATProto uses $link “as the key name instead of /”. And, there are practical limits too — for example, Bluesky's data validation guide suggests at most 32 levels of nesting, and 1 MiB per record (as CBOR). (See: ATProto Record.)

Records can contain floating-point numbers.

Floats are not allowed in the data model — they do not round-trip reliably, and the bytes must be exact for hashing.

You can compute a record's CID by hashing its JSON.

The CID is a hash of its DRISL-CBOR encoding. JSON is not byte-exact.

A missing field and a null field mean the same thing.

They are different — and both are different from false, 0, or an empty array.

Every record in a repository is valid against its lexicon.

By default, a PDS only checks records whose lexicon it knows (“optimistic validation”, or “fail-open”). Validate what you read.

A record with fields its lexicon does not mention is invalid.

Unexpected fields should be ignored — “at worst as warnings”. (Validating a post with an extra mood field against app.bsky.feed.post passes. See: ATProto Lexicon.)

“Record deletion is supported without leaving a trace or "tombstone" of previous contents.”

Deleting a record removes it from the Internet.

Deleting a record removes it from the user's repository. But, by then, copies may already be elsewhere — the creation went out on the PDS's firehose, and relays, AppViews, feed generators, search indexes, backups, and anyone else watching may have kept it.

The deletion goes out on the firehose too, and the specifications expect other services to follow it. The accounts specification says “When accounts remove records from their public repositories, hosting services should remove public access to that content.” And, the sync specification says mirrors should “respect repository updates (eg, record deletion) … in a timely manner (within seconds or minutes)”. But, “should” is not a guarantee — nothing forces every service to comply, and a copy someone else kept (or a screenshot) is out of the user's control.

(And, since the data was signed, such a copy can still be shown to be genuine. Treat anything written to a public repository as published.)

It is a name — a reversed Internet domain plus a name. (See: ATProto NSID.)

The Internet domain part is not case-sensitive, but the name is — getRecord is not getrecord. “Implementations should not force-lowercase NSIDs.”

Implementations reject an NSID whose Internet domain part is longer than 253 characters.

The specification says 253 — but the official test vectors list a 283-character one as valid, and Bluesky's TypeScript and Go code only check the 317-character total.

If _lexicon.feed.bsky.app does not exist, try _lexicon.bsky.app.

Lexicon resolution is not hierarchical. If the exact record does not exist, resolution simply fails. (See: How-To Resolve a Lexicon.)

The app.bsky.* lexicons are in the bluesky-social/atproto repository on GitHub.

Not anymore — its main branch has no lexicons/app/bsky/ directory. Resolve them from the network instead (they are published by did:plc:4v4y5r3lwsbtmsxhile2ljac).

A union in a lexicon lists every type you will ever see there.

Unions are open by default — new types can be added. (The live app.bsky.feed.post lexicon's embed union includes app.bsky.embed.gallery, which older code will not know about.)

It can change — in compatible ways (new optional fields, more union types, etc).

You need a special library to talk ATProto.

XRPC is plain HTTP and JSON. curl works. (See: ATProto XRPC.)

A server returns the error names listed in the end-point's lexicon.

Not always. resolveHandle's lexicon lists HandleNotFound, but public.api.bsky.app answered an unknown handle with InvalidRequest.

The specification itself warns that “many services will return generic load-balancer or reverse-proxy HTML error pages.”

An end-point a server does not have returns 404.

A Bluesky PDS answered a made-up end-point with 401 AuthMissing.

Treat it as opaque. (One server's listRecords cursor happens to be the last record key — do not depend on that.)

Every PDS has its own firehose, and there are several relays — for example, Bluesky's bsky.network and the Blacksky team's atproto.africa. (See: ATProto Relay.)

A follow is an app.bsky.graph.follow record — stored in the follower's repository, with the followed account's DID as its subject. So, a user's PDS knows exactly who the user follows, but not who follows them — those records are spread across everyone else's repositories, on every PDS. (See: How-To Count an ATProto Account's Followers.)

Likes and replies live on the author's post.

They live in the repositories of the people who liked or replied. A like is an app.bsky.feed.like record in the liker's repository, whose subject is a strong reference (uri and cid) to the post. A reply is an app.bsky.feed.post record in the replier's repository, with a reply field pointing at the thread's root and the parent post. (Reposts work the same way.) The author's post record itself has no list of likes or replies, and no counts.

So, like and reply counts — and threads — are put together by services that index the network, like an AppView or a backlink index. For example, for one of @bsky.app's posts (app.bsky.feed.post/3n2opitxdyc2j), on November 22nd, 2026, public.api.bsky.app said 1951 likes and 774 replies — and so did the Constellation backlink index. (For a recent post, they agree. For older ones, they may not — see the follower counts, below.)

It is one service's opinion. For the same account (reiver.blacksky.team), at the same time (November 22nd, 2026), public.api.bsky.app (Bluesky's AppView) said 292 followers, api.blacksky.community (the Blacksky team's AppView) said 196, and the Constellation backlink index said 134. (See: ATProto AppView and How-To Count an ATProto Account's Followers.)

With enough work, a follower count can be computed exactly.

You would have to check every repository on every PDS — and you can never be sure you found them all, since a relay only knows the hosts it crawls. By the time you finished, the answer would have changed. And, what counts as a follower is a choice — for example, the app.bsky.graph.follow lexicon says “Duplicate follows will be ignored by the AppView.” (See: How-To Count an ATProto Account's Followers.)

It sends a skeleton — a list of post URIs. The AppView fills in the posts. (See: ATProto Feed Generator.)

A label is a signed annotation. What to do with it (hide, blur, warn, nothing) is up to each app and user. (See: ATProto Labeler.)

Account status (active, deactivated, etc) can be verified cryptographically.

“Unlike other aspects of atproto, account status is not self-certifying”. It is passed along hop by hop — so different services may disagree. When in doubt, ask the account's own PDS (com.atproto.sync.getRepoStatus).

Bluesky is one app built on it. Others use their own lexicons — for example, site.standard.document, community.lexicon.calendar.event, and actor.rpg.sprite.

Microblogging (short posts, like Bluesky's) is just one thing built on it. The overview describes ATProto as “a decentralized protocol for large-scale social web applications”. Nothing in the core protocol is about posts — records, repositories, XRPC, and sync work the same for any record type. What a record is comes from its lexicon, and anyone with a domain can define new ones.

For example: long-form documents (site.standard.document), calendar events (community.lexicon.calendar.event), game sprites (actor.rpg.sprite), custom feeds (app.bsky.feed.generator), and, in the spaces proposal, bookmarks, private forums, and group chats. Even the protocol's own lexicons are published as records (com.atproto.lexicon.schema).

(Falsehoods that come from comparing ATProto with ActivityPub, the Fediverse, and Mastodon.)

Unlike ActivityPub (and the Fediverse, and Mastodon), ATProto does not use JSON-LD.

DID documents are JSON-LD. plc.directory serves them with the content type application/did+ld+json, and each one starts with an @context:

(That is from plc.directory/did:plc:scewmn2pl3oz36mxme2b6czz. A did:web document has one too — for example, api.bsky.app/.well-known/did.json.)

What is true is that ATProto's own data — records, lexicons, XRPC — is not JSON-LD. And, ATProto software usually reads DID documents as plain JSON — the ATProto DID specification says which fields to read, and does not call for JSON-LD processing.

Like on Mastodon, an ATProto handle includes the user's server — @user@server.

On Mastodon, a user's full address is a user name and a server — Mastodon's documentation says it is “in the form @username@domain”, and that “@user@example.com is not the same as @user@example.org.”

An ATProto handle is just one domain name — like reiver.blacksky.team — and it says nothing about the user's server. The server (PDS) is found separately, from the DID document. (A handle shown as @reiver.blacksky.team has just one @, as a decoration.)

ATProto has nothing like a Fediverse “instance”.

The difference is that it is more hidden. It is not part of the user's identity or handle — reiver.blacksky.team does not say which PDS hosts it. It is not what decides what a user sees — that is mostly the AppView. And, a user can move to another PDS while keeping the same DID, handle, posts, and followers.

Like Mastodon, ATProto looks up handles with WebFinger.

Mastodon uses WebFinger (/.well-known/webfinger) — its documentation says “WebFinger is required for fully interoperating with Mastodon.”

ATProto does not. A handle is resolved with a DNS TXT record at _atproto., or with https:///.well-known/atproto-did. (See: How-To Resolve a Handle to a DID.)

Like on Mastodon, when a user moves to a new server, their posts stay behind, and their followers have to be moved over.

On Mastodon, moving an account moves followers — but Mastodon's documentation says “Your posts will not be moved, due to technical limitations”, and that “Mastodon currently does not support importing posts or media”. Moving also has to “force everyone to unfollow your current account and follow your new account”.

On ATProto, moving to a new PDS includes “migrating data from the old PDS to the new PDS” (from the accounts specification) — the whole repository, posts and all. And, the account keeps the same DID. Since follow records point at the DID, followers do not have to be moved at all. (See: ATProto PDS.)

Like ActivityPub servers, ATProto servers send posts to each other's inboxes.

In ActivityPub, a server pushes each activity to its recipients — the ActivityPub specification describes it being “inserted into the actor's inbox (delivery)”, by HTTP POST.

Like in ActivityPub, to trust a copy of a post, you have to check it against the server it came from.

The ActivityPub specification says servers should do “something at least as robust as checking that the object appears as received at its origin”, and that “No particular mechanism for verification is authoritatively specified”. (Mastodon uses HTTP Signatures, to check who sent an activity.)

ATProto data checks itself. Repository commits are signed with the account's key, and records are identified by their hash (CID) — so a copy can be checked no matter who it came from. The data model specification says this “makes it possible to redistribute content and trust copies even if coming from an untrusted party.” (See: ATProto Record.)

ATProto and the Fediverse cannot talk to each other.

They are different protocols — but there are bridges. For example, Bridgy Fed describes itself as “a decentralized social network bridge. It connects the fediverse, the web, and the Atmosphere (Bluesky).” With it, people on one network can follow, reply to, like, and repost people on the other.

(These are about the spaces proposal, which is not yet part of the specification.)

“Atproto spaces provide access control, not confidentiality. They are not end-to-end encrypted.”

Each member's records stay on that member's own PDS. “The space does not colocate records on a single network host.”

A copy of space data proves who wrote it.

Space data is authenticated with MACs, not signatures — on purpose, so that it “should not carry proof of authorship that survives a leak outside its access boundary.”

Most of these come from the same idea: ATProto separates things that are usually tied together.

So, the safe defaults are: key everything by DID; resolve, do not assume; validate what you read; ignore what you do not understand; and expect other servers to disagree with yours.

Charles Iliya Krempeaux has been an Open Social Web developer since the year 2021, and is both an active member of the Fediverse developer community, and the ATProto (ATmosphere) developer community. Charles was an early engineer (one of the 1st 4 senior engineers) at the social media company Hootsuite. He created the second hosting company on the Fediverse — SpaceHost — and as a result has a deep understanding of hosting Fediverse servers. He has worked on a number of ActivityPub server software and client apps. And, he implemented the ActivityPub protocol from scatch — in the Go programming language (golang). Charles is the organizer and founder of the Fediverse conference: FediCon. And, he implemented the ATProto protocol from scatch — in the Go programming language (golang). He created the 2nd custom feed generator for ATProto: RobinFeed. He created the 1st real-time search engine for the Fediverse and ATmosphere (ATProto): Now. He is a founding engineer at the ATProto social media company Blacksky. And, he works on a Rust programming language impementation of ATProto known as rsky.

#9700. NGINX2Root: Remote Code Execution vulnerabilities in nginx

Xint is reporting that it has discovered a collection of five critical vulnerabilities in the NGINX web server. The worst flaw, it says, would allow an unauthenticated attacker to execute commands on an affected nginx server with HTTP/2 enabled. The company also reports a local-privilege escalation (LPE) kernel vulnerability, which was introduced in the 4.15 kernel, in the Stream Control Transmission Protocol (SCTP) subsystem. If chained with the NGINX vulnerability, it would allow an attacker to gain root privileges on the host. A kernel patch for this is not yet available.

Xint recommends updating to NGINX 1.31.9, which was just released, and to block the SCTP module on hosts that do not need it until a kernel fix is available. See the mitigations section of their report for more information.

Anyways, go give your distro security team a hug.

More seriously, it looks like the 'most severe' of the attacks requires sending 128 gigabytes of data; so with luck, we won't see this one be seriously exploited over the internet.

From my perspective, this is not about corpos "putting immense strain on a public utility" – if free security audits and reports now are an "immense strain on a public utility", we have a fundamental misunderstanding here. We developers must not forget one thing here: security researchers are helping us.

We are the ones who shipped broken software, and they invested the resources to figure that out and report it. They are neither maintainers, nor necessarily even developers – they are security researchers, so at this point, they already did their job. Everything else – an initial patch request, whatever – is an extra cherry on the top of an already free service.

The vulnerabilities are already there, whether they contact us about it or not changes nothing about our code being broken – and if our code is broken, malicious third parties might exploit it already. It's not as if the researchers made things up, or that if they said nothing, the vulnerabilities magically would not exist somehow too.

We should be happy that someone invested their time to report things on the mailing list; but instead we blame them because they didn't do enough – they give us the inch, but we immediately expect the mile, and shame them if don't deliver. Security vulnerabilities don't go away if we don't keep them secret for weeks until the devs finally decide to move, you know? I understand that and that is technically correct (the best kind :-) but the existence of a vulnerability isn't the only important consideration when it comes to risk, the likelihood of someone using that specific vulnerability is also a significant factor, and likelihood changes based on how popular a particular bug is, at least for criminal gangs and script kiddies. No software is going to be completely free of security bugs, but the Internet keeps working because not everyone cares to develop working exploits and actually leverage every available bug, even if they know about them. So the existence of a fancy website and good marketing by a security researcher can change the ultimate risk even for known bugs, which is why the normal procedure is to keep quiet until the fix can be developed at a normal bugfix cadence, not just "drop everything and PANIC", and the researcher is only justified in promoting their bug early if the vendor is dragging their feet, which would be weeks or months of stalling, not just a few business days.

I don't have the best visibility on the security "weather" on the Internet but my understanding is that while there have been a lot of automated LLM-directed code fuzzing bug reports recently listed as critical severity, there hasn't been a corresponding increase in criminal actors actually using those bugs, some are harder to reliably exploit in practice and maybe there are so many that there aren't enough criminal actors to develop reliable exploits for every one, or the ones they already use are working well enough that they don't feel pressure to develop new malware variants, in any event the risk hasn't gone up as much as predicted because the likelihood of exploiting these now-known security bugs seems low.

And as a side note, because this isn't totally applicable in this case as nginx and Linux have plenty of commercial support, the calculus of who is responsible is different when there is a vendor consortium who maintains a project for commercial use, and when a widely used project is someone's volunteer/hobby project, in the case of a commercial maintainer, sure they have responsibility to respond to security reports and you can just hand off to the vendor once they are notified, but volunteer/hobby projects are not vendors and while it's not against the license to just drop a bug report and bail, it's a bit rude to not help and volunteer if you want something changed. I don't think a volunteer/hobby project has any responsibility to field and fix security bugs, although most are highly motivated to do so, and those companies who repackage to sell volunteer code they find on the Internet should be responsible for setting up some kind of vendor consortium to handle maintenance and security bug reports. Just offering code for free can't make one responsible for every possible downstream user of that code, the people choosing to use/license that code need to take responsibility for that choice and fund maintenance themselves.

Here I tend to disagree, for multiple reasons. First of all, by that definition, any bug report without a PR would be rude – individual mileage may vary here, but personally speaking, I really disagree with that. But even from a more objective poverty, it is a mixup of competencies – a security researcher is not a software engineer. Of course, they generally have some developer skills; but being able to understand and write some code is a hugely different set of skills from writing PRs in the context and style of an arbitrarily managed project – and let's be honest here, lot's of open source projects have very high and very specific standards, and even long time members don't get their MRs merged on the first or second or even third try.

Also, I think that "if you want something changed" is probably also a bit of an assumption or different perspective here, because it puts the security researcher into the position of the supplicant. We should not forget they are not: they find a vulnerability, and they communicate it – and with that, they provide a free service of significant value to us as well as the users. Then they go on – because I might be a dev by hobby or paycheck, and they are a security researcher by hobby or paycheck. In fact, we have to consider they might not use our software at all; and even if they do, they know about the mitigations, or have their "not good enough" v1 patch.

In practice, the "significant value" they provide predominantly goes to the would-be attackers, with only rounding error going to the maintainers. End-users largely get screwed.

Worth noting that even if a project has "commercial maintainers", if you're not a paying customer/supporter, you're in the AS-IS boat as nearly everyone else; fixes will happen on *their* timeline, not yours.

That is not true in Germany, at least. "Produkthaftung"/product-liability is independent of payment.

Worse: you cab point LLM at the binary without any source or debug symbols and it would easily recognize common parts and reason about them — even for piece of proprietary shit that it never saw before! That part may even be more drastic, long term: LLMs may not not “understand”, fully, a well-designed piece of code with comments — yet they “understand” obfuscated binary almost as well as well-commented source… it's still not clear what would be the long-term implications of THAT.

Security researcher reports are heavily skewed. One finds a problem in X, everyone else tests X in other software. That does not mean X is the only thing with holes and that does not mean would-be attackers also focus on X, that means security researchers have herd mode on. It is quite unsurprising to find problems in HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 implementations. They are quite new and complex. They are also trendy, so security researchers will focus on them (hype mode on). HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 also replace and streamline a babel tower of JS and proxy hacks people deployed to try to make HTTP/1 suck less. You bet no researcher is going to focus on those because they are one-of-a-kind site-specific setups. Someone who wants to hole a specific site, OTOH, will have no such scruples.
