#9685. tokenizers v1: encode, decode and scaling, measured

The tokenizer has not historically been the bottleneck within ML workflows. Compute-wise, tokenization is light compared to the heavy modeling happening in the rest of the pipeline. Yet, in some cases, it has rapidly become key to accelerating (or slowing down) your machine learning work.

As models become faster and workloads scale, that balance begins to shift. Training on massive datasets, serving many concurrent requests, or repeatedly processing long inputs can put enough pressure on the tokenizer that it starves the model of data.

This is why we have chosen to heavily focus on performance for the upcoming version 1 of tokenizers. Tokenization should be light and should scale with your workflow. Your GPUs should never sit idle waiting for the CPU to complete its tokenization.

In this article, we look at what makes v1 faster than v0.23, often by tens of times.

This work was entirely possible thanks to the rest of the ecosystem. Tokenization is a very active area of open source work, and libraries such as gigatoken, tiktoken, kitoken, tokie, fastokens, wordchipper and ai-tokenizer, as well as many others, have each pushed on what a fast tokenizer can be. We read that work, and several of the ideas below reached us because another project showed they were worth trying.

Before this refactor, tokenizers was nowhere near the performance it could have had, so contributing to it may not have seemed worth it. With this refactor, we hope to make clear that we intend tokenizers to be a library worth contributing to.

We also thank IBM, NVIDIA, and the ExecuTorch team for contributing patches and helping us test across a wide range of hardware to broaden platform support.

We showcase results for the release candidate of tokenizers v1 against other widely used alternatives. We go over single-threaded, multi-threaded, scaling across threads, per-model comparison, per-language comparison, latency, decoding throughput, memory heap, as well as crate size.

We run this from the tokbench repository, and add a command to rerun the benchmarks on your hardware if you would like to do so.

v1 will produce the same token IDs as v0.23. The goal was to preserve the output, the API, the vocabulary and the merge ranks, and improve everything that can be improved. That includes breadth. The library stays general across tokenizer families rather than specialising on BPE, so v1 loads everything v0.23 loaded.

A tokenizer converts text into the list of integers a model reads. tokenizers runs that conversion in four stages. Normalization applies operations such as lowercasing or Unicode normalization to the raw text. Pre-tokenization splits the text into smaller pieces called pre-tokens. The model turns each pre-token into tokens and maps them to IDs in its vocabulary. Post-processing adds any special tokens the model expects.

The model stage is where most of the work described here happens. Eight of the ten model families measured in this article use byte pair encoding, or BPE. BPE starts from the bytes of a pre-token and repeatedly joins the highest ranked adjacent pair until no ranked pair remains. The ranking is learned when the tokenizer is trained and ships with it, so the same text always produces the same IDs. A merge never crosses a pre-token boundary. The other two families use WordPiece and Unigram, the two other model types the library supports.

The tokenization pipeline page documents the four stages. Tokenization algorithms documents BPE, WordPiece and Unigram.

Each stage was worked on. These are the changes that mattered:

BPE models use a regular expression to split the input text into smaller, easier to process chunks called pre-tokens. Merges happen inside a pre-token and never across the boundary between two of them, so this split decides what the rest of the pipeline sees.

That regular expression is a fixed parameter of the model. It ships with the tokenizer and never changes at runtime, so there is no need for a general-purpose regex engine to interpret it on every encode. An equivalent splitting function can be written by hand, once, for the pattern a given model actually uses.

A hand-written function can then use the SIMD instructions (single instruction, multiple data) of a modern CPU, which apply one operation to many bytes at once and suit UTF-8 text well. bitcannon views the input's bytes as parallel streams of bits, so boundaries fall out of boolean operations across whole registers instead of a scan that advances one character at a time. It decides 64 bytes per register operation. The same idea drives Parabix for text processing and simdjson for JSON.

This depends on recognising the pattern. A handful of grammars cover most byte-level BPE models, and a tokenizer whose pattern is not among them keeps the regex path and none of this speed-up. That is why the gains above vary as much as they do.

Real text contains many repeated words. Because BPE always produces the same token IDs for a given pre-token, v1 can save the result after processing it once. A thread-local cache maps each pre-token's bytes to its token IDs, allowing later occurrences to skip the merge process.

Naturally, as the input grows, the number of unique words can grow more slowly than the total number of words. Repeated words then account for an increasing share of the input. New words still appear, which accounts for the occasional misses in the animation below.

Caching works best when the input contains repeated pre-tokens. Input with few repeated pre-tokens can pay for lookups without receiving many hits.

The next major cost comes from the BPE merge loop. For each pre-token, the loop repeatedly finds the highest-priority adjacent pair and merges it. The previous implementation allocated new memory for every call and built a new priority queue for every pre-token.

v1 reuses a scratch buffer owned by the caller, removing those repeated allocations. It stores symbols in a flat array and links adjacent symbols by their positions in that array, which makes updates during merging cheaper. It also processes a batch of pre-tokens in a single model call.

Each candidate pair is also packed into a single 64-bit value, with the merge rank in the high bits. Comparing two candidates is then just comparing two integers, and "no merge here" is the largest possible value, so the loop finds its next merge without a branch.

Small differences in benchmark design can produce large differences in tokenizer performance. We used the following rules to keep the comparison consistent across engines.

Repeatedly encoding one document can be faster than encoding a stream of distinct documents on the same build. The first approach measures performance when the entire document is already represented in the cache. The second measures performance on new input while allowing previously seen pre-tokens to remain cached.

Both conditions are sometimes described as "warm," even though they measure different workloads. Our headline results use distinct documents, and the complete corpus is too large to fit in the cache. Tokenizer benchmarks should identify which workload they use because the choice can dominate the result.

Across the ten model families v1's encode path covers, it encodes text 3 to 30 times faster than v0.23 with one thread on an Apple M4 Max. The low end is t5-base, the high end gpt2. It scales at 76% of linear across eight workers. Throughout these changes, v1 produces exactly the same token IDs as the released library.

The overall improvement comes from several changes working together: a hand-written splitter in place of a regex engine, a cache that answers a repeated word without merging it again, a merge loop that never touches the allocator, and one model call per batch of pre-tokens instead of one per pre-token. Each reduces the work done at a different point in the pipeline.

The next priority is support for more model families. We will move additional models onto the new merge loop before 1.0.0. Once the release candidates stabilize, the next step will be bringing about the improvements within the transformers library and the rest of the ecosystem which depend on the tokenizers library.

This post is generated from tokbench results and will be updated as support expands.

A release candidate for v1 is on crates.io. The API you call is the one you already call, so the only thing that changes is which build you install.

Training is behind a default-on feature that pulls a C++ dependency with it. If you only need to encode, turn it off to exclude the training implementation:

Encoding is unchanged: same call, same ids.

Every figure in this post was measured against this crate. The Python bindings wrap the same code and are built from bindings/python, but they add per-call overhead that none of these measurements include.

The benchmarks in this post cover the completed release-candidate work listed first. The remaining sections show what is still required for 1.0.0 and what we plan to explore afterward.

This work is in the Rust pre-release on crates.io:

Will have to try it out. Data seems real good.

Sadly, the app requires an Apple Music or Spotify subscription. In this blog post, Iâll go down the rabbit hole of reverse engineering the Android app and bypassing their very, very sloppy attempt at hiding the data.

First, we need to understand how the game works.

On the front of each card, youâll find the artist or band name, the year the song came out, and the song title. On the back, thereâs a QR code. Scanning it takes you to a URL with two things in its path: the gameâs region (DE in my case) and the card ID. The music then starts playing in the app or through Spotify.

This means thereâs a mapping from Card ID â Spotify Track. There are also multiple card versions per region, so the card ID alone isnât enough to identify a song. Card ID 1 might be âWet Dreamâ in the UK, but âTage wie dieseâ in Germany.

After getting the appâs APK from some sketchy Android APK download website, I used jadx to get the decompiled Java code.

I ran a tool to identify the format, and it came back as Base64. Thatâs an encoding, so I decoded it first. The result still wasnât readable, and I guessed it was encrypted with AES or something similar.

Iâd never reverse engineered an Android app before, so I just searched globally for AES. And guess what? There was a file called k43.java with the entire decryption process laid out in front of me:

So letâs walk through this step by step.

The function f takes two strings as inputs. The first, str, contains the Base64-encoded data, which it decodes:

It then checks whether the decoded data is at least 28 bytes long:

Next, it passes a bunch of data to the function o, which handles the final stage of decryption:

The first argument is the first 12 bytes of the decoded data. Thatâs our IV, or nonce. The second argument is the entire decoded byte array.

The third argument is where things get interesting. It takes the total length minus 28 and passes that, along with str2, to the function m. Those 28 bytes account for the 12-byte nonce and the 16-byte authentication tag.

Inside m, the remaining length is converted to a string and joined with str2. That combined string is then hashed using SHA-256 to produce the AES key.

So str2 isnât the AES key itself. Itâs the secret string used to derive it, and we havenât found it yet.

It sets up AES-GCM with the derived key and nonce, then decrypts the data after the first 12 bytes.

Thatâs the decryption process figured out. Now we just need the secret string.

I was doing this in a Discord call in the Rust Language Community server, and someone pointed out that I should look for a byte array with a length of 32 bytes.

I first searched for byte[32], but didnât find anything useful. I then tried this pattern:

That led me to m17.java, which contained these two super cool arrays:

We then tried to figure out how to turn these into something useful. After a bit of experimenting, someone suggested XORing the two arrays together. We interpreted the resulting bytes as text and got this:

Using this string, I wrote a little decryptor in Rust:

That gave us this awesome test.txt file with around 31,000 lines of mappings from card IDs to Apple Music and Spotify tracks, plus ISRCs, across multiple regions.

We then looked around the code a little more and found out that all of this wasnât really needed.

If weâd searched for an HTTPS URL first, we wouldâve landed on this:

https://hitster.jumboplay.com/hitster-assets/

https://hitster.jumboplay.com/hitster-assets/gameset_database.json

There was the entire thing. No encryption.

We spent around 18 hours chasing a file that, in the end, wasnât even a real secret.

InfoQ Homepage News Grafana 13.3 Adds Shared Dashboard Variables and Notebooks

Nov 21, 2026 2 min read

Grafana Labs has released Grafana 13.3 with cross-dashboard variables that let teams manage shared dashboard controls in one place. The release also introduces Notebooks for collecting panels and investigation notes in a document that colleagues can share.

The release announcement describes cross-dashboard variables as a public preview across all Grafana editions. Teams can define a variable once and use it in multiple dashboards, avoiding separate configurations for a selector such as an environment or a region. Grafana says managing those copies separately can lead to configuration drift.

Cross-dashboard variables address a longstanding user request. In a 2021 GitHub discussion, Grafana user Darth-Bobo described having to maintain the same variables separately across dashboards, warning that configuration differences could become "unmanageable over time". More recently, an early tester described shared variables as useful for evaluating Git Sync without Terraform templating.

Variables can have global scope, which makes them available throughout a Grafana organisation, or folder scope, which limits them to dashboards in the same folder. An editor can add the available variables from a dashboard sidebar, either individually or all at once. Viewers can still change the selected value on a dashboard, while the variable configuration remains centrally managed.

Teams running Grafana themselves must enable the grafana.dashboardGlobalVariables feature toggle to try the preview. Grafana places the management screen under Dashboards > Variables, separate from the dashboard editor where users add the shared controls.

Notebooks are also in public preview across all editions. A notebook can hold panels from dashboards or Explore alongside written observations, with findings from Grafana Assistant included as well. Teams can use the document to record how they investigated an issue or to prepare a post-incident review with relevant panels already in place.

Users can create a notebook manually or through Grafana Assistant, then save and share it. Grafana is rolling the feature out gradually to Grafana Cloud. Self-managed installations need the dashboard.notebooks feature toggle enabled.

Grafana’s Notebooks joins similar investigation-document workflows from other observability vendors. Datadog Notebooks combines live graphs with rich text and supports simultaneous editing, inline comments and reusable postmortem templates. New Relic Notebooks, generally available since August 2026, combines NRQL queries, visualisations and Markdown, with natural-language query translation and notebook-wide variables.

The release also changes how Grafana Assistant builds dashboards. In public preview, dashboard plans let a user describe what they want to monitor and review a proposed layout in chat before building it. The plan covers the title and the proposed panels, including visualisation types and variables. A read-only preview lets the user refine the plan before choosing to build and save the dashboard.

A separate Assistant feature, Undo turn, is generally available across all editions. It restores the previous dashboard state after an Assistant edit, including when one request changed multiple panels. The Assistant dashboarding guide notes that undo is unavailable if the dashboard has changed since the Assistant's edit.

Grafana 13.3 also previews a visual refresh with revised themes and interface components. Grafana Labs says the visual refresh preserves existing navigation and workflows and introduces no breaking changes for plugins. Plugins using standard Grafana components and theme tokens pick up the new appearance; those with custom styling can migrate separately. Self-managed users can enable grafana.visualDesignRefresh to try it and switch back to the previous design.

#9680. Jun Kim, oMLX creator and maintainer, joins Hugging Face to support the MLX community

We are super excited to welcome Jun as our newest team member 🔥. We are completely invested in local AI, and MLX is a central piece of the ecosystem. We are delighted that Jun chose us to set up home and continue contributing to MLX.

MLX is Apple's framework for local AI, especially optimized for Apple Silicon. We are big MLX supporters since it was the Christmas present from Awni and Angelos in 2023, and proud that Hugging Face is the Hub where people find MLX models and contribute their own. Usage of open, local AI is accelerating, and we believe in a healthy ecosystem where people can find the tools that work for them.

Stability, and hopefully faster development! Graduating from a side job to a fully maintained and funded project will allow Jun to better guide the contributors and build for the long-term. oMLX stays Apache 2.0, and Jun keeps leading it as before.

Our end goal is to unblock the community to run local AI in any shape or form, and provide the tools and building blocks to make that happen. We expect oMLX to serve as a testbed for new ideas, while leveraging the foundational work of the dependencies it already relies upon, such as mlx-lm or mlx-vlm. We believe that strong modeling and inference libraries help the community, so we'd love to upstream work to wherever it makes sense. We have been collaborating with many projects mlx-lm, mlx-vlm, LMStudio, and we hope we can strengthen the relationship with Cheng, Prince, Yagil, and their teams to better serve the community together.

Concretely, one focus area is the quick transition from a transformers model definition to a reference MLX implementation that can be consumed by different engines, so each one can focus on the unique features they provide. The transformers library has become the reference for ML model definitions, we want to streamline the process to make new transformers models run on MLX.

We are incredibly excited about the future.

#9679. Beyls: Wrapping up LLVM's relicensing effort

Kristof Beyls has published a summary to the LLVM discussion forum to announce that the project is declaring success and bringing its relicensing effort to a close after eight years.

We've been asking past contributors to relicense their work since 2018. New contributions have come in under Apache-2.0 WITH LLVM-exception since January 19, 2019. Code contributed before that date was under LLVM's earlier licenses (UIUC/NCSA, plus MIT for some runtime libraries), so we needed permission from its authors to move it over. [...]

Today, more than 99.5% of all lines of code ever contributed to LLVM are either covered by the new license, too small for copyright to apply, or no longer in the repository.

Rather than trying to "chase the last tiny fraction forever" LLVM is winding up the effort. Any contributors with code contributed before January 19, 2019 who have not signed a relicensing agreement and do not want their contributions made available under Apache-2.0 with the LLVM-exception can still reach out to the project to ensure their code has the appropriate SPDX license identifier.

The LLVM exception to Apache-2 Posted Nov 21, 2026 13:13 UTC (Sat) by coriordan (guest, #7544) [Link] For anyone who doesn't know (like me until 5 minutes ago): The LLVM exception: https://merlijn.sebrechts.be/blog/what-is-the-apache-2-ll... It says two things. (Based on my quick read; corrections welcome) 1. That Apache-2 licensed compilers (which insert some compiler code into the executables they create) don't create Apache-2 obligations for the programs they create. 2. It fixes incompatibility with GPLv2 by saying that, for a combined work of Apache-2 plus GPLv2 code, if an authority decides that any clause of Apache-2 is incompatible with GPLv2 then that clause of Apache-2 doesn't apply. (Which I guess they decided is fine because the places where there could be conflicts, such as patents, using the GPLv2 version isn't enough of a problem to be worth incompatibility.) So, the LLVM exception looks like a pretty good instrument.

#9678. Illiterate Programming

Get new articles delivered to your inbox →

My family comes from a part of the world where writing is held in very high esteem. Our poets are national heroes, our role-models are dissident essayists, and our governments, unlike those in Australia and New Zealand, had the good grace to actually attempt to persecute writers because, if nothing else, they knew that those writers would be read. Even now, it's still a cultural expectation that a middle-class Polish adult is at least a little well-read, and they should be able to identify and have read at least three or four poets.

It's probably not a surprise, then, that I grew up surrounded by books and grew into a voracious reader as a child. I've always been good at reading and read a lot and, once I'd read enough, I turned out to be a pretty damned effective writer as well. Reading and writing have, in short, always been a massive part of my life to the extent that I almost did an arts conjoint with my engineering degree and when I was dissuaded from that by my parents (one of the biggest regrets in my life, if I'm to be honest), I still did my absolute best to keep up with the humanities as I did my engineering degree (I spent altogether too much time in the library trying to unpick the Latin of the Vulgate bible). And my literacy, little though you might expect it, did me some considerable favours. Being able to write well and lucidly saved me in a couple of engineering courses where I was struggling with the maths, I suspect, and I was able to contribute to magazines and online publications which kept me socially connected despite being a socially awkward mess.

It was a jolt, therefore, when I started my third job and found myself, for the first time, interacting with actual programmers. My first job was for an acoustics consultancy, and I was more than a little lucky with it, truth be told: the place was full of sensitive and intelligent music-lovers, some of whom were literary and the rest of whom were at least interested in something worthwhile. My second job involved working heavily with biologists: again, quite a literate crowd, even if some of them were wilfully obtuse about the humanities in the way scientists often are. My third job, though? Nope. Never have I had the misfortune to spend so much time with wilfully ill-read, obtuse, uncultured philistines. And this isn't just me complaining that they don't read Eliot or what-have-you: they had only the barest familiarity with Shakespeare, the bible or any novel at all. Hell, they thought Brandon Sanderson unbearably intellectual, and Sanderson is pretty pulpy as an author.

Writing is often a precarious way to make a living, both directly and indirectly. While our situation is stabilising, it's a slow process, which means that if you derive value for my writing, I fear I must ask, as always, for your support. If you'd like to contribute to helping keep me writing, then, you can do so via Patreon, Liberapay or Stripe.

In short: programmers don't read, and this vexes me sorely. The immediate irritation is simply that I feel quite lonely: in being fairly literate and writing about it, I quite often find myself labelled as suspect or as "not a real tech person": that kind of problem, you know? More problematically, I genuinely find it hard to build a rapport with your average non-reading programmer. And I am not bad at communicating: if I was, quite frankly, this blog would not be a thing, nor would it be half as well-read as it is. No, there's something about the non-reading programmer that, for want of a better word, makes it difficult to communicate with them: try as I might, my best attempts mostly bounce off them entirely.

Which poses an issue. After all, I'd probably not be offended if a roofer or an electrician didn't read, at least not beyond the general kind of "bemoaning societal illiteracy" that I tend to engage in. My general assumption with tradies or people outside my general literati bubble is that they don't need to be reading lots of hard books in order to lead happy, fulfilling and socially valuable lives. I don't think that my plumber needs to read Goethe in order to be able to fix my toilet well. And yet with programmers, not reading sticks in my head as a massive moral defect. Why?

Some light can be shone on the matter by the fact that the best programmers and engineers (as opposed to the general run of the profession) buck the general trend and read quite a lot: Efron Licht, to give just one example, reads quite widely and in real depth. Even if they don't quite engage in the way that I'd like them to, they make the effort, and consequently they usually have something interesting to say. The engineers that don't read, by contrast, I've always found very difficult to talk to productively.

As it happens, this generalises. The better a software engineer is at programming (and I mean this both in a moral and in a technical sense), the wider a range of interests they tend to have. Good programmers do all matter of different weird and wonderful things, while the kind of programmer who's only interested in programming and tech in general tends to be a second-rate software developer at best. What this suggests to me is that a large part of my issue is that not reading bespeaks incuriosity. As some long-forgotten Chinese poet had it:

The powerful don't read, The illiterate are loaded, Fuck up and you'll get promoted

The complaint being made here is quite similar to mine: powerful and influential people lack the most basic curiosity about the world and things beyond their immediate sphere, and it shows. Importantly, the issue is that of power, as the poet doesn't complain about peasants or artisans not reading. This is an insight of some importance.

Programmers as a class have occupied, and often still do (mass layoffs aside) a position of considerable cultural power in our society. And a lot of them don't read. They don't wish to learn about times and places other than their own. They are basically dull-minded and incurious people, which makes them manifestly unfit for the position of power they occupy.

After all, being in a position of power means that you're in a position to make choices that impact other people, often quite a lot of them. If you're a software developer writing an interface, your choices will influence how other people interact with the software you've written. If you're writing accounting software, you influence whether people get access to loans or not. Your decisions have a lot of influence on how people interact with the world.

To do this task well, you need to be able to exercise curiosity about other people and how they live. You need to be able to learn what's important to them and what isn't, how they work, what they find confusing... while one might possibly (if not plausibly) learn to exercise exactly the kind of curiosity needed for your work and only that curiosity, it's far easier just to start by being curious in general. Lack of curiosity, as indicated by an unwillingness to read, thus indicates that you're bad at your job.

So, that's one part of the irritation: what's the rest?

Be the first to know when a new article drops! Sign up to the newsletter too for exclusive updates on my thinking and news about deadSimpleTech and our projects.

Get new articles delivered to your inbox →

The incuriosity is, in itself, bad enough, but it doesn't explain the whole phenomenon. One could, after all, imagine programmers doing work similar to that of plumbing: writing glue code that's important for infrastructure but that doesn't really require much communication with other people (although I think you'll find that even plumbing and electrical work take quite a bit of communication: it's just that even the worst communicator is able to communicate "the toilet broke and is spewing sewerage everywhere" pretty well mosst of the time). Unfortunately, code doesn't really work that way.

Any act of programming or producing code is an act of written communication, and doing it well exercises much the same skills as writing an essay does. To give one example of this, wide structure in a codebase involves basically the same considerations as wide structure in an essay: you want to make sure that different subjects are separated out correctly and each subject is placed in a logical grouping with other subjects of its kind. Similarly, you want to make sure that these groupings are logically arranged together in a way that flows well and leaves the reader edified at the end. A codebase, in short, is a written communication to a reader first and something executed by a machine second.

This is easily enough evidenced: unmaintainable or unreadable code is, in the long run, useless, no matter how effective it might be initially. If you can't change the code and adapt it to fit your situation, or if you can't read it to see what it does, it doesn't matter what it does do: it's mostly useless to you. The basic functions of code, then, are quite fundamentally tied up with its role as a written communication directed at other people.

And here's the rub: to be good at communicating, curiosity is essential. After all, when you write to communicate, you have to imagine yourself, at least partially, in the reader's head: to figure out how they'd interpret a given set of words, to consider the connotation of what's written (butt-dial and booty call are, after all, denotatively identical) and to make ethos, pathos and logos work together for your particular audience. This applies to technical writing just as much as to the writing of fiction or essays. You have to have a healthy curiosity about who your audience are and what they're like, otherwise your writing is simply bad.

And this, I think, is the second great sin of the non-reading programmer: they feel entitled to do what they will without putting any effort into either communicating or being communicated with. It puts me in mind of the job interviews I've been in where I've been told that I'm excellent technically and communicate well, but that I "lack relatability": what this means, I think, is that by virtue of who I am, your average programmer will have to put a little effort into communicating with me. It's only a little, and it's the amount that implicitly exists when you're communicating with someone who isn't exactly like you, but even that mote is too much for a non-reading programmer.

The consequences are as you might expect: they range from bad documentation and unreadable code on the relatively trivial end, to the fact that people are willing to work for OpenAI on the grossly immoral end of things. Programmers like this are, quite honestly, just horrible to work with, let alone spend time with. And aside from these problems, there are half-a-hundred other little irritations that spin off from them: the weird rationalist cults, the repeated reinvention of eugenics and phrenology, DHH...

Unfortunately, our non-reading colleagues have one major advantage over us in the job market in that they can usually be relied on to smile and nod and say "yes, boss" to whatever inane diktats have come down from management on any given day. It doesn't matter that the code will be an unreadable, unmaintainable mess, nor that the request may, in point of fact, have been physically impossible: the high-ups, who by and large also don't like reading, nor communicating or being communicated with, see work happening, so they're happy. Us unlucky folks, who feel the need to communicate and be communicated with, are shit out of luck.

It's too much to hope for, alas, that this problem might be fixed by forcing the non-reading programmer to read a novel a month or whatever: high school English classes show what happens when you try that. Still, it wouldn't hurt to try a bit of social engineering: weird manosphere shit was able to get people to read (and horribly mangle) Marcus Aurelius, so getting people to read Shakespeare should be doable. Creating the expectation that engineers should be cultured seems worth a try, and it could be quite doable by people like me. If you're a tech blogger and you read, then, please let people know. Create the impression that the tastemakers think being cultured again. Otherwise I fear that someday I'll have to sit through another insufferable office Christmas party, and I don't think I can survive that.

#9676. Transformers now runs llama.cpp quants

We're adding support for running GGUF models efficiently in transformers, so you can use checkpoints sized for your laptop's memory through the familiar transformers APIs. Pick a GGUF from the Hub, load it with from_pretrained, and start generating on your own machine.

Running AI models on your laptop has become much easier, and llama.cpp has been a big part of that. Its inference engine powers local AI tools such as Ollama, LM Studio, and Jan. Alongside projects like MLX, it has helped make local inference a practical option for everyday use.

A recent example of what local AI can feel like:

This is where we are right now. And i’m not gonna lie it feels pretty magical 🧙‍♀️Qwen3.6 27B running inside of Pi coding agent via Llama.cpp on the MacBook ProFor non-trivial tasks on the @huggingface codebases, this feels very, very close to hitting the latest Opus in Claude… pic.twitter.com/lsIxLoUneU

GGUF, developed by the llama.cpp team, is a widely used format for local inference. The team also shares quantized checkpoints under ggml-org on the Hub. Publishers such as Unsloth, LM Studio Community, and bartowski also provide ready-to-use GGUF checkpoints in a range of quantizations, so users can pick the version that fits their machine. GGUF models have been downloaded millions of times.

We want to make it easier to run these models locally with transformers, too. Compatibility is only useful if the model is pleasant to run. To bring performance close to llama.cpp, we're reusing its underlying ggml kernels through the kernels library, and reducing overhead in generate. Our initial focus is local inference on Apple Silicon, starting with the Qwen3.5 architecture.

GGUF packages model weights and metadata, including tokenizer information and an optional chat template, in one file. It supports different quantization levels, letting you trade some precision for a smaller memory footprint. Variants such as Q4_K_M mix tensor precisions, using mostly 4-bit weights while keeping sensitive tensors at higher precision.

Here's how quantization changes the file size of Unsloth's Qwen3.5-4B:

We suggest starting with Q4_K_M, then trying Q5_K_M or Q6_K if you have more memory available. More aggressive quantization can help larger models fit, but the quality tradeoff depends on the model and the task. Evaluate it on the work you actually want the model to do. The Hub's GGUF documentation describes the available quantization types.

To load a GGUF model, pass its Hub model_id and filename as gguf_file to from_pretrained.

No extra configuration is needed: when the weights stay packed on Metal, transformers automatically loads the compatible ggml/Metal layer kernels and uses ggml-org/ggml-attn as the attention implementation. If that kernel cannot be fetched, the model falls back to "sdpa" with a warning, and you can always force "sdpa" by passing attn_implementation="sdpa" explicitly. See the GGUF documentation for more loading options.

That is the only GGUF-specific step. Everything after it is the standard transformers API:

Without a compatible quantization kernel, the loader falls back to dequantizing the model and uses more memory.

You can also use the same checkpoint with transformers serve, which exposes an OpenAI-compatible API:

The model argument uses :.gguf: before the colon is the Hub repository (unsloth/Qwen3.5-4B-GGUF), and after it is the file to load (Qwen3.5-4B-Q4_K_M.gguf). This selects a specific quantization from a repository that may contain several.

For models whose chat template supports thinking, add --reasoning off to skip it or --reasoning on to enable it. The default, --reasoning auto, follows the chat template’s default. See the reasoning options for details.

You can connect a client such as Jan or Pi by adding a custom OpenAI-compatible provider with these settings:

transformers runs the model on your Mac, while the client provides the conversation interface. The same endpoint can be used by other clients that support this API.

Our reference for local inference performance is llama.cpp. The comparison below focuses on three GGUF checkpoints: a small dense model, a larger dense model, and a mixture-of-experts model.

The llama.cpp column comes from the llama-bench tool (build 5f55650a7, release b10200, Metal backend from ggml 0.18.0), run as llama-bench -m -p 0 -n 128 -r 3, which reports tg128: the token-generation rate over 128 decoded tokens, averaged across three repetitions, with prompt processing excluded. The transformers column is generate producing the same 128 tokens from a 12-token prompt, best of three warmed runs, and it includes prefill.

Measured on a MacBook Pro M2 Max, 32 GB unified memory, macOS 26.6, PyTorch 2.12.1, kernels 0.17.0, plugged in.

Transformers is close to llama.cpp across all three checkpoints. The chart uses the same measurements described above; it does not imply identical benchmark conditions, since the Transformers measurement includes prefill while llama-bench reports decode-only throughput.

When GGML and llama.cpp joined Hugging Face, we described their complementary roles: llama.cpp provides a foundation for local inference, while transformers provides a foundation for model definition. GGUF support brings those two closer together.

llama.cpp remains our recommended engine when your priority is efficient local inference. Its dedicated runtime, memory management, and broad hardware support are built around that goal. This integration gives developers a convenient way to work with the same GGUF checkpoints inside transformers:

For that last case, use GgufConfig(dequantize=True):

The bigger opportunity is bringing ggml's performance to models that llama.cpp does not support.

transformers already provides the PyTorch implementations of these architectures. With ggml kernels and quantization schemes available in PyTorch, we can work toward accelerating their supported operations without first implementing the entire model in llama.cpp. This is especially useful for new architectures, research models, and custom variants that may never receive a dedicated llama.cpp implementation.

That opportunity extends beyond the GGUF format itself. A kernel operates on tensors; it does not require the whole model to come from a GGUF file. The same building blocks can be integrated into other transformers models and loading workflows. This also opens a path to other modalities: computer vision models, audio models, and multimodal models could reuse compatible attention, normalization, and matrix multiplication kernels without first having a full implementation in llama.cpp. Each architecture still needs integration and validation; the initial GGUF examples here cover text generation.

We also wanted to show how far we can get while keeping the model and generation loop in Python. With the right kernels and an efficient generation loop, Python and PyTorch can deliver strong local inference performance. The kernels handle the heavy computation, while the generation loop keeps the GPU busy by avoiding unnecessary synchronization.

Our focus was to make eager execution fast without requiring torch.compile. For interactive use, we wanted a quick start and a steady stream of tokens, without compilation pauses or recompilation when input shapes change. The two main pieces of that work are the kernels and generate itself.

A kernel is a small program that performs an operation on the GPU. PyTorch supplies general-purpose implementations; a specialized kernel can do less work, combine several operations, or read quantized weights directly in their stored format.

The kernels library lets us distribute compatible builds of ggml's Metal kernels on the Hub and call them from transformers. That brings ggml's work into the PyTorch model without replacing the model with a separate inference runtime.

The first four packages build on ggml's kernels; the top-k kernel addresses a separate bottleneck in MoE routing. Together they reduce the GPU work needed for each generated token.

To show the contribution of the layer kernels, we compare the same packed GGUF checkpoints with and without them. The quantization kernel stays enabled in both configurations: disabling it would also change how weights are represented and would measure a different tradeoff.

Faster kernels only help if the GPU has work to do. During generation, the CPU schedules GPU operations and controls the loop that produces the next token. Reading a result back from the GPU can force the CPU to wait until queued operations finish. Repeating even a small wait for every token can noticeably reduce throughput.

Two changes address this in generate, which results in improvements for all transformers models (not just when running GGUF files):

These changes improve the generation loop around the model, so their usefulness extends beyond GGUF. They complement the kernel work: kernels reduce the cost of an operation, while fewer synchronization points let CPU scheduling and GPU execution overlap.

These measurements keep all layer kernels enabled; the bars isolate the changes to the generation loop.

The initial target is a single interactive conversation on Apple Silicon. There are a few boundaries to keep in mind:

If you have a GGUF model you would like to use in transformers, open an issue with the checkpoint and your use case. That will help us prioritize support for the models people are running locally.

We would like to thank Arthur Zucker for initiating this work and reviewing all of my PRs, and Cyril Vallez for the generate PRs. We are grateful to Sayak Paul, the llama.cpp team, and Bertrand Chevalier for their help integrating the kernels. We also thank Aritra Roy Gosthipaty and Pedro Cuenca for reviewing this blog post, and Lysandre Debut for overseeing the project.

#9673. Africa Retakes Top Spot as Most Attacked Region, Led by Nigeria Surge

Breaking cybersecurity news, news analysis, commentary, and other content from around the world, with an initial focus on the Middle East & Africa, the Asia Pacific, Europe, and Latin America.

Nigeria faced more than double the cyber threats of the previous year, with Angola and Kenya also in the top 5 most-attacked countries globally.

Organizations in Africa faced an average of 3,834 cyberattacks per week in October, a jump of 38% from a year earlier, making the continent the most-attacked region for the first time in more than a year.

Nigeria, Angola, and Kenya were among the top-five most targeted countries, with Nigeria topping the list with nearly 6,700 attacks targeting organizations in the country every week; that marks a 140% increase over October 2025, according to data published by Check Point Research earlier this month. The nations are among those rapidly pushing technological transformation of their infrastructure, expanding connectivity, investing in digital services, and putting sensitive data in network-connected applications and storage.

The fast transformation is exposing more opportunities for attackers, says Shayimamba Conco, chief technology officer and security evangelist in the Office of the CTO at Check Point Software.

Related:Chinese AI Project Scouts Spies in Taiwan Chip Industry

"All this rapid digital expansion is now happening within the region, but then, at the same time, this [expansion] is outpacing improvements in security maturity," he says, adding that security improvements are uneven across the continent. "Yes, some areas — let's say for example, South Africa — it's adopting cybersecurity at a much quicker rate than the rest of the Africa region, but there will be those regions which are still lagging behind a bit."

The significant increase in average weekly attacks pushed African organizations past those in Latin America as the favored targets of cyberattackers. In the first quarter of 2026, Latin America averaged more than 3,000 attacks per week, surpassing the approximate 2,700 attacks targeting African organizations. In September, the two regions essentially tied in terms of attacks, with Africa once again becoming the most popular target in October.

Globally, organizations experienced an average of 2,550 weekly cyberattacks in October, down 9% from September but up a third from the previous year. While Africa encountered the most weekly attacks, both Latin America and Asia-Pacific regions saw a greater-than-average number — 3,483 and 3,436, respectively.

Globally, cyberattacks focused heavily on the education sector, with the average academic institution suffering more than 5,900 attacks per week, up a third from the same month in 2025. The education sector has topped the global list of popular targets every month, with organizations made attractive to attackers because of their large data sets and reliance on legacy systems, says Conco.

Related:Malicious Linux Implants Mimic Asian Mail Security Products

"There is a lack of budget when it comes to not just IT, but specifically cybersecurity," he says. "A junior IT engineer has to manage these vast environments, which are hard to lock down by nature, because you've got all these students who need access to all these applications and resources."

In Africa, however, cyberattackers most often targeted financial services, government agencies, and the energy sector, according to Check Point's data.

The countries are racing to improve their cybersecurity postures and address persistent threats. Nigeria's National Information Technology Development Agency (NITDA) continues to work on the details of the nation's cybersecurity and cloud-sovereignty policies. Last month, Operation Serengeti 3.0 — a joint task force between Interpol and 20 African countries — led to the arrest of more than 1,500 suspects and the recovery of $105 million in stolen funds. In August, Operation Jackal IV targeted West African crime syndicates, leading to more than 200 arrests.

Check Point also flagged the use of AI in companies as a potential weak point, finding that about 2.9% of prompts to generative AI and large language models (LLMs) posed a high risk of leaking sensitive information. The risk is steadily increasing over time, from 2.3% in August to 2.5% in September.

Related:UAE, Saudi Arabia Face Onslaught of Increasingly Complex Cyberattacks

Interpol has also observed that attackers are increasingly using AI in a way that has impacted African nations. In its African Cybercrime Assessment Report 2026, Interpol found that 55% of reported cybercrimes across Africa used AI to some degree.

"Cybercrime has emerged as one of the most significant criminal threats to the region," Neal Jetton, Director of Interpol’s Cybercrime unit, said in a statement in August. "AI is automating every stage of a cyberattack from reconnaissance and phishing to extortion and evasion. However, we see that when countries work together, cybercriminal infrastructure can be identified, disrupted and dismantled."

Rob is an award-winning, veteran technology journalist of more than 30 years, reporting on global cybersecurity issues, the latest offensive and defensive technologies, malware incidents, cyber conflict, and AI's impact on software and cybersecurity.

A former research engineer, Rob has written for more than two dozen publications, including CNET News.com, Dark Reading, MIT's Technology Review, Popular Science, and Wired News. He has received five awards for journalism, including Best Deadline Journalism (Online) in 2003 for his coverage of the Blaster worm. Rob also analyzes data on various trends using Python and R for both his reporting and his clients. Recent reports include analyses of the shortage in cybersecurity workers, annual vulnerability trends, and annual threat reports.

Rob holds degrees from Cornell University in Electrical Engineering and Computer Science (double major).

InfoQ Homepage News AWS Lambda Now Runs GPU Inference with 48 Concurrent Invocations Sharing One Model per GPU

Nov 22, 2026 4 min read

AWS has added GPU support to AWS Lambda: Event Functions running on Lambda Managed Instances can now run on EC2 G-series instances (G4dn, G5, G6, G6f, Gr6, Gr6f and G6e at launch), deployed as container images, and triggered by the same event sources as any other function. The feature is generally available in the commercial regions where both Managed Instances and G-series instances exist. It is priced at the EC2 On-Demand rate plus a 9.75 percent management fee and the standard $0.20 per million requests.

As InfoQ reported last December, Managed Instances let a function run on EC2 capacity the customer selects and pays for, with Lambda handling provisioning, patching and scaling and several invocations sharing one execution environment. GPUs were missing at that launch. Daniel Abib, senior specialist solutions architect at AWS, describes the operator's side of the change:

You build an OCI image, point the function at it, and let Lambda handle provisioning, scaling, and event integration. There are no GPU drivers, CUDA versions, or AMIs to reconcile, and no clusters or device plugins to operate.

A capacity provider lists the allowed instance types, the VPC and a vCPU ceiling; Lambda picks the newest generation with capacity and falls back to older generations when newer ones are short:

The function declares its GPU memory through a new AcceleratorConfig block, next to memory, timeout, storage, and a per-environment concurrency:

Concurrent invocations in one environment share a single copy of the model in GPU memory, up to 48 per environment, and scaling follows GPU utilization, CPU utilization, and concurrency. Publishing a version provisions the environments, downloads the weights, and warms the engine before the first event arrives; Seekable OCI lazy loading can cut environment start time by up to 70 percent.

AWS ships five GPU base images: CUDA only, CuPy, PyTorch, vLLM, and SGLang. The two inference servers need no handler code; a MODEL_ID variable points to a Hugging Face or ModelScope repository, an S3 prefix, or a local path, and a model swap is a configuration change followed by a new version:

The limits are in the launch post: container images up to 32 GB, 32 GB of ephemeral storage, 2 to 32 GB of memory, 3 to 48 GB of accelerator memory, 15,000 vCPUs per capacity provider, and a timeout of up to 90 minutes for asynchronous and event source mapping invocations. Abib draws the line against the competition in one sentence: serverless GPU services that hide the same work "often sit outside your AWS environment, with no native event sources, identity, or networking."

The first hands-on reports came within a day. Classmethod's Akaike, who had corrected a conference talk in December after finding that no G-type was accepted, tried every accelerated instance type in us-east-1 and found 37 of 81 accepted, all G-family; P-family, G7, Inferentia, Trainium, and the Graviton-based g5g were refused, as were zip packages. A PyTorch benchmark ran about 66 times faster on the L4 than on the instance's CPU. Still, neither Terraform nor the Cloud Control provider knew AcceleratorConfig yet, and the GPU vCPU quota in a fresh account is zero: "if you use g6.xlarge (4 vCPU) with the default three instances, you need a quota of 12 vCPUs." A Terraform provider issue and pull request, opened on 16 November by a user named sasidhar-aws, and a pull request from the same user remain open.

A second test, by an AWS Community Builder writing as xbill, put Gemma 4 E2B on a single g6.2xlarge through the vLLM image, with Google's 4-bit QAT weights and a speculative-decoding drafter baked into a 9 GB image. One environment served all 48 simultaneous requests and every one of 417 calls succeeded, at roughly 130 tokens a second for a single request and 3,400 to 3,600 at 48. The friction was in the pipeline rather than the GPU: 484 seconds from publish to an active version, a Docker image index that Lambda rejected until it was pushed as a single-platform manifest, and a handler that returns complete replies, so time to first token could not be measured. His verdict keeps to that scope:

For a model behind events, queues or other AWS services, the Lambda GPU function is the simpler road: one image, one function, and Lambda keeps the server alive and routes the requests. Keep the drafter on for a chat with a few users at a time, and publish without it for heavy batch load.

When streamed replies or full control of the server are needed, he writes, "run vLLM on an EC2 G6 yourself."

The pricing model is the one Managed Instances introduced, with a lower fee for GPUs than the 15 percent charged on CPU instance types. Savings Plans and Reserved Instances apply to the instance, and there is no duration charge, so an instance bills for as long as the minimum environment count is above zero. Yan Cui's December analysis of the model, written when it still carried the line "GPU instances are NOT supported," applies to the GPU case unchanged:

Regular Lambda functions can scale rapidly by tapping into a large, shared pool of EC2 instances. With managed instances, it takes tens of seconds to launch new EC2 instances. As such, it's not a good fit when you have large, unpredictable spikes in traffic.

Managed Instances still support only Event Functions, so the GPU path does not yet reach Web Functions, the HTTP-server shape Lambda gained this year, and AWS has not said whether it will.

#9671. How UK AISI and EvalEval Are Making Benchmark Results Reproducible

The EvalEval Coalition is thrilled to share that the UK AI Security Institute (AISI) is using EvalEval's infrastructure to openly share evaluation results, supporting more reproducible and verifiable evaluation science.

AISI and EvalEval have previously collaborated on research that began at a joint workshop alongside NeurIPS 2025, and feedback from the Institute has helped shape the Every Eval Ever (EEE) schema. This next phase of the collaboration puts that shared infrastructure into practice.

As AI deployment accelerates, evaluations are becoming increasingly important sources of evidence about model and system performance. Yet results are reported across many formats, platforms, and outlets, often without enough information to reproduce them. Running the evaluations again may itself be prohibitively expensive.

EvalEval's mission is to improve this ecosystem through a shared reporting schema, Every Eval Ever, and an open platform, Evaluation Cards, that brings evaluation results and the information needed to interpret them into a common structure.

This builds naturally on AISI's work to make evaluation more efficient through OptStop, more statistically rigorous through HiBayES, and more standardised in areas including transcript analysis and capability elicitation. Together, AISI and EvalEval are working to diagnose gaps in evaluation reporting and build shared infrastructure to close them.

Transcript-level transparency matters not only for reproducibility, but also for analysis and diagnosis. In this new phase of the collaboration, AISI is making publicly reported evaluation methods and findings available through Evaluation Cards where appropriate. The release includes verified results, context, and configuration information for the five benchmarks in the paper's main experiment:

These results cover six frontier models: Claude Opus 4, Claude Opus 4.5, Claude Opus 4.6, GPT-5, GPT-5.2, and GPT-5.4. The release also includes results from two related cyber evaluations—Cyber CTFs and The Last Ones—which use a different, partially overlapping set of models. The data accompany AISI's paper, How Inference Compute Shapes Frontier LLM Evaluation, which studies how benchmark performance depends on inference-time compute and evaluation protocol.

Performance on Humanity's Last Exam changes with evaluation protocol and inference compute. Each curve shows the cumulative share of attempted tasks solved within a given token count, using the earliest observed success per task. When models received correctness feedback from an oracle after each attempt, they continued to solve additional tasks as token use increased.

When results are openly released with setup information, researchers and practitioners can examine individual studies more closely and compare findings across the wider ecosystem. Where other reports lack these details, releases like AISI's provide verified reference points for interpreting evaluations in context—for example, by helping researchers understand how setup choices may influence reported performance. As more evaluators adopt EEE, open comparisons like these can support broader and more reliable meta-research.

AISI's Terminal-Bench 2.0 results alongside other reported evaluations for the same models, under different evaluation setups.

We are excited about this adoption and look forward to further standardising and sharing evaluations with AISI and other AI evaluation organisations.

The EvalEval Coalition is a research community developing scientifically grounded research and robust deployment infrastructure for the evaluation ecosystem. Its goal is to improve evaluation science, address the lack of consensus around documenting evaluation applicability and utility, and broaden coverage of the impacts that matter for scientific research and policy analysis.

The coalition's flagship projects include Every Eval Ever, a shared schema and repository for evaluation results, and Evaluation Cards, which combines benchmark metadata, evaluation-run data, and model metadata into interpretable records. Together, they make it easier to understand when apparently similar scores were produced under meaningfully different conditions.

The UK AI Security Institute is a research organisation within the UK government's Department for Science, Innovation and Technology. Its mission is to equip governments with a scientific understanding of the risks posed by advanced AI. AISI conducts research and builds infrastructure to understand advanced AI capabilities and impacts, develop and test mitigations, and inform policy.

The line that matters for practitioners is quiet: apparently similar scores can be produced under meaningfully different conditions.

Once you've watched a benchmark move just by changing inference-time compute or the elicitation protocol, "Model A beat Model B on X" without a card is marketing, not comparison. Evaluation Cards that ship verified results with configuration — especially transcript-level context where it's appropriate — are how eval becomes a contract instead of a leaderboard screenshot.

One ask I'd put to teams adopting EEE: which fields get skipped first under deadline pressure (seed, tool access, attempt budget, oracle feedback), and do you treat a missing field as "do not cite the delta" rather than "assume defaults"?

Reproducible reporting won't remove disagreement. It will make the disagreement about the right variables.

#9669. Welcome RL Environments to the hub

Reinforcement Learning environments give new capabilities to agentic AI systems, and they’re a great way to measure and improve performance in your agents. Therefore, Hugging Face Hub now has a special place for RL Environments.

An environment gives an agent a task, responds to its actions with observations, and scores the outcome. The resulting rewards can measure an agent's performance during evaluation or provide a learning signal during training. For an introduction to this interaction loop, see our blogpost on environments. Within the environment, the agent will perform a set of tasks that are represented as datasets. Therefore, environments can be split into broadly two parts: tasksets and runtimes. In this release, we are focusing on the tasksets.

An RL environment on the Hub is a dataset repo that shows up in the new RL Environments filter. The Use this dataset button gives you the command to run it in that framework. There is no new repo type, no registry, and no sign-up. There are already environments in Harbor, Verifiers, and NVIDIA NeMo Gym.

Every RL paper or framework uses its own way to find environments. Custom hubs, runtime registries, independent task datasets, or a GitHub list of tasks with a custom loader. This means that many of the published environments are siloed: if you publish an environment for one framework, users of the other three can’t load it. If you want to train on an environment from another framework or a new paper, you’ll need to port it by hand.

We think this is the wrong shape. An environment is tasks, tests, containers, and a reward rule, which are data with a runtime on top. The Hub already stores data, versions it, gates it, previews it, and serves it to millions of people. It does not need a second system to hold environments. It needs a way to say "this data is an environment, and here is how you run it."

The frameworks keep doing what they are good at. The Hub does what it is good at, which is hosting, discovery, and versioning. Nobody has to own the catalogue. In fact, catalogues can run on other platforms too, powered by the hub.

The dataset repository hosts your environment files. The framework runs them locally or on a supported cloud backend. Hugging Face Jobs can run cloud workloads, and Hugging Face Sandboxes, built on Jobs, provide interactive command execution. The tags describe compatibility and generate loading commands; adding a tag does not start a job or sandbox.

The RL Environments filter. Go to huggingface.co/datasets?other=rl-environment. Every dataset with the rl-environment tag appears there, whatever framework it works with.

Framework tags. Four environment frameworks are registered as dataset libraries:

Each framework tag puts the framework's icon on the dataset page and adds a generated snippet to Use this dataset.

A dataset can carry more than one framework tag. That is the point. Tags describe compatibility, and compatibility is not exclusive. Each listed framework must support the files in the repository; adding a tag does not convert them.

Choose the example for your framework and run it in a separate Python environment with the prerequisites listed below.

Harbor can load task directories from a Hub repository. The oracle agent runs the task's reference solution, then the verifier scores the result. It does not call a model.

The viewer shows the task's reward, verifier output, and logs. This checks the task and its reference solution before you try a model agent.

The Harbor integration of verifiers v1 can run the same task directories in different runtimes, such as Docker. It also supports different harnesses, including a minimal bash harness.

Here repo is the full Hugging Face Git URL, while dataset is the name and version in that repo's registry.json. This loader uses Harbor's registry conventions, so a bare Hub repo ID cannot replace both values.

OpenEnv's Harbor integration can run the same task directories with an agent such as OpenCode and return the verifier's reward alongside the agent's trace.

The command downloads the dataset's tasks/ directories, runs one task in Docker, and writes the result. The default connection uses a temporary Gradio tunnel so the sandboxed agent can reach OpenEnv's model proxy. Read the verifier result and the number of model calls:

A reward of None means no verifier reward was produced; inspect error before interpreting the run as a model failure. This path expects Harbor task directories.

NeMo Gym supports evaluation and RL training: its environments collect trajectories and compute rewards, while a training framework updates model weights. For example, the Structured Outputs dataset pairs prompts with JSON schemas. Its verifier rewards schema adherence; it does not check whether the generated content is factually correct.

The best part is that this gives one repo and one discussion tab where people report broken tasks from all major frameworks. So when an author fixes a bad test, every framework gets the fix on the next pull.

Open your dataset card and add this to the YAML header:

That is the whole integration. Keep rl-environment, then list every framework that can load your files. If your environment works with a framework we have not registered yet, open a PR to the list of supported libraries.

We opened PRs to tag some of the environments people already train on. If you maintain one of these, merge the PR and your environment shows up in the filter.

The first version generates one default snippet per framework. Per-config snippets are next, so a repo with several task sets can show the right command for each. After that we will look at structural detection for frameworks with strict layouts. It would also be really cool build custom task UIs, we’ve been experimenting with this here:

The bigger goal is for framework tagging to be automatic everywhere. OpenEnv already does it on upload. If you maintain Harbor, Verifiers, Nemo Gym, or any other environment framework, add the tags in your push path. It is a few lines, and every environment your users publish becomes visible to everyone else.

If you train agents, go browse the filter. If you build environments, publish and tag them, whether they cover coding, tool use, games, robotics, or another task. Include the files, a working run command, and the rule that produces the reward so others can use them. If your framework is missing, contribute it to the list of supported libraries.

CachyOS, a performance-focused distribution based on Arch Linux, has announced its November 2026 release. Notable changes in this release include a new recovery environment ("cachyos-recovery") for rolling back broken systems, Easy Anti-Cheat (EAC) v2 support for games that require EAC to run, version 2.0.0 of the CachyOS Package Installer, and more.

1. DRM and anticheat are, to a large part, one and the same, including that they're trying to best-effort solve a theoretically impossible problem by locking down clients.

Not purchasing DRM-requiring games is really the best way to do this. Until then, refuse to help deploy such mechanisms (can't really not help with implementation unless you also think that no one should be able to do lockdown-like things to their own hardware or avoiding contributing to any such thing). Game studios certainly have the right to release games that require it. It's just better if no one buys them then.

After that came Secure Boot, which when enabled (and the security hysteria is that you must always have it enabled, even though its driving use case of "not allowing any untrusted code to run before the antivirus starts" is not very relevant for Linux) makes it harder to use a self-compiled kernel. It seems that, outside of source-focused distributions, we've grown complacent and got too comfortable letting someone else compile the software we use. Quick question: can you, with a single command, download and rebuild any package of your favorite distribution (in a way which allows easily applying local changes to it), or does it require deep developer knowlege and a bunch of esoteric commands with a long list of magic options?

InfoQ Homepage News Google Announces Agent Compute Engine for Secure AI Agent Execution

Nov 22, 2026 2 min read

Google recently announced Agent Compute Engine, a managed service that runs AI agents in isolated microVMs, with checkpointing capabilities to suspend and resume execution environments. The design keeps credentials, API keys, and OAuth refresh tokens outside the agent sandbox, using an external Agent Gateway to authenticate requests and inject the required secrets.

Google designed Agent Compute Engine to address three requirements at global scale: keeping sandboxes free of exploitable credentials, even when agents make mistakes; minimizing the cost and latency of resuming idle agents; and preserving persistent workspaces across sessions and operating system updates. The infrastructure team writes:

Agent Compute Engine achieves this by using copy-on-write memory sharing to run multiple agents on a single operating system template, and pausing idle microVMs via fast checkpoint and restore.

In the deep dive "Inside Agent Compute Engine," Ramanathan Venkatapathy and Rohit Jnagal, distinguished engineers at Google, describe the service’s architecture, covering microVM isolation, credential management, agent identity, storage, and scheduling at scale. They explain the strict separation between the agent harness and sandbox:

The orchestration harness (the brain) runs completely outside the execution sandbox (the hands), helping ensure that untrusted guest environments only execute explicit commands dispatched by the harness and stream output back. This boundary establishes a deterministic audit trail correlating every harness-initiated tool call with expected compute activity inside the sandbox.

The architecture supports four main workload categories: interactive consumer and enterprise agents that execute code, browse the web, and perform actions; persistent Linux workspaces for autonomous software engineering; large-scale parallel environments for model evaluation and reinforcement learning; and lightweight, sandboxed execution environments for dynamic logic in Google services.

Venkatapathy and Jnagal also describe how the cloud provider uses the platform internally for Gemini, Gemini for Business, the agentic development platform Antigravity, and model evaluation workloads.

Separately, Google offers Agent Substrate, an open-source, Kubernetes-native runtime for running AI agents in isolated environments. Agent Substrate manages sandbox lifecycles independently of the underlying compute infrastructure, allowing idle agents to be suspended while preserving their state and resuming execution on available workers when needed.

In the article "Google's Agent Compute Engine: A MicroVM Sandbox With No Credentials Inside, and What Google Has Not Shipped Yet," Harel Asaf, AI specialist at Elementor, examines the security architecture, the separation of credentials from agent execution environments, and the gaps between Google's announcement and what is currently available. Asaf warns:

The deep dive gives no boot time, price or density figure for Agent Compute Engine itself. It says developers will control each environment's image, identity, network access and lifecycle, while Google manages the fleet, and that the service is targeted for preview in the coming months. The numbers in the announcement belong to Agent Substrate.

Google is not the only provider offering managed, isolated execution environments for AI agents, with AWS and Azure providing similar capabilities through Bedrock AgentCore and Foundry Agent Service. However, Google’s approach keeps credentials outside agent sandboxes and injects them through an external gateway.

Google also expanded its agent governance capabilities with centralized identity and policy enforcement: the governance stack includes Agent Gateway for traffic control and policy enforcement, Agent Registry for tracking approved agents and tools, SPIFFE-based Agent Identity for authentication and auditing, and OpenTelemetry-compatible observability for monitoring model calls and tool invocations.

Agent Compute Engine is not yet available, and pricing has not been announced. The cloud provider is targeting a preview in the coming months. While Agent Substrate is portable across Kubernetes environments, Agent Compute Engine itself is limited to Google Cloud.
