InfoQ Homepage News PostgreSQL 19 Released with Online Table Repacking and Query Planning Controls

Nov 22, 2026 2 min read

The PostgreSQL Global Development Group released PostgreSQL 19, introducing changes to database maintenance, query planning, replication, and application development. The release focuses on reducing administrative overhead and improving performance, with new tools for reorganizing tables without downtime and controlling query plans.

One of the main additions is REPACK, which reclaims unused table space and can reorder data to match an index. Its CONCURRENTLY option allows the operation to run without blocking reads or writes, making it a potential replacement for common uses of VACUUM FULL and CLUSTER. PostgreSQL 19 also introduces pg_plan_advice and pg_stash_advice, extensions that let administrators influence query plan selection and apply stored advice to queries by identifier, without changing application code.

Other maintenance improvements include parallel index vacuuming, changes to autovacuum prioritization, and additional monitoring views. EXPLAIN ANALYZE and related logging now report asynchronous I/O activity and WAL generated for full-page images. PostgreSQL also reports that changes to foreign key checks made bulk inserts nearly twice as fast in testing. Query planner improvements include more efficient anti-joins for eligible NOT IN clauses and eager aggregation before joins.

The release adds several features for replication and application development. Logical replication now supports sequence values, and PostgreSQL automatically raises the effective WAL level to logical when the first logical replication slot is created. The new WAIT FOR LSN command lets applications wait until a standby has replayed a specified WAL position before querying data, providing read-your-writes consistency. Developers also get INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO SELECT for get-or-create operations, JSON output from COPY, additional SQL/JSON string methods, and IGNORE NULLS support for window functions.

Security and compatibility changes include server-side TLS Server Name Indication (SNI), which allows a server to present different certificates based on the hostname used by the client. PostgreSQL 19 also warns after successful MD5 password authentication. MD5 was deprecated in PostgreSQL 18 and is planned for removal in a future release, with SCRAM recommended instead. JIT compilation is now disabled by default because its cost estimates proved unreliable, while LZ4 becomes the default TOAST compression method when supported by the build.

The release has also prompted discussion on Hacker News about whether production users should wait for PostgreSQL 19.1.

Another user recommended waiting for the first minor release on critical production systems:

Personally, I would say, for critical production systems, it's still good to wait for the .1 release.

PostgreSQL 19 is available now. The complete list of changes is available in the official release notes.

#9651. Introducing Falcon ASR

Arabic WER: 20.92% · Parameters: 1.6B · Emirati WER (TII evaluation): 22.73%

We’re introducing Falcon-ASR, our 1.6 billion parameter speech recognition model for Arabic, with a particular focus on the Emirati dialect. Developed at the Technology Innovation Institute (TII) in Abu Dhabi, it also supports English, French, Spanish and Portuguese.

In our evaluation, Falcon-ASR achieved an average word error rate of 20.92% across six Arabic test sets, compared with the best published result of 23.17% in the leaderboard snapshot we used. On our internal Emirati evaluation, it recorded the lowest word and character error rates among the systems we compared.

We also support word-level timestamps for transcriptions, linking each transcribed word to its position in the audio.

Arabic speech varies by region, speaker and setting. A model that handles a formal news broadcast may still struggle with a conversation in Emirati or with speech recorded over a phone line. Dialectal Arabic also has fewer transcribed resources than Modern Standard Arabic (MSA), which makes training and evaluation harder.

We trained Falcon-ASR on Emirati, MSA, other Gulf and Arabic dialects, and English. Our aim is to transcribe the words people use in everyday speech, including dialectal forms and changes between languages.

The Open Universal Arabic ASR Leaderboard, maintained by the ELM Research Center, ranks systems by the equal-weight average WER across six test sets. It also reports character error rate (CER). Lower values are better for both metrics. Our Falcon-ASR evaluation follows this protocol.

WER = Word Error Rate; CER = Character Error Rate. A lower value indicates better performance.

We evaluated Falcon-ASR on the same six benchmarks using the leaderboard’s pinned manifests. Competitor figures are the published leaderboard averages checked on 30 September 2026. Falcon-ASR’s average WER is 2.25 percentage points better than the best published result in that snapshot.

Public evaluation data already includes Emirati: Casablanca has a UAE subset. We complement that coverage with an internal evaluation of additional Emirati and Gulf speech, using held-out recordings and human-validated transcripts to assess transcription accuracy beyond the public UAE subset.

In our internal Emirati evaluation, Falcon-ASR achieved 22.73% WER and 10.19% CER:

Falcon-ASR has the lowest WER and CER among the systems compared here. Its WER is 4.07 percentage points below Qwen3-Omni, the next best result. The results show improved transcription accuracy at both the word and character level on this evaluation.

We included background noise, overlapping speech, music, room reverberation and telephony effects, as well as variations in speed and pitch. We applied the same treatment to Emirati recordings, exposing the model to a range of conditions it may encounter in meetings, calls and other everyday recordings.

Falcon-ASR also transcribes English with the same model weights. In our evaluation on the seven public English test sets used by the Hugging Face Open ASR Leaderboard, it achieved a mean WER of 5.74%.

The model also supports French, Spanish and Portuguese. All five languages use the same weights, without requiring a language flag. The output is a transcript in the language spoken.

Falcon-ASR builds on our Falcon3-Audio work. The architecture and training approach for Falcon3-Audio are described in Competitive Audio-Language Models with Data-Efficient Single-Stage Training on Public Data.

Our Hugging Face Demo Space lets you try Falcon-ASR and explore its transcription capabilities. API access and native applications are planned. We invite you to try the Demo with your own recordings.

We thank the team behind the Falcon-Emirati model for their support with Arabic foundation models. Read about their latest work in the Falcon-Emirati blog post.

We also extend our sincere thanks to Mikhail Lubinets for continued support with the compute infrastructure.

نقدّم Falcon-ASR، نموذجنا للتعرف على الكلام العربي بحجم 1.6 مليار معلمة، مع اهتمام خاص باللهجة الإماراتية. طوّرنا النموذج في معهد الابتكار التكنولوجي (TII) في أبوظبي، وهو يدعم أيضًا اللغات الإنجليزية والفرنسية والإسبانية والبرتغالية.

في تقييمنا، حقق Falcon-ASR متوسط معدل خطأ في الكلمات بلغ 20.92% عبر ست مجموعات اختبار باللغة العربية، مقارنةً بأفضل نتيجة منشورة بلغت 23.17% في نسخة لوحة المتصدرين التي استخدمناها. وفي تقييمنا الداخلي للهجة الإماراتية، سجّل النموذج أدنى معدلات خطأ في الكلمات والأحرف بين الأنظمة التي قارناها.

ندعم أيضاً الطوابع الزمنية على مستوى الكلمات في عمليات التفريغ النصي، بحيث ترتبط كل كلمة بموضعها في التسجيل الصوتي.

يختلف الكلام العربي باختلاف المنطقة والمتحدث وظروف التسجيل. فقد ينجح نموذج في تفريغ نشرة إخبارية رسمية، ثم يجد صعوبة في تفريغ محادثة باللهجة الإماراتية أو تسجيل عبر الهاتف. كما أن الموارد الصوتية المفرّغة نصيًا للهجات العربية أقل من تلك المتاحة للعربية الفصحى، مما يزيد صعوبة التدريب والتقييم.

درّبنا Falcon-ASR على اللهجة الإماراتية والعربية الفصحى ولهجات خليجية وعربية أخرى، إلى جانب الإنجليزية. وهدفنا هو تفريغ الكلمات التي يستخدمها الناس في حديثهم اليومي، بما في ذلك الصيغ اللهجية والانتقال بين اللغات.

ترتّب لوحة المتصدرين المفتوحة الشاملة للتعرف على الكلام العربي، التي يديرها مركز ELM للأبحاث، الأنظمة وفق متوسط معدل خطأ الكلمات عبر ست مجموعات اختبار، بوزن متساوٍ لكل مجموعة. وتعرض أيضًا معدل خطأ الأحرف (CER). وكلما انخفضت قيمة أي من المقياسين، كان الأداء أفضل. ويتبع تقييمنا للنموذج هذا البروتوكول.

WER هو معدل خطأ الكلمات؛ وCER هو معدل خطأ الأحرف. تشير القيمة الأقل إلى أداء أفضل.

قيّمنا Falcon-ASR على مجموعات الاختبار الست نفسها، باستخدام قوائم العينات المثبّتة في لوحة المتصدرين. وأرقام النماذج المنافسة هي المتوسطات المنشورة في اللوحة، والتي جرى التحقق منها في 30 سبتمبر 2026. وكان متوسط خطأ الكلمات للنموذج أفضل بمقدار 2.25 نقطة مئوية من أفضل نتيجة منشورة في تلك النسخة.

تتوافر بالفعل بيانات عامة لتقييم اللهجة الإماراتية، إذ تضم مجموعة Casablanca قسمًا خاصًا بالإمارات. ونكمّل هذه التغطية بتقييم داخلي لتسجيلات إضافية من الكلام الإماراتي والخليجي، باستخدام تسجيلات مخصّصة للاختبار ونصوص مرجعية خضعت لمراجعة بشرية، لتقييم دقة التفريغ على مواد إضافية إلى جانب البيانات الإماراتية العامة.

حقق Falcon-ASR في تقييمنا الإماراتي الداخلي معدل خطأ كلمات قدره 22.73٪ ومعدل خطأ أحرف قدره 10.19٪:

سجّل Falcon-ASR أقل معدل لخطأ الكلمات والأحرف بين الأنظمة المقارَنة هنا. وكان معدل خطأ الكلمات أقل بمقدار 4.07 نقطة مئوية من Qwen3-Omni، صاحب النتيجة التالية. وتُظهر النتائج تحسنًا في دقة التفريغ على مستوى الكلمات والأحرف في هذا التقييم.

ضمّنا بيانات التدريب ضوضاء خلفية وكلامًا متداخلًا وموسيقى وصدى الصوت وتأثيرات الاتصالات الهاتفية، إلى جانب تغيّرات في سرعة الكلام وحدّة الصوت. وطبّقنا المعالجة نفسها على التسجيلات الإماراتية، لتهيئة النموذج للتعامل مع ظروف مختلفة قد يواجهها في الاجتماعات والمكالمات والتسجيلات اليومية الأخرى.

يفرّغ Falcon-ASR الكلام الإنجليزي باستخدام أوزان النموذج نفسها. وفي تقييمنا على مجموعات الاختبار الإنجليزية العامة السبع المستخدمة في لوحة Hugging Face المفتوحة للتعرف على الكلام، بلغ متوسط معدل خطأ الكلمات 5.74٪.

يدعم النموذج أيضًا الفرنسية والإسبانية والبرتغالية. وتستخدم اللغات الخمس أوزانًا واحدة، دون الحاجة إلى تحديد اللغة مسبقًا. ويكون الناتج تفريغًا نصيًا باللغة المنطوقة.

يستند Falcon-ASR إلى أعمالنا في Falcon3-Audio. وتعرض ورقة Competitive Audio-Language Models with Data-Efficient Single-Stage Training on Public Data بنية Falcon3-Audio ونهج تدريبه.

يتيح عرضنا التجريبي على Hugging Face تجربة Falcon-ASR واستكشاف قدراته في تفريغ الكلام. أما الوصول عبر واجهة API والتطبيقات الأصلية فهو مخطّط له. ندعوكم إلى تجربة النموذج باستخدام تسجيلاتكم.

نتوجّه بجزيل الشكر إلى الفريق القائم على تطوير نموذج Falcon-Emirati على دعمهم في مجال النماذج التأسيسية للغة العربية. ويمكن الاطّلاع على أحدث أعمال الفريق من خلال المقال المنشور حول Falcon-Emirati.

كما نتقدّم بخالص الشكر والتقدير إلى Mikhail Lubinets على دعمه المستمر للبنية التحتية الحاسوبية.

#9649. Swapping Jolt's sorted collections to a B+tree

Until recently, sorted-map and sorted-set in Jolt were a straight port of Clojure's PersistentTreeMap, which is backed by a persistent red-black tree. Using a red-black tree has worked well for Clojure, and it provides a solid foundation for backing these data structures. However, red-black trees have a downside, which is that every entry gets its own small node, meaning that every step of a lookup follows a pointer to a different place in memory.

So, naturally I got curious to see if a different data structure could be used for the same job which might have a lower overhead. Turns out that a red-black tree can indeed be swapped out for a B+tree here. I updated Jolt's sorted collections along with the java.util.TreeMap and TreeSet shims to use a persistent B+tree, which dropped peak memory by 40% while making most operations faster at every size, as we'll see later in the benchmarks.

Each red-black node in Jolt was a five-slot Scheme vector holding a color along with the key, the value, and its two children. And all that translates into 48 bytes of metadata per entry on top of the key and value themselves. A map with 4 million entries needs a tree around 22 levels deep, so, a lookup can end up visiting about 22 nodes scattered across the heap. And once the tree outgrows the CPU cache, each of these visits is likely to be a cache miss as well.

As you might've guessed, writes also have a similar problem. Since a persistent tree can't modify a node in place, an assoc has to copy every node on the path from the root to the change, which results in 22 small allocations followed by rebalancing at that size.

The key advantage of using a B+tree is that it keeps data in leaves of up to 16 entries and branches through inner nodes of up to 32 children with each node being a single Scheme vector. In this layout, a leaf is written as #(#t k0 v0 k1 v1 ...) with keys and values sitting side by side in one contiguous block. An inner node also stores the largest key below it right next to each child.

Now, the same tree of 4 million entries becomes just 5 levels deep instead of 22. On top of that, a lookup within each node has to only search through adjacent slots that are already in cache. Writes still have to copy the path from the root, but that's now a quarter of the work with each one being copied as a block.

Unsurprisingly, memory use improved significantly, since a full leaf holds 16 entries in 34 machine words, needing only 17 bytes per entry against the red-black tree's 48. Nodes are also allowed to drop to half before they merge, so 34 bytes per entry ends up being the worst case here. It would be ideal to keep the common case near full as much as possible, and a trick that can be used here is to start a fresh node when append goes past either end of the tree rather than splitting a full node into two half-empty ones. A common case for this would be building from ascending keys, which ends up packing every node using this approach. Similarly, deletes end up borrowing entries from a neighbour or merging with it to keep the tree balanced without needing rotations.

Of course, nothing in life is free, and B+trees do have a weakness of their own. While they're much faster for large collections, building small ones of tens to hundreds of entries one insert at a time ended up being around 15% slower than the red-black tree. The reason goes back to the respective structure of each data structure. Once a map has 17 entries, that requires a root with two leaves, and every insert needs to copy the whole path. So, at smaller sizes the B+tree has to move more bytes per insert than the red-black tree, which is the trade-off.

Luckily, there is a way around the problem by changing how collections get built. We can first collect the inputs for into, the sorted-map and sorted-set constructors, and multi-argument conj/assoc to check whether they're already in order, then skip the sort if they are. Additionally, we can drop duplicate keys by keeping the first key along with the last value, which allows us to bulk-load the leaves. The batches can now get merged with the collection that already has entries. Meanwhile, small sources of 8 or fewer entries that go into an empty collection continue to use plain conj, because the overhead of buffering would end up costing more than it actually saves. With these changes in place, the worst remaining case ends up being a 4 entry map at 1.05x, which is effectively as good as a red-black tree.

So, now that we've discussed how B+trees work, and what makes them a good alternative to red-black trees in this scenario, let's look at some actual benchmark numbers comparing the two approaches. The numbers were measured using optimized binaries across several runs on an M1 Max with 64 GB. The JVM comparisons use Clojure 1.12.6 on OpenJDK 20. A ratio under 1.0 means the B+tree is faster.

Times are for the whole operation over the collection, which includes building it, doing a lookup for every key, removing every key, and replacing every value. Keys are also scrambled to avoid a degenerate sequential case.

As we can see, lookups win at every size, by 23 to 33%. Builds and writes stay flat below 64 entries. Notably, even a 4 entry map ends up being a single leaf searched in place, meaning that it doesn't pay for the extra machinery.

The reduce-kv result stands out because it's a result of a fix in the new layout. The original red-black tree code built a map entry for every pair going through the generic sequence path. Walking the leaves and passing each key/value pair straight to the function avoids having to allocate memory for each slot. And since the B+tree can seek to a key to start reading from that leaf without having to rebuild a stack of nodes from the root on every call, repeatedly taking the first element of a subseq gets faster as well.

From here on out we hit a cliff where the cache matters more than anything else.

While performance looked good for thousands of elements, it was also important to check what would happen with collections having millions of entries in order to make sure nothing broke or regressed badly at this scale. The following benchmark builds a sorted map and a sorted set from scrambled keys and then runs a mix of operations over them.

And the good news is that every operation at this scale is also faster than the previous version. Not only that, but Jolt is now faster than the JVM at building sets, walking, reducing, and range queries, while the two are roughly even on contains? and the map build. Finally, point lookups and deletes are still about 1.5x slower than the JVM, which uses a red-black tree backed PersistentTreeMap thanks to the magic of the highly optimized JIT that the JVM enjoys.

Peak resident memory for the 4M run nearly halved, going from 1.73 GB to 1.04 GB with the B+tree. It's worth noting that the process holds a 4M entry map with its 4M entry set, along with the garbage from building them. So, the numbers here reflect the whole program rather than just the trees themselves. And the JVM run peaked at 4 to 6 GB, but that's mostly an artifact of how the JVM collects garbage with its default settings, so we shouldn't read too much into that.

You might have noticed that the scrambled builds slow down sharply somewhere between 1M and 2M entries. The JVM also shows the same jump with its sort going from 16 to 93 ms. In both cases, the cause is that the working set ends up falling out of cache, making lookup more expensive.

As I mentioned earlier, Jolt's TreeMap and TreeSet shims are built on the sorted map. These were implemented using a naive approach where they went through it one generic operation at a time. Each put looked up the key and then inserted it, having to walk the tree twice, while navigation methods like floorKey built a subseq and took its first element.

Now, all of these operations have been updated to use the tree directly, meaning that a put or remove is one walk, while operations like floorKey are a single seek. The size of a bounded view can now be computed by adding up whole leaves and only scanning the two partial leaves at the edges. Times are for 20,000 operations.

That's 4 to 70 times faster than the original version, with headMap size beating the JVM, which needs to walk the view in order to count it. But the writes are still about 4x the JVM, and can't be closed with this design because the Java mutates its nodes in place, while Jolt's TreeMap is a mutable wrapper around a persistent tree. So, there's no way around each put having to copy about five nodes.

Iteration order, which key is kept on a duplicate, which value wins, the argument order passed to custom comparators, and returning the identical collection from a no-op assoc all work as they did before. But there is one thing that's different from the JVM, which stems from the layout of the trees. Building a 1,024 entry map from ascending keys now calls the comparator 1,023 times while the JVM's red-black tree calls it 12,301 times. So, code that counts comparator calls will see different numbers on Jolt.

What this exercise shows is the importance of the memory layout used by the backing data structure. All the operations do the same logical work as before, but they now have to touch about a fifth as many nodes with the data inside each node being contiguous.

Switching to use a B+tree was not a free win, though, since it required a separate batch build path to make the switch efficient for code that builds lots of medium-sized maps, which adds some complexity to the implementation. If you're making a similar kind of optimization, always be sure to measure the middle sizes along with the extremes.

#9648. The model that didn't exist, so you made it yourself

Last week, I wanted a small version of the prompt rewriter that ships with Qwen-Image 2.1. The official one is a 9B model that needs about 20 GB of memory and thinks for thousands of tokens before writing a single paragraph. On the Hub, I found only compressed copies of that same 9B model. So I described what I wanted to ML Intern, and the next day I had a 0.8B version that runs on a CPU. It returns valid output 99.7% of the time and uses about a quarter of the teacher's tokens. The compute for the whole project, including having the 9B model label 8,797 example requests, came to USD 16.

Over the course of the next few days, I made five more models the same way. Each one started as a message in HuggingChat with ML-intern switched on, and each one ended as a public model on the Hub with its evaluation in the model card. ML-intern plans the work, asks me for a budget before it spends anything, runs a small test before the real job, then trains, evaluates and publishes on Hugging Face hardware.

The first message is where I spend my effort. My first prompt, for the citrus model shared below, was about 450 words. By my 6th project it was closer to 2,000, because each project taught me something I wanted in the next one. All seven prompts are on GitHub at yvrjsharma/ml-intern-prompts, exactly as I wrote them.

A prompt starts with the idea in one line and why I want it. Then it names the exact pieces: the dataset, the base model, the training script. Anything I have already checked goes under a heading that literally says "Verified facts, do not re-derive", so the agent spends its budget on the work instead of rediscovering what I know. For the camera-angle LoRA that section listed which trainer had just added transparent-image support, and which open GitHub issues made the fallback trainer risky.

Two lines in the prompt are critical. The first asks for a baseline before any training. For example, the citrus prompt says: "Also report the base model's zero-shot score on the same metric before training so we can see the gain." Without it you get a trained model and no idea whether it is better than what you started with. The second is a smoke test with a check attached. For the image LoRAs I asked for 50 training steps, then a check that the saved weights had actually changed, before paying for the full run.

At the end of the prompt, I lay out the expected deliverables and limit the cost. I define what belongs in the model card and include a instruction like: "Cap total spend at USD 12 and ask me before exceeding it." Because ML-intern begins every task with zero dollar budget and needs permission before executing paid jobs, this spending limit stays strictly enforced. When you leave out a budget, the agent suggests a couple of paths depending on project size and asks which one you prefer.

You don't necessarily need all of that on your first attempt. For example, I didn't have the verified-facts section in my citrus brief and ML Intern still produced a model that more than tripled the accuracy of the Qwen3.5-2B model. Let me walk you through 6 things I built with Ml-Intern in just a couple of days.

A general vision model can describe a yellowing citrus leaf. However, telling you whether it is a mite problem or a magnesium deficiency, and the bio and non-bio remedies to treat the plant is very hard. Using Claude, I put together a training dataset merged from three sources hosted by the Project-AgML organization on the Hub. The resulting citrus-disease-vlm-instruct is a dataset containing 3,017 annotated images across 21 distinct pests, illnesses, nutritional gaps, and treatment approaches. ML-intern handled the fine-tuning of Qwen3.5-2B using these examples, making sure to benchmark the foundation model beforehand.

On the 335 test photos, the base model named the right problem 14.9% of the time. After two epochs on one A10G, the fine-tuned model got 52.8%. Compute cost, about USD 1.90.

Check out: Model · Dataset · Citrus Doctor App

Image models know plenty of characters. Huggy, drawn in the flat style of the Hugging Face brand assets, was not one of them. I asked ML-Intern for a LoRA on FLUX.2 klein base 4B, trained on 84 captioned drawings from Chunte/huggy_for_training dataset.

The agent saved a checkpoint every 100 steps and drew the same set of prompts with each one, which made choosing easy. Step 200 was the first where Huggy was fully on-model. From step 500 on, Huggy's style started bleeding into prompts that had nothing to do with Huggy! The trained LoRA also works on the distilled klein model at 4 steps. Compute cost, about USD 7.60.

Check out: Model · Dataset · Huggy Generator App

ML-intern rendered 1,030 scanned household objects from Google Scanned Objects at 24 angles each, 24,722 transparent images, on a CPU job that cost a few cents. It later finalised 461 objects for training and 40 held out for testing, and 1,844 before-and-after training pairs spread evenly over 23 camera instructions.

Training ran 2,000 steps in about 90 minutes on one A100 (~USD 3.75). The whole project took about half a day and 48 jobs, counting the ones that failed on missing packages or wrong paths and had to be resubmitted by ML-Intern. Total compute cost, about USD 16.

Check out: Model · Dataset · Viewpoint Orbit App

No dataset existed for this, so my prompt described how to make one. Start from a real photo in Open Images, remove one object with the LaMa inpainting model, and draw a scribble where the object used to be. The untouched photo is the target. ML-intern wrote and tested the pair-building scripts in a CPU sandbox, then ran them as GPU jobs, recording the author and license of every source photo along the way. It built 6,042 training pairs and a 160-pair test set, where 40 of the test pairs come from 23 object classes kept out of training entirely.

Before training, it measured the base model on its own and with the Viggle turbo LoRA, and checked that running edits in batches produced identical images, which made the evaluation cheaper. Training ran 2,000 steps in 1 hour 38 minutes on one A100 (~USD 4), and a comparison of the saved checkpoints on 48 test pairs picked step 500.

Paired with the Viggle turbo LoRA at 6 steps the LoRA performed really well. 67.5% of objects detected where they were drawn, at 4.7 seconds per edit. Objects from the 23 unseen classes landed as reliably as the rest (65.0% versus 64.2%). The project took a little over a day and 59 jobs. Total compute cost, about USD 24.

Check out: Model · Dataset · Doodle-in App

Training the 0.8B and 2B students took 12 and 18 minutes on an A10G (USD 0.75 for both). The 0.8B also ships as an 812 MB GGUF file for running on a CPU. The project took about 11 hours and 24 jobs. Total compute cost, about USD 16.

Check out: Pocket rewriter 0.8B Student · 2B Student · Dataset · Pocket Studio App · Compare the teacher-student in Rewriter Arena

It took two runs. The first cached 155,000 training images as latents, baked the guidance into the model, then cut the step count in stages from 16 to 8 to 4, all on A100s. The 4-step student beat the teacher run at the same 4 steps on GenEval and FID, after that ML-intern exported it to ONNX for the browser. This run took about 13 hours and USD 22.

I did a second training run by asking ML-Intern to improve the 4-step student a bit more. It then made 24,000 more image pairs with the teacher at 16 steps and fine-tuned the 4-step student against them for about an hour. GenEval went from 0.509 to 0.536, against the teacher's 0.563 at 50 steps, with just 4 steps (one-fourth the compute). ML-intern re-exported the browser version. The second run took about 8 hours. Total compute cost across both runs, about USD 37.

Check out: Agate 4-step model · Dataset · Run Agate in your browser · Agate 4-step LIVE

These are the GPU and CPU job charges reported for each session.

ML-intern is in HuggingChat. Switch on ML-intern mode and paste a prompt. If you want a starting point, my example prompts are free to copy. Start from a model you wish existed and a dataset you have, or one you can describe. Give it a small budget, ask for a baseline and a smoke test, and read what comes back before you raise the cap.

If you make something with it, share it on X and tag @Gradio and @HuggingFace. We would love to see the models you make that nobody else would think to build for you.

#9647. UQ researchers send an unblockable message using gravity

Professor Matthew Davis, Dr Charles Woffinden and Professor Andrew White inside the elevator they used to send a message.

(Photo credit: The University of Queensland. )

University of Queensland researchers have used gravity to transmit a message through a brick wall using an elevator and a sensitive gravimeter.

The unusual experiment took place in UQ’s Parnell Building, where the team of physicists sent the elevator back and forth between 2 levels, moving its 1.8-tonne counterweight between positions representing binary 0 and 1.

A gravimeter in an adjacent bathroom detected the changes in the gravitational field and translated the message into a single word, ‘Gravity’.

Dr Charles Woffinden from the School of Mathematics and Physics said gravitational communication had an intriguing advantage.

“Unlike the electromagnetic signals used in modern wireless communication, a gravitational signal cannot simply be screened out by placing ordinary material in its path,” Dr Woffinden said.

“Anyone who has lost phone reception in a tunnel or struggled with Wi-Fi through a solid wall will understand the appeal.

“While the present system is far from practical, it demonstrates the possibility of communicating using a method that ordinary physical barriers cannot block.”

Dr Andrew Groszek said the idea came from a project to develop a contactless weighbridge.

“We were aiming to determine the mass of trucks and other large vehicles by measuring their tiny gravitational pull,” Dr Groszek said.

“Once we had shown that the idea worked, we realised the same physics could be used to encode and transmit information.”

Professor Andrew White said the biggest limitation to future gravity-based communication was its slow speed.

“Our lift was snail-paced – it’s from the 1950s – so our experiment transmitted just 1 bit per minute, meaning it took an hour to send a single word,” Professor White said.

“The speed of gravity communication would come down to how big the mass is, how fast you can move it and the sensitivity of the detector.

“It took more than 100 years to go from the first telegraph system to the mobile phone, so while gravity communication is not practical today, it could be in the future.”

A gravimeter in an adjacent bathroom detected the changes in the gravitational field from the elevator's movement and translated the message.

(Photo credit: The University of Queensland.)

Professor Matthew Davis said the UQ team had established an important underlying principle.

“It’s not often that you get to demonstrate an entirely new way of communicating,” Professor Davis said.

“We have shown experimentally that information can be encoded in the gravitational field and recovered at the other end.

“Our experiment used a classical gravity sensor, but our modelling indicates that quantum sensors could, with rather ambitious assumptions, support ranges of up to about 500 metres and data rates of around 15 bits per minute.”

Such sensors could eventually support communication in environments where radio waves, light and other conventional signals cannot penetrate.

Read the research published in Science Advances.

#9646. Run fast, private agents on-device with LFM2.5-24B-A2B

LFM2.5-24B-A2B is a 24B-parameter reasoning model with just 2B active parameters, built for fast, private agents on-device. It thinks before it answers, calls tools, and works through multi-step tasks inside popular agent harnesses. Because only 2B parameters are active per token, each reasoning token is cheap, so you can run agents continuously on your own hardware.

LFM2.5-24B-A2B builds on LFM2-24B-A2B and keeps its architecture: 40 layers, 64 experts per MoE block with top-4 routing, and the same hybrid of gated short convolutions and GQA. The context window grows from 32K to 131K tokens, and an in-place tokenizer expansion doubles the vocabulary from 65K to 128K tokens for better non-Latin tokenization. Unlike its predecessor, it is a reasoning-only model that produces an explicit chain of thought before its final answer.

Pre-training was scaled up from ~17T to ~33T tokens. Mid-training then adds 2T tokens at 32K context, weighted toward reasoning, math, code, instruction following, and multilingual text, and 300B tokens at 131K context, weighted toward long-context data. Tool calls and multi-turn trajectories appear throughout both phases. Post-training turns the base model into an agent in five stages:

We evaluated LFM2.5-24B-A2B against Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, Gemma-4-26B-A4B-it, and Nemotron-3.5-Lightning on 16 benchmarks covering tool use and agentic workflows, knowledge, instruction following, math, and coding. It is the smallest model in the group, yet it is competitive with MoEs with ~50% more total and active parameters.

*All the models were evaluated with vLLM, using each benchmark's recommended generation parameters.

For your app, the strengths are tool use and instruction following. LFM2.5-24B-A2B leads or matches the competition on five of the eight tool-use and agentic benchmarks (AutomationBench, BFCLv4, ToolSandbox, LiveClaw, and τ³-Bench Banking), and on AutomationBench it scores more than three times the next-best model. It also leads on all three instruction-following benchmarks. Larger models keep an edge on knowledge-heavy benchmarks like GPQA Diamond, HLE, and AA-Omniscience, and on coding benchmarks like SWE-Bench Verified (OpenCode) and SciCode, so pair LFM2.5-24B-A2B with retrieval or web search for knowledge-heavy workloads.

These results make LFM2.5-24B-A2B a strong foundation for agents that need to reason, call tools, and run reliably on your device.

LFM2.5-24B-A2B ships with day-one support across the inference ecosystem, including llama.cpp, MLX, vLLM, SGLang, and ONNX.

Edge inference. LFM2.5-24B-A2B is the fastest of the compared MoEs, decoding 184 tokens/s on an M5 Max and 114 tokens/s on a Ryzen AI Max+ 395. That is up to 1.7x faster than the next-best model, while using the least memory.

GPU inference. LFM2.5-24B-A2B is the fastest model in its size class, reaching over 21K output tokens per second at high concurrency on a single B300.

Reach for LFM2.5-24B-A2B when you need agents that reason, call tools, and run reliably on your device.

InfoQ Homepage News QCon San Francisco 2026: The Harness Is the New Operating System

Nov 22, 2026 4 min read

At QCon San Francisco 2026, Manju Rajashekhar, founder and CEO of Mad Labs, opened the conference with the keynote "The Harness Is the New Operating System."

Rajashekhar argued that the harness around an AI model, rather than the model itself, decides what an agent can do and how safely it does it. Each part of a harness, the keynote proposed, maps onto a job that operating systems already perform.

Rajashekhar began with a split that shaped computing history. Applications encoded behavior, while operating systems abstracted the hardware beneath them, and that separation made portable, composable software possible.

AI agents break that arrangement because they generate behavior at runtime. Software therefore needs a new layer that makes that behavior useful, reliable and repeatable, and Rajashekhar called that layer the harness.

In Rajashekhar's framing, model plus harness equals agent, and the harness is "everything in an agent that isn't the model." It supplies the tasks, context, tools, state, permissions, feedback loops and a definition of done.

The simplest agent is a model running in a loop that the harness controls. But "a loop isn't enough. Every iteration has to count," and Rajashekhar described four parts of the loop that make each iteration count.

Context works like virtual memory. The harness assembles what the model needs for its next decision inside the hard limit of the context window, and the advice was to "give the model a pointer, not the whole thing."

The interface works like system calls and "puts a ceiling on the agent's effective capability." Rajashekhar pointed to the SWE-agent paper, in which GPT-4 Turbo resolved 11.0% of SWE-bench Lite issues through a plain shell and 18.0% through an interface designed for agents.

Execution works like processes and permissions. The harness enforces boundaries through isolation and scoped credentials, such as a test database with no production access, because "instructions guide. Boundaries enforce."

Feedback works like return codes. The harness keeps "tests failed," "could not run" and "outcome unknown" apart, so the model does not have to guess what happened.

That matters because errors compound. On a 20-step task with a 95% chance of each step going right, the whole job succeeds 36% of the time, and catching 80% of errors lifts that to 82%.

When an agent goes in circles, Rajashekhar said, most engineers swap the model. A better first step is to keep the model and change the harness.

DeepSeek's model card for DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash reports the same model scoring from 65.5% to 74.2% on DeepSWE across eight harnesses. The minimal harnesses scored highest, which Rajashekhar read as a sign that more harness is not automatically better.

In a second study, Qwen3.8-27B passed 66.8% of 100 hard LiveCodeBench problems with a single call. Inside a manager-worker scaffold with a shared ledger, it passed 92.4%.

Rajashekhar made a related point on LinkedIn earlier this year. Frontier models are forgiving, the post said, while "open-weight models are less forgiving. They make you think deeply about the harness and how it aligns to the model."

The harness also determines what an agent is allowed to affect. Rajashekhar contrasted an agent that fixes failing tests with one that deletes the tests so they pass, observing that "the difference isn't ability. It's authority."

The example offered was the July 2026 incident in which OpenAI evaluation agents on a capture-the-flag benchmark reached the internet through an open code sandbox. They held admin access on Hugging Face's internal clusters for about two and a half days.

Human approval alone is a weak gate, Rajashekhar argued, citing Anthropic's work on Claude Code auto mode, which InfoQ covered in May. People approve the large majority of permission prompts, and "a tired gatekeeper is a rubber stamp."

The keynote extended a talk Rajashekhar gave at QCon AI Boston 2026. That talk argued that production agents "are just distributed systems in disguise" and proposed the actor model as their runtime.

In the Boston design, each agent task owns its state, receives events through a mailbox, writes each state change to a durable store and runs under a supervisor. The talk closed with a variation on Greenspun's tenth rule, suggesting that any sufficiently complicated agent loop contains half of an actor system.

The San Francisco keynote widened the lens from the runtime to everything the model sees, calls and runs inside. Rajashekhar brings a systems background to that question, having led caching systems on Twitter's early engineering team, which open-sourced twemproxy.

The talk arrives as "harness" has become the common term for everything around the model. Thoughtworks Distinguished Engineer Birgitta Böckeler described it in a February memo as covering "the tooling and practices we can use to keep AI agents in check."

Rajashekhar closed on why a harness design is never finished. Every component "encodes an assumption about what the model can't do," and those assumptions expire as models improve.

Anthropic's harness for long-running apps needed context resets because Claude Sonnet 4.5 showed "context anxiety" near its context limit. That behavior largely disappeared with Opus 4.5, as InfoQ reported in April.

The reverse also holds. LangChain moved checks the model kept skipping into the harness and lifted GPT-5.2-Codex from 52.8% to 66.5% on Terminal-Bench 2.0 without changing the model.

Rajashekhar asked attendees to open an agent they already use and read its system prompt and tool list. Then, on a task where it struggles, change one part of the loop and rerun what already worked.

Developers interested in learning more can watch InfoQ in the coming weeks for video of the keynote and can view the keynote abstract and resources here.

#9644. Navigating Vulnerability Hysteria in the AI Era

Cybersecurity In-Depth: Feature articles on security strategy, latest trends, and people to know.

This installment of the Reporters' Notebook video series examines the fallout from recent high-severity flaw disclosures, exploring how fears of AI-assisted exploits trigger widespread panic, operational disruptions, and growing warning fatigue.

The pressure on cybersecurity teams to patch critical vulnerabilities is reaching a boiling point, exacerbated by incessant coverage and rapid-fire disclosures of AI-discovered bugs. Last month it was PHP2Shell. This week it's Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938), a 9.2 CVSS flaw in OpenJDK's Base64 decoder unearthed in just one hour using OpenAI's Codex by Calif Research, and NGINX2Root (CVE-2026-123007), a 9.2 CVSS critical integer underflow vulnerability affecting nginx HTTP/2 discovered by Rapid7 MDR.

In the latest installment of the monthly Reporters' Notebook video series, TechTarget Cybersecurity's Alissa Irei, Cybersecurity Dive's David Jones, and Dark Reading's Fahmida Y. Rashid discussthe PHP2Shell vulnerability and examine whether the industry is falling victim to communal panic.

PHP2Shell refers to two critical PHP vulnerabilities — CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 — discovered by Calif (the same company that found Java4Shell) and rated 9.2 on the CVSS scale. Caused by out-of-memory corruption and stale global state errors, the flaws enable unauthenticated remote attackers to execute arbitrary code on Web servers without requiring credentials or prior access. Following a rocky, coordinated disclosure process marked by accidental leaks on X, many organizations preemptively pulled websites and critical services offline, fearing that threat actors leveraging artificial intelligence (AI) would rapidly launch automated attacks before Web servers and applications could be patched.

Related:NIST Enrichment Reductions Impact CVE Coverage, Accuracy

However, the anticipated wave of machine-speed exploits failed to immediately materialize during "Black October," raising questions about whether extreme preemptive shutdowns do more harm than good. While AI accelerates vulnerability discovery, complex exploit paths, hardware dependencies, and flawed proof-of-concept code mean that severe flaws do not automatically lead to immediate compromises, even when attackers use AI. Constantly shuttering operations or broadcasting catastrophes can create early-warning fatigue, akin to ignored national weather alerts, leaving organizations numb when a genuine emergency strikes.

A similar wave of urgency surrounds Java4Shell, where researchers demonstrated unauthenticated remote code execution in widely deployed enterprise tools like Keycloak and Jenkins, prompting CISA to call for immediate patching. However, Java4Shell does not have a universal exploit, meaning attackers must consider each application's memory layout and timing, how Base64 is used, and take application-dependent steps to exploit it.

Related:Java4Shell Flaw Threatens Global Enterprises, Java Application Ecosystem

A CISO's primary responsibility is not to unilaterally order costly operational shutdowns or carry sole accountability for business risk, but to clearly communicate technical and operational risks to executive leadership equipped to weigh security threats against business continuity. Staying calm, focusing on risk-based prioritization, and adhering to core security fundamentals remain the most effective defenses against modern threats.

Learn more in the video, and also check out other Reporters' Notebook episodes, available here, for insights and coverage from across Informa TechTarget's network of cybersecurity sister sites.

This transcript has been edited for clarity, readability, and length by Informa TechTarget's internal AI assistant and human editors. For the full experience, please watch the video.

Dark Reading's Fahmida Y. Rashid: Hi, and welcome to this month's installment of Reporters' Notebook, featuring reporters from Dark Reading, TechTarget Cybersecurity, and Cybersecurity Dive. I'm Fahmida Rashid, editor-in-chief of Dark Reading. This month, we are going to be talking about scary security vulnerabilities and the lessons we should take about how they're disclosed. So, joining me are Alyssa and Dave.

Related:Major Brazilian Signature Apps Enable RCE & Fraud

Why don't you introduce yourself quickly before we start the topic?

TechTarget Cybersecurity's Alissa Irei: Sure. I'm Alissa Irei, senior reporter with TechTarget, covering cybersecurity news.

Cybersecurity Dive's David Jones: David Jones. I'm a reporter at Cybersecurity Dive

DR's Fahmida Y. Rashid: All right, let's get started. We had what researchers have been calling PHP2Shell, which were essentially two security vulnerabilities found in some versions of PHP. In some software, using PHP is pretty serious. We're talking memory corruption, the ability to run code on a Web server without logging in.NNNNNNNNNN

We know it was serious and pretty scary because, on the CVSS score, it was a 9.2 out of 10. That's pretty big news. And whenever you tell anyone that by exploiting vulnerabilities, an attacker will be able to run their code on the Web server without logging in, it gets people worried. I believe the patches were out. There was a whole coordinated disclosure.

TTC's Alissa Irei: This struck me as a pretty big deal. Our colleague James Walker wrote a couple of articles on the vulnerabilities themselves and also the disclosure process, which I believe got a little bit rocky in terms of accidental early disclosures on X, and then there was a lot of racing to patch and companies taking their websites down. But yeah, PHP is in use, in, I think, 70% of the world's websites.

Anything that enables remote code execution seems like a really big deal to me. So, I thought it was noteworthy. I know, Dave, your take seems to be a little bit "this meeting could have been an email." Maybe when all is said and done, it was somewhat overblown.

CD's David Jones: I thought it was absolute chaos. I'm still trying to understand exactly what happened last month because the initial rollout of the patch, the disclosure, as you mentioned, was more than a little rocky and the hype around the entire situation in terms of what was actually at risk. That was kind of a bit of a moving target.

We've had situations in the past where there's a lot of concern that you're going to have what is considered systemic risk on such a global scale that large institutions will not be able to manage that risk in a timely manner. Obviously, there are a couple of factors that kind of played into this.

One was the fact that AI was involved in the discovery. With the fact that malicious actors are able to exploit vulnerabilities faster than they ever have been before. There's a great deal of concern in terms of are you able to address these vulnerabilities in a fast-enough method to get those patched, tested, and verified before malicious actors have a chance to attack them? I think what we saw last month was just a lot of preemptive action where major institutions all over the world were basically preemptively taking their sites offline because they had no way of triaging the potential fallout in time to properly address whether or not they were fully protected.

It's still a bit of a mystery to me exactly what happened, whether there was an initial overreaction, whether there were elements of the exploit that we just didn't understand. There was a lot of bad code in a lot of the proofs of concept, and it just never quite amounted to the emergency that it was set up to be.

Maybe it was a good exercise. But we're still trying to get to the bottom of exactly what took place and how we can avoid some of the exaggerated threat that we saw.

DR's Fahmida Y. Rashid: You brought up two really important things that I want to make sure we dig into. The first one was, there was a bit of a fear that because the adversaries have AI, we don't know how fast they're going to be able to launch an attack. And I think that was the reason for some of this panic … you know, take down the website so that we have time to figure it out.

With Log4j, what was it, three days before we started seeing proofs of concept? And I think there was this sense that we don't have those three days anymore. I think, Dave, you make a really good point that maybe this was a good exercise. Maybe we now know that at least for now, it will not be the same day. We're not going to see an attack the day we see the vulnerability.

TTC's Alissa Irei: Well, the tricky thing about that, though, is can we say that? Because AI can move so quickly, it can also move much more slowly than we anticipate. But is today the day? I do think that there's a big question mark around, you know, sophisticated machine-speed AI-enabled attacks that we're not seeing yet. But also, you don't want to be the organization that is the Wikipedia entry for the big one.

DR's Fahmida Y. Rashid: Yes. That's true. But I definitely do think that part of that entire response was driven with we don't know when those attacks were coming. But, Dave, you also noted a second point which I thought was really interesting. That even with AI, the exploit path was a lot more complicated to exploit. I think we've always said in our beat that just because there is a vulnerability, just because there is a way to exploit, does not mean it will automatically be exploited. Sometimes the process to do it is hard, and not all attackers are going to take that harder route. And I think this was an example.

CD's David Jones: I think, you know, in a way it's good that we're thinking about how we respond to these types of things. Maybe we're better prepared, but at the same time, I think we don't want to get into a situation where we're crying wolf ahead of time. And at the end of the day, what actually happened?

Was Black October deserved? I mean, was it really that bad a month? Because I've seen worse.

TTC's Alissa Irei: It's a good point. It reminds me of, you know, national disaster weather warnings. At some point, if you go through enough of them and nothing much happens, people become inclined to ignore them. And at some point, that can be quite dangerous. So, I think it's a fair point.

Do you think that this sort of … I think we used the word hysteria in a previous conversation, communal hysteria, if you will. Do you think that this is specific to the AI age? It has this tendency to overreact. Has it grown in the age of AI and given us our fears about adversarial AI, or do you think that this is a pre-existing tendency that we as an industry have?

CD's David Jones: When you're a security team, particularly a security team with limited resources, you can't respond to every critical flaw or even medium- or high-severity flaw.

Whenever you want to, the resource is not there. You have to prioritize; you have to make decisions about the vulnerabilities that are going to affect the most critical technology.

Can I take the proper steps to either slow this process down or stop it before it gets out of control and I lose control over exactly how my operation continues? Because you have certain businesses where you may be operating in an OT environment where you can't afford to shut down for a certain amount of time. You may be running a hospital; you might be running a factory. You might be running fuel through a pipeline. You can't necessarily afford to be offline for a certain amount of time.

It's a difficult thing. I mean, there are probably a lot of organizations that were basically shut down for a certain amount of time, and they lost money, they lost time, they lost productivity. I don't think we can do that each and every time there's a critical situation.

DR's Fahmida Y. Rashid: That's actually the one thing that occurred to me, when Web people were like, we need to take the site down while we figure things out. And I was like, just a couple of weeks prior, we had people taking down their Citrix boxes because there was a vulnerability and we didn't know what was going on. We don't know what's going on, so turn it off. And to Dave's point, we can't turn everything off. So, it's getting to be a priority, but to also understand when something is so bad that it is a turning-off incident. Because I'm worried that we're kind of moving into this state of turning it off every time, and that's just not practical.

DR's Fahmida Y. Rashid: One thing I want to make sure we get a chance to talk about, and I love that Dave mentioned Log4j, because I think it's one of the biggest concerns. So, with Log4j, as a refresher for everyone, it was a vulnerability in a logging framework used by Java applications. And the challenge was that it's used in all sorts of different applications. And so, you could be like, nope, I looked, but I don't have Log4j, not realizing your suppliers were using it. And I think there was a bit of a worry that this might be the same, where I might not be using it, but I don't know who else is.

Which I think is a very legitimate concern. You need to know not just what you have, what your suppliers have, what your partners have. And I think that was the one aspect of PHP2Shell that kind of got a little obscure. That entire concept of thinking broader and bigger is something that really reminded me with this one that vulnerabilities are not just in your stuff; they're in other people's stuff too.

TTC's Alissa Irei: I think it's a great point. And I do worry about the smaller open source projects that have one or two maintainers, and it seems like everyone is drowning in vulnerabilities these days. And what does that mean for teams that are barely teams, and what does that mean for the software supply chain? I think it's a legitimate worry.

CD's David Jones: I'm not sure that a CISO or a frontline security operations team has the authority to take anything out of service without having a conversation higher up the food chain. I mean, you've got to be in a situation where … let's say there's an emergency, you've got to have people kind of above your pay grade where you have conversations where, yeah, we're not going to be producing food for the next few days, maybe. Or we've got to stop these surgeries if you're in a hospital system. The nuclear plant is not going to be, you know, cooling down for maybe a few hours. You've got to have this thought out in terms of, OK, can you explain to somebody who may not be a trained engineer, who may not be versed in these various systems, why you have to move forward and disrupt the entire business operation for a certain amount of time, because if you let it continue, and let's say somebody gets into your IT environment or your OT environment, and you may not be able to see them.

Are you willing to take that risk? Are you going to be held responsible for taking that risk? And who's going to be the C-suite person or the operational leader whoever makes that call that's going to say, "Yeah, go ahead and pull the plug"?

TTC's Alissa Irei: It's a good reminder that ultimately a CISO's job in some of these cases is communicating risk, not deciding how to manage the risk. Because if I'm a CISO, I wouldn't want to be making that decision about shutting down a hospital or a nuclear power plant. It becomes about being able to quickly and accurately communicate the operational risk to someone who is paid to make those decisions.

DR's Fahmida Y. Rashid: We're increasingly seeing situations where the CISO is the one left holding the bag. So yeah, it's definitely a bigger calculation. To Alyssa's point, communicate it; make sure everyone understands what this means so that it's an informed decision.

TTC's Alissa Irei: Actually, this makes me think of two comments that have come up in recent conversations. One was with an analyst who said the CISO's job is and has always been to manage risk to the best of their ability and then take the blame when things go wrong. And she was very clear that that has not changed in the age of AI; it is the continuation of a pattern.

You know, debatable, but on some days I'm sure that feels true if you're a CISO. Another conversation I had recently was about CISO risk and the need for … I think there's some growing murmurs in the CISO community about the need to push back on the risk that is not actually security's bag to hold and be a little bit more vocal and clear about offloading some of that risk to people who are really better equipped and paid to hold it.

DR's Fahmida Y. Rashid: I think overall it's worth saying that yes, this is serious, yes, this is huge, here's a priority list. But you know what? Maybe it is the time to be a little bit contrarian.

Dave, what would you say is the one lesson you want our listeners, our readers, to be taking away?

CD's David Jones: Well, I guess the question I would have is: Are you prepared and properly set up to address such a situation the next time it happens, because it might happen over Thanksgiving.

Let's agree that AI has the ability to find critical flaws that might take a human team days, weeks, or months to find.

There are state actors and sophisticated criminal actors that can get access to an AI-assisted or automated attack. Find out how to best attack a vulnerability. That could happen within the space of days or hours.

You can't have a team on standby 24/7 all the time responding to every alarm that goes off. It's not cost-effective. It's unrealistic. But to be fair, you have to be prepared to respond to that in some way.

DR's Fahmida Y. Rashid: Definitely. Alissa, what would you say yours would be?

TTC's Alissa Irei: Mine is much broader and much less useful.

I think I saw it on a tea towel somewhere, but stay calm and look for signs. I think that's what I'm trying to do. I don't really have a good handle on where this is going next. I don't know that anybody does. So, it seems like that's the best that any security team can do. You know, focus on risk, focus on potential impact and prioritizing actions based on that. And in the meantime, to Dave's point, we'll try to avoid communal hysteria and do what we can do when we can do it, as fast as we can do it, and as smartly as we can do it. And I think that's all anybody can ask because, you know, we've never been here before.

DR's Fahmida Y. Rashid: My thought was kind of similar to yours, that the fundamentals still matter. Know what you're securing, keep an eye on how you're working, you know, keeping an eye on your alerts. Yes, everything is a little new because we're now kind of in this age of, you know, things are being found more complicated, faster, but it's still the fundamentals, right? We need to know what we have so that we can secure it quickly and efficiently communicate it. To Dave's point, let's hope that we don't have these kinds of disastrous months every single month because I don't think we're going to be able to keep up with that volume

So, I'm going to say thank you so much for joining me for this month's Reporters' Notebook. I hope you enjoyed the conversation as much as I did. And see you next month.

Fahmida Y. Rashid is an award-winning B2B cybersecurity journalist with over two decades of experience covering enterprise technology. As editor-in-chief, she leads Dark Reading's editorial strategy. She breaks down news events and industry trends to demystify security technology for IT professionals, cybersecurity practitioners, and business managers. She takes an interdisciplinary approach to explain security concepts through the lens of psychology and economics. She also analyzes data to uncover insights to help CISOs do their jobs.

In her reporting and writing, she focuses on the following areas: application security; cloud, network, and infrastructure security; identity and access management; third-party and supply chain risk; governance and compliance; and cybersecurity data analytics.

Past leadership roles include Executive Editor at VentureBeat, where she led the newsroom's transition to focus editorially on AI and data technologies; co-founder of the cybersecurity magazine Decipher; and serving as founding editor-in-chief of the RSAC Conference. Her work has appeared in various business and tech trade publications, including CSO Online, InfoWorld, and eWEEK. She also reviewed networking technologies as an analyst at CRN Test Center and PCMag. She began her career writing financial briefs at Women's Wear Daily.

Before becoming a journalist, she spent over 10 years as an IT professional and has experience as a network administrator, database administrator, software developer, management consultant, and product manager.

#9643. Most Frequently Asked Questions About NFTs(Non-Fungible Tokens)

Non-fungible tokens (NFTs) are the most popular digital assets today, capturing the attention of cryptocurrency investors, whales and people from around the world. People find it amazing that some users spend thousands or millions of dollars on a single NFT-based image of a monkey or other token, but you can simply take a screenshot for free. So here we share some freuently asked question about NFTs.

NFT stands for non-fungible  token, which is a cryptographic token on a blockchain with unique identification codes that distinguish it from other tokens. NFTs are unique and not interchangeable, which means no two NFTs are the same. NFTs can be a unique artwork, GIF, Images, videos, Audio album. in-game items, collectibles etc.

A blockchain is a distributed digital ledger that allows for the secure storage of data. By recording any kind of information—such as bank account transactions, the ownership of Non-Fungible Tokens (NFTs), or Decentralized Finance (DeFi) smart contracts—in one place, and distributing it to many different computers, blockchains ensure that data can’t be manipulated without everyone in the system being aware.

The value of an NFT comes from its ability to be traded freely and securely on the blockchain, which is not possible with other current digital ownership solutionsThe NFT points to its location on the blockchain, but doesn’t necessarily contain the digital property. For example, if you replace one bitcoin with another, you will still have the same thing. If you buy a non-fungible item, such as a movie ticket, it is impossible to replace it with any other movie ticket because each ticket is unique to a specific time and place.

One of the unique characteristics of non-fungible tokens (NFTs) is that they can be tokenised to create a digital certificate of ownership that can be bought, sold and traded on the blockchain.

As with crypto-currency, records of who owns what are stored on a ledger that is maintained by thousands of computers around the world. These records can’t be forged because the whole system operates on an open-source network.

NFTs also contain smart contracts—small computer programs that run on the blockchain—that give the artist, for example, a cut of any future sale of the token.

Non-fungible tokens (NFTs) aren't cryptocurrencies, but they do use blockchain technology. Many NFTs are based on Ethereum, where the blockchain serves as a ledger for all the transactions related to said NFT and the properties it represents.5) How to make an NFT?

Anyone can create an NFT. All you need is a digital wallet, some ethereum tokens and a connection to an NFT marketplace where you’ll be able to upload and sell your creations

When you purchase a stock in NFT, that purchase is recorded on the blockchain—the bitcoin ledger of transactions—and that entry acts as your proof of ownership.

The value of an NFT varies a lot based on the digital asset up for grabs. People use NFTs to trade and sell digital art, so when creating an NFT, you should consider the popularity of your digital artwork along with historical statistics.

In the year 2021, a digital artist called Pak created an artwork called The Merge. It was sold on the Nifty Gateway NFT market for $91.8 million.

Non-fungible tokens can be used in investment opportunities. One can purchase an NFT and resell it at a profit. Certain NFT marketplaces let sellers of NFTs keep a percentage of the profits from sales of the assets they create.

Many people want to buy NFTs because it lets them support the arts and own something cool from their favorite musicians, brands, and celebrities. NFTs also give artists an opportunity to program in continual royalties if someone buys their work. Galleries see this as a way to reach new buyers interested in art.

There are many places to buy digital assets, like opensea and their policies vary. On top shot, for instance, you sign up for a waitlist that can be thousands of people long. When a digital asset goes on sale, you are occasionally chosen to purchase it.

To mint an NFT token, you must pay some amount of gas fee to process the transaction on the Etherum blockchain, but you can mint your NFT on a different blockchain called Polygon to avoid paying gas fees. This option is available on OpenSea and this simply denotes that your NFT will only be able to trade using Polygon's blockchain and not Etherum's blockchain. Mintable allows you to mint NFTs for free without paying any gas fees.

The answer is no. Non-Fungible Tokens are minted on the blockchain using cryptocurrencies such as Etherum, Solana, Polygon, and so on. Once a Non-Fungible Token is minted, the transaction is recorded on the blockchain and the contract or license is awarded to whoever has that Non-Fungible Token in their wallet.

You can sell your work and creations by attaching a license to it on the blockchain, where its ownership can be transferred. This lets you get exposure without losing full ownership of your work. Some of the most successful projects include Cryptopunks, Bored Ape Yatch Club NFTs, SandBox, World of Women and so on. These NFT projects have gained popularity globally and are owned by celebrities and other successful entrepreneurs. Owning one of these NFTs gives you an automatic ticket to exclusive business meetings and life-changing connections.

#9642. Welcome FLUX.3 Image Klein in Diffusers

Black Forest Labs FLUX.3 Image Klein is here, and it runs in Diffusers from day one. One model does text-to-image and multi-reference image-to-image, and it adds something new, the layout control. You write bounding boxes into the prompt to say where each part of the image should go, or which parts of a reference image to move.

Both open checkpoints are in the FLUX.3 Image Klein collection:

You can head on to the Hugging Face space and generate some images right now!

Install the latest diffusers and transformers (for the Qwen3-VL text encoder):

Load the distilled checkpoint and generate an image:

FLUX.3 responds best to a full scene description with the subject, the setting, the light, the composition, and the style. The official prompting guide from Black Forest Labs has more tips. The distilled checkpoint generates a 1024 × 1024 image in 16 steps by default. Pass height, width, or num_inference_steps to change them.

Pass a reference image (or more) with the image argument. Write the prompt as a caption of the image you want, with the change included.

With several references, refer to them in the prompt as , , ... in the order they are passed to image:

Add a JSON list of regions after the caption. Each region has an id, a bbox, and a desc, and the caption mentions it as .

Boxes are written as [y_min, x_min, y_max, x_max], y first, on a 0–1000 scale. Because the scale is normalized, the same box works at any image size.

For edits, each region says where its content comes from (src_bbox in the reference) and where it goes (tgt_bbox in the output). A region with the same two boxes stays where it is.

This example moves the knitted knight up and to the left, and pins the backdrop, the cliff, the needle, the dragon, and the fire:

Everything above uses the distilled checkpoint. The base checkpoint runs 50 steps with classifier-free guidance, and it's the one to fine-tune (see LoRA finetuning).

Black Forest Labs also ships the transformer as a single file, in bf16 and in two quantized formats: fp8r (rowwise FP8) and nvfp4. Load any of them with from_single_file, then load the other components by name so the bf16 transformer isn't downloaded too.

For the unquantized single file, use https://huggingface.co/{model_id}/blob/main/model.safetensors and drop quantization_config.

FLUX.3 works for both text-to-image and image-to-image, which makes it a great base for custom LoRAs. diffusers ships DreamBooth LoRA training scripts for both tasks (you can also train with Ostris' AI Toolkit).

Here is a text-to-image example that learns a tarot-card style from the multimodalart/1920-raider-waite-tarot-public-domain dataset, triggered with trtcrd:

To reduce memory usage, add a few optimization flags:

--gradient_checkpointing recomputes activations in the backward pass (lower VRAM, slightly slower), --cache_latents pre-encodes the images and frees the VAE, and --use_8bit_adam keeps the optimizer states in 8-bit.

A couple of knobs are worth experimenting with. The grid below trains the same tarot style with different LoRA ranks and optimizers; the adapters are on the Hub at diffusers-modular/flux3-tarot-lora. More training features and configurations are documented in the DreamBooth FLUX.3 README.

For instruction-based editing, the image-to-image script (train_dreambooth_lora_flux3_klein_img2img.py) trains on (reference image, target image, instruction) triplets, where the reference is addressed in the prompt as .

See the DreamBooth FLUX.3 README for all options and the full image-to-image example.

In this section, we will talk about the memory consumption and the speed of generation of the models.

End-to-end timings for the distilled checkpoint (16 steps), averaged over three runs after a warmup:

Single NVIDIA H100 80GB, no offloading, default attention backend.

A reference image roughly doubles the time. Reference tokens join the same sequence as the text and the image being generated, so a 1024 × 1024 reference adds 4,096 tokens to every transformer call

Let's open the model up, one piece at a time. The model takes three kinds of tokens:

FLUX.3 is a latent-space flow model for image generation. This means that the denoiser takes latents as inputs and produces latents as outputs. We use a VAE to decode the latents back to pixels. FLUX.3 uses the same VAE architecture as Flux.2.

The FLUX.2 VAE compresses an image 8× in each direction into 32 channels, and then every 2 × 2 patch of that latent is packed into a single token with 128 channels.

So one token covers a 16 × 16 pixel patch, and a 1024 × 1024 image becomes a 64 × 64 grid of 4,096 tokens. The noisy image starts as random noise of exactly that shape. A reference image goes through the same VAE encoder and packing, and keeps its own size.

The text encoder is Qwen3-VL, a vision-language model. FLUX.3 doesn't just take its last layer. It reads the hidden states of eight of its 36 layers (layers 4, 8, …, 32) and stacks them, so each text token becomes a 8 × 2560 = 20,480-dimensional vector before a linear layer projects it to the transformer's width of 3072.

This gives the transformer features from several depths of the language model, not just its final layer. The prompt is padded to a multiple of 80 tokens, and the transformer attends to the padding too, which is why the pipeline takes one prompt per call.

The transformer processes the tokens in two stages:

The two stages differ in who can attend to whom.

In stage 1, each stream only attends to itself, so each kind of token gets refined on its own terms first. In stage 2, everything attends to everything, where the image learns from the text and from the references. For comparison, FLUX.2's double-stream blocks also give text and image separate weights, but let them attend to each other from the start. FLUX.3 keeps the streams fully apart first, then merges them.

At the end, the text and reference tokens are simply dropped. Only the image tokens go through the output layers, which predict how to move them one step toward a clean image.

Every block, in either stage, has the same shape. Attention and the MLP run in parallel on the same normalized input, and their sum is added back to the residual stream.

Each block starts with a LayerNorm that has no learned scale or shift of its own. The scale, shift, and gate come from a timestep embedding instead (this is called modulation). Inside the attention, the queries and keys are RMS-normalized and get rotary position embeddings (RoPE), which we look at below.

In a joint block, all tokens share the same weights, but text, image, and reference tokens each get their own scale, shift, and gate.

In FLUX.1 and FLUX.2, one timestep embedding modulates every token. In FLUX.3, the modulation depends on the kind of token.

The noisy image tokens are modulated by the current timestep t. The text and reference tokens are always modulated by timestep 0, which means "clean, nothing to denoise here". So even a reference that looks almost the same as the output is marked as given context, not as something to generate.

The distilled checkpoint is a flow map. It is also told the timestep each step jumps to. That second timestep gets its own embedding, which is added to every token's modulation, so each of its 16 steps can make a larger jump.

Attention on its own doesn't know where a token is (this phenomenon is called permutation equivariance). RoPE fixes that by rotating each query and key by an amount that depends on the token's position. FLUX.3 uses four position axes, (t, h, w, l) (timestep, height, width, length of sequence), and gives each one a quarter (32 dimensions) of every 128-dimensional attention head:

Text tokens line up along l, like words in a sentence. The image and the references are 2D grids in (h, w), separated from each other along l. Because a reference uses the same (h, w) coordinates as the output, "the same spot in the reference" has a precise meaning to the model, which is what the src_bbox / tgt_bbox editing relies on.

FLUX.3 is a flow-matching model. Generation starts from pure noise, and at each of the 50 steps the transformer predicts a velocity. This is the direction from noise toward a clean image. The scheduler takes one step along it.

At every step you can also read off the model's current guess of the final image. Decoding that guess at a few steps shows how the image takes shape:

The fox, its pose, and the light are already in place by step 10, while the noise level is still 0.97. The snow-laden branches and the texture of the fur only appear in the last few steps. FLUX.3's scheduler uses a large time shift (6.93), which keeps the noise level high for most of the run: 44 of the 50 steps happen above σ = 0.5. We built this figure by adding one small block to the pipeline, which brings us to Modular Diffusers.

If you are new to flow matching, we have a beginner friendly tutorial and a video for you to understand how it works.

FLUX.3 ships as a Modular Diffusers pipeline.

You can list the workflows and print the exact blocks of each one, without loading any weights.

get_workflow() resolves the auto branches and gives you the plain sequence of steps that will run. print(blocks.get_workflow("image_conditioned").doc) prints the components, inputs, defaults, and outputs of that workflow.

Pop the text encoder out, encode the prompt once, free it, and generate from the cached embeddings.

The denoising figure above came from one extra block that records the model's guess of the clean image at every step:

Built something with FLUX.3? Share your LoRAs and pipelines on the Hub. We'd love to see them! 😎
