InfoQ Homepage News Claude Code Adds Experimental Code Mode to Orchestrate Tool Calls with JavaScript

Nov 23, 2026 3 min read

Anthropic has added Code Mode to Claude Code, an experimental feature in which the model writes JavaScript to drive its tools instead of requesting each Bash, Read, or Edit call separately. Code Mode is off by default, requires Claude Code v2.1.323 or later, and is enabled with the CLAUDE_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_CODE_MODE=1 environment variable. Anthropic warns it may change or be removed in any release.

In a normal session, Claude asks for one tool call, reads the full result, and decides the next step. In Code Mode, one script can run commands in parallel, pass one result into the next call, and return only the output the model needs. The documentation's example finds a file with rg, raises a retry limit, runs the tests, and returns just the path and test output. The conversation still shows each tool call and diff, while the generated code sits in the transcript viewer. Anthropic recommends it for edits repeated across many files, searches that need filtering, and independent commands. Code that Claude waits on stops after ten minutes; sessions started in auto or bypassPermissions mode can push it to the background for up to two hours while the conversation continues.

The permission model is the part architects should read first. Each call inside a script still goes through deny and ask rules and PreToolUse hooks, but in auto mode the classifier reviews the script before it runs, not each call, and cannot see values computed at run time. A git push can now reach a hook as cd 'app' && git push, so hooks must check every part of a command; a hook matching the REPL tool can read the JavaScript from tool_input.code. Project settings cannot enable Code Mode, so a cloned repository cannot switch it on, and administrators can block it through managed settings.

Code Mode runs only in interactive terminal sessions of the native build, on Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, Haiku 5.5, or Fable 5.2, through a Claude subscription or Console account. It does not work with -p, the Agent SDK, the VS Code panel, the Desktop app, Amazon Bedrock, gateways, or zero-data-retention organizations. Agent teams need v2.1.326. Anthropic has published no token or latency figures for it.

George (@bolyki) compared Code Mode with normal mode across eight interactive Sonnet 5.5 runs and posted:

Same results every time. Context 20-25% smaller. On the bigger task: 37% fewer tokens, 19% lower cost. But it is not faster, and on a tiny task it cost more.

Ravi Madabhushi, who builds agent auth infrastructure, pushed back on claims that the feature makes MCP obsolete:

It doesn't materially change anything wrt authentication, authorization and audit policy layers; Your agent still makes those same MCP calls, with the same auth tokens and context and what materially changes is how much context gets into the model window and how much can be discarded.

The idea, and the name, predate Anthropic's release. Cloudflare introduced Code Mode for MCP converting MCP tools into a TypeScript API that models code against inside sandboxed Workers, where bindings keep API keys away from generated code. Anthropic's own post on code execution with MCP described one workflow dropping from 150,000 to 2,000 tokens, and the Claude API offers programmatic tool calling in a remote code execution container. Code Mode instead runs the script in the developer's local session, against Claude Code's built-in tools and permission system.

Code Mode remains opt-in and experimental, and Anthropic collects feedback through /feedback. Setup steps and troubleshooting are in the Claude Code documentation

#9635. TorchNeuron: running HF models on AWS Trainium is easier than ever

TorchNeuron provides a new native backend for PyTorch on AWS Trainium. Transformers, Diffusers and Kernels natively support it, making it easier than ever to run models on Trainium and to share them on the HF hub.

TorchNeuron is a PyTorch plugin that brings a new backend for Trainium enabling support for eager mode, torch.compile and native distributed APIs like FSDP and TP. Read the Pytorch blog to learn more about TorchNeuron.

Starting Oct. 20, 2026, TorchNeuron will be available as a public beta. Researchers and developers will be able to install it with pip install torch-neuronx.

To date, the Hugging Face experience on AWS Trainium and Inferentia — AI chips designed respectively for cost-effective training and inference at scale — has been delivered through optimum-neuron. This library relies on the torch-neuronx package, which is based on PyTorch XLA. It was the natural choice at the time, but it meant thinking like a compiler: lazy tensors instead of eager execution, static shapes only, a recompilation for every graph break. Optimum Neuron existed to hide that complexity, and maintained custom code (modeling classes, trainers, etc) to do so.

TorchNeuron changes this. It integrates directly into PyTorch and exposes neuron as a native device, with eager execution, PyTorch's own distributed primitives (DTensor, FSDP2) and torch.compile.

For the Hugging Face libraries, Trainium becomes a device like any other: Transformers, Diffusers, Accelerate, PEFT and TRL run on it directly, with the same classes and scripts you would use on any other accelerator. From now on, we recommend that Neuron users use these libraries directly instead of going through Optimum Neuron.

Text generation is now natively supported in Transformers for a wide range of models. With TorchNeuron, 89% of the top 100 most-used text-generation model architectures are supported out of the box, compared to 46% with Optimum Neuron v0.4.5. You just need to pass the device_map=neuron argument in your code and your model will be moved to the Neuron devices.

The following is an example of text-generation with tensor parallelism, which will enable to fully benefit from your Neuron instance. Note that it uses a static cache for generation as this is strongly recommended with Neuron to prevent frequent recompilations.

Now that Neuron is a native PyTorch device, training on Trainium uses the same Hugging Face libraries as any other accelerator: Transformers, Accelerate, PEFT and TRL. You no longer need a dedicated trainer or a Neuron-specific fork of the model code. A standard TRL fine-tuning script runs on a Trainium instance with only a few Neuron-specific settings.

Here is a supervised fine-tuning script built on TRL's SFTTrainer. If you have fine-tuned a model with TRL on GPUs before, it should look familiar.

Parallelism is handled natively by Transformers. You put a DistributedConfig with the tensor-parallel (TP) and FSDP sizes in model_init_kwargs, SFTTrainer passes it to from_pretrained, and the model is sharded as its weights are loaded. The Trainer sees that the model is already distributed and does not wrap it again. You don't need an --fsdp flag or an Accelerate FSDP config.

Nothing in the script is tied to Trainium: the same code runs on any hardware. A few things are worth knowing when you run it on Trainium:

The command below launches training with torchrun, which starts one process per NeuronCore. TP_SIZE and FSDP_SIZE set the parallelism layout, and their product is the number of processes: here 4 x 8 = 32, matching --nproc_per_node. The 32 processes form a 4 x 8 grid. Tensor parallelism splits each layer across the 4 cores of a TP group, and FSDP shards the parameters, gradients and optimizer state across the 8 TP groups.

We ran it on 8 Trainium2 chips (32 NeuronCores), which is half a trn2.48xlarge instance.

Training runs to completion, and trainer.save_model writes a standard Transformers checkpoint. Nothing in it is tied to Neuron: you can push it to the Hugging Face Hub as is and load it on any other hardware.

Many pipelines from the Diffusers library are compatible with TorchNeuron in eager and compiled mode. FLUX.1-dev, FLUX.2, Qwen-Image, Qwen-Image-2.1 and H3 are also compatible with tensor parallelism to make the most of your Neuron devices. The following is an example showing how you can use TP:

You can run this piece of code with: NEURON_LOGICAL_NC_CONFIG=2 torchrun --nproc_per_node=8 run.py.

More and more pipleines will be compatible with TP. If a pipeline you like is not, you can also add support for it following this guide.

Make sure to check out the kernels from the Neuron team as more and more Neuron kernels will become available on the Hub to speed up your models. Neuron kernels can be written using the Neuron Kernel Interface (NKI), which gives lower control to optimize operations. This way, users can run their own custom operations and share them on the hub.

You can use for example this kernel to speed up your vision transformers with up to a x2.4 speedup on Trainium!

Special thanks to the AWS team for their work on TorchNeuron and for their reactivity to our feedback to make the HF integration as good as possible.

hi, which models are supported with this? is mobernbert and t5gemma2 on the list?

Hi, we now have a space where you can chek if a model is supported: https://huggingface.co/spaces/aws-neuron/torch-neuronx-model-support

#9634. Sneakernet

NOTICE: Sneakernet is a work in progress. The documentation makes some promises that are not reflected in the current state of affairs. Links to to-be-written parts of the documentation are indicated in red.

Sneakernet is a system for securely1 sending digital messages to other people without using the Internet. Instead, messages are automatically passed on to other Sneakernet users on your local network – at your hackerspace, an event or conference, your local cafe, etc — and then physically carried to their destination on your “sneakers”, where they will be automatically delivered to any recipients on the same network (or handed over to be carried further on by someone else).

Sneakernet encourages slow, thoughtful participation in community and face-to-face meetings with the users who will carry your messages onwards to their destination, and entrust their own messages to you.

⇒ Head to Getting started to set up Sneakernet on your device.

Many applications can be built on top of sneakernet’s general-purpose messaging system, provided that they are tolerant of high latency and out-of-order messages. Some examples include:

Building your own sneakernet applications is easy, too, in any programming language – see Building applications for more details.

All messages are authenticated and all private messages are also encrypted. People who carry your messages along cannot tamper with them and cannot read your private messages. See Security for more details.

#9633. Critical PHP Flaws Allow Code Execution, but Don't Panic 'PHP2Shell'-Style

November's monthly security release patches seven critical PHP flaws that should be addressed ASAP, though experts say exploitability varies and depends heavily on configuration.

The PHP team has released a new security update that fixes a wide swath of vulnerabilities and issues, but compared with last month's PHP2Shell chaos, it's harder to pin down how much these bugs will appeal to attackers.

That's because, according to PHP's maintainers, the seven issues rated "critical" in the latest monthly security update "require either non-default configuration or uncommon setups." The update, published Nov. 19, affects all supported versions of PHP, and maintainers strongly encourage users to upgrade promptly.

This latest update comes on the heels of threat actors targeting PHP2Shell — a pair of vulnerabilities (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619) capable of remote code execution (RCE) in PHP — en masse. PHP is an open source scripting language common in Web development and present in much of the server infrastructure keeping the Internet afloat. Given PHP's ubiquity, the rush to patch created a fervor across the security industry hardly seen since Log4Shell in 2021.

Related:Cursor Traces Malicious Claude Code Extensions to Third-Party Breach

PHP versions 8.2 through 8.5 now have patches available through the project's downloads page, in the form of 8.2.36, 8.3.37, 8.4.28, and 8.5.13. 8.6.0; the latest major release of PHP also launched today with fixes included.

Of the dozens of issues accounted for in the changelog, the seven marked critical (CVSS 9.2) on GitHub were: session serializer mismatch RCE flaw CVE-2026-115560; use-after-free via repopulation of last_fatal_error_backtrace global after shutdown flaw CVE-2026-129182; time zone cache use-after-free RCE vulnerability CVE-2026-129496; use-after-free after interrupted session shutdown bug CVE-2026-129481; use-after-free in magic method backtraces RCE bug CVE-2026-129474; PHP-FPM request smuggling through an unread HTTP request body bug CVE-2026-129289; and PHP file-based session handler RCE vulnerability CVE-2026-126714.

While maintainers included workarounds in most critical advisories (barring CVE-2026-115560), they're considered temporary mitigations, and users should upgrade as soon as they can.

Justin Moore, director of adversary operations at Arctic Wolf, tells Dark Reading that two challenges organizations will run into when patching these issues are business continuity for servers running critical functions and visibility.

"A lot of organizations don’t have a complete inventory of where PHP is running, especially with legacy applications, internally developed Web services, managed hosting environments, or third-party software. It's baked into CMS platforms, hosting control panels, vendor appliances, and old internal apps," he says. "When a vulnerability is disclosed, the primary challenge is identifying every aspect of the business that is affected. The reality is that Internet-facing PHP systems should move toward the front of the patch queue because attackers have repeatedly demonstrated an interest in rapidly exploiting PHP vulnerabilities when a path to code execution exists."

Related:Grok Bots Attempt to Access Corporate Data Without User Approval

Among the critical flaws, there are some that experts recommend focusing on first. According to Upwind, which published an analysis of the security release, PHP-FPM bug CVE-2026-129289 is the one to close first, because it "gives an unauthenticated attacker PHP code execution with a single request," with no memory corruption, gadget chain, or race required to exploit. Although Upwind assesses it's the most direct route to code execution, "It does need a front end that reuses FastCGI connections and an application path that opens php://input without reading it to the end."

Upwind also noted that three of the vulnerabilities address gaps introduced by the PHP2Shell fixes last month. "PHP ties CVE-2026-129481 and CVE-2026-129182 to cases the October fix for CVE-2026-109619 did not cover," according to the analysis. "A third, CVE-2026-129474, became remotely reachable through a change introduced in 8.5.12."

Related:F-Secure Identifies 26 Ways AI Can Harm Consumers, and Where to Stop Them

All three depend on specific configurations and versions. CVE-2026-129474 and CVE-2026-129182 are only applicable to PHP 8.5, while CVE-2026-129481 excludes PHP 8.2. CVE-2026-129474 and CVE-2026-129182 both rely on PHP 8.5's fatal error backtrace engine feature, which was introduced with that version; for CVE-2026-129481, the session cleanup behavior it exploits was introduced in PHP 8.3.

Finally, among the other recommendations the analysis makes, one broader tip may ring true for a wide range of PHP-using organizations: "Don't forget container images and appliances that bundle their own PHP build. They need a rebuild or a vendor update."

Meanwhile, WatchTowr's Jake Knott tells Dark Reading that CVE-2026-115560, CVE-2026-126714, and CVE-2026-129289 are the ones the firm expects attackers to go after first.

In any case, while not the same level of emergency as seen last month, users should absolutely apply this latest update as soon as they can.

Just because a vulnerability is rated critical does not necessarily mean it applies to all organizations equally or that threat actors will target each issue like the PHP2Shell bugs last month.

Knott, who is WatchTowr's head of threat intelligence, says organizations must consider factors such as how a vulnerability is exploited and how likely real-world exploitation is. And more specifically, whether that organization uses the affected configurations or meets the prerequisites for exploitation. Only then can one determine where attackers have a viable path and how defenders can prioritize securing their environments.

He says the best place to start is with three questions. First, how is PHP being run (be it PHP-FPM, Apache mod_php, php-cgi, or something else)? Second, how are sessions configured, and is session upload progress enabled? And third, what settings is PHP running with, and where are errors being logged?

"Organizations should absolutely take these vulnerabilities seriously, and many of the other critical and high-rated vulnerabilities from this week," Knott says. "There is a stark difference in business-as-usual accelerated patching in response to a critical vulnerability, and panic driven by trivially exploitable default configuration vulnerabilities that typically carry the product2shell monikers, which these aren't."

He adds, "Answers to these questions will quickly rule out many of these vulnerabilities and let organizations patch prioritized sets of assets from a position of understanding and actual risk."

Alex is an award-winning writer, journalist, and podcast host based in Boston. After cutting his teeth writing for independent gaming publications as a teenager, he graduated from Emerson College in 2016 with a Bachelor of Science in journalism. He has previously been published on VentureFizz, Search Security, Nintendo World Report, and elsewhere.

At Dark Reading, he covers a variety of cybersecurity topics, including the cybercrime ecosystem, open source security, and the intersection between AI and threat actors. In his spare time, Alex hosts the weekly Nintendo podcast, "Talk Nintendo Podcast," and works on personal writing projects, including two previously self-published science fiction novels.

He has received numerous awards, including TechTarget's Writer of the Year in 2022 as well as more than 10 Azbee awards for his reporting between 2022 and today.

#9632. MPS in PyTorch 2.15

If you run models on your Mac or use MPS as your primary acceleration tool for computing, there's plenty to look forward to in PyTorch 2.15! FP8 arrives on MPS, language-model decoding gets faster paths through linear layers and softmax and new Metal kernels tackle some surprisingly expensive parts of audio, video and training workloads.

A quick word about who we are: we're the PyTorch team at Hugging Face. We contribute across PyTorch, and one of our focus areas is the MPS backend, where the goal is to make your Mac a first-class place to run and train PyTorch models. At the start of 2026, running even small models on MPS often meant working around unsupported operations, performance cliffs and unexpected memory growth. So we run real models from the Hugging Face Hub across language, image and video, find where MPS falls short and fix it upstream in PyTorch, more and more often by replacing MPSGraph with dedicated Metal kernels. Much of this post is the result of that work, done together with the PyTorch maintainers and community contributors.

If you run models on a Mac with transformers, diffusers or tools like ComfyUI, here's what 2.15 changes in practice:

You'll need an Apple silicon Mac with macOS 15 or later and Python 3.11 or later (see the 2.15 compatibility matrix). If your OS is too old or no Metal GPU is available, the MPS availability check now tells you why.

To try the release candidate in a separate environment:

FP8 gives you another way to save memory on your Mac. PyTorch 2.15 adds torch.float8_e4m3fn tensors on MPS: one byte per value, half the storage of FP16 or BF16.

You can multiply these tensors with F.scaled_mm, which supports both tensorwise and rowwise scaling. Here's a small example with one scale per tensor:

Every LLM has a prefill phase and a decode phase. During decode, each new token goes through the model as a single row, so the big matrix multiplications turn into matrix-vector products. PyTorch 2.15 speeds up both kinds of layers that dominate this step: dense linear layers and mixture-of-experts layers.

MPS has had GEMV kernels for torch.mm since 2.14, but F.linear still went through MPSGraph. PyTorch 2.15 connects them to F.linear, so the common [1, 1, hidden_size] decoding input uses them directly, with eligible bias additions fused in. Across 96 BF16 layer shapes from real models, that's a 1.23× geometric-mean speedup. The biggest wins land on small projections, such as the gates in MoE models, where the old path left most of the memory bandwidth unused. Large layers and LM heads were already close to bandwidth-bound, so they stay near 1×.

A mixture-of-experts layer sends different numbers of tokens to each expert. Grouped matmul handles those uneven groups in a single operation, and 2.15 gives MPS a native implementation.

In 2.14, grouped matmul copied the group offsets to the CPU and looped over the groups. The new Metal kernels read the offsets directly on the GPU, using Metal Performance Primitives where available and a separate Metal path elsewhere. Small groups, the common case during decoding, get their own kernel as well.

For example, 64 tokens can be split into groups of 16, 32, and 16:

The decoding kernel shows up directly in token throughput. On an M3 Ultra with torch.compile, MoE models generate about 1.3× more tokens per second:

Working with complex tensors gets easier. complex64 LU factorization, LU solve and triangular solve now run on MPS, which also unlocks the operations and gradients built on them, such as complex determinants. Here's a small system solved directly on the GPU:

Small matrices get fast kernels too. For camera geometry and image transformations, batches of FP32 matrices up to 4 × 4 are inverted in a single Metal kernel that combines factorization and solving. Larger problems get attention as well: QR uses blocked updates, and triangular solves turn much of their work into efficient matrix multiplication.

Gated DeltaNet workloads get a dedicated fast path for batches of 16 × 16, 32 × 32 and 64 × 64 FP32 triangular systems with at least eight right-hand sides.

SVD is also more robust at numerical extremes. It now correctly handles very small singular values, very large or very small input magnitudes and basis completion with full_matrices=True, which in turn makes pseudoinverse and least-squares results more reliable.

Audio models, video decoders and training loops have their own expensive operations. This release gives several of them new paths through Metal:

Token sampling gets faster in 2.15 as well. softmax and log_softmax now run on dedicated Metal kernels, and large vocabularies benefit the most: an FP32 softmax over a [1, 128256] row of logits drops from 57 µs to 7 µs, about 8× faster than the MPSGraph version. The speedup holds across other common vocabulary sizes:

One of the most striking results in this release comes from the constant-padding change. The VAE decode in Wan-AI/Wan2.2-TI2V-5B-Diffusers makes 8,764 padding calls over a full 28-tile decode. With padding on Metal, peak driver memory drops from about 270 GiB to 8 GiB:

You can now pick which MPS stream runs your work, directly from Python. torch.mps.Stream and the torch.mps.stream context manager provide the interface, and Tensor.record_stream lets the allocator track a tensor's use on another stream.

Here's a small example that sends work to a separate stream and synchronizes before reading the result:

Several more operations now run on MPS: torch.frexp, torch.logspace, torch.take and Tensor.put_, torch.heaviside, torch.special.laguerre_polynomial_l and unsigned-integer comparisons. logspace doesn't yet support integer or boolean outputs with more than one element.

Attention gets a correctness fix too: the MPS math implementation of scaled dot-product attention now handles batch and head broadcasting correctly.

Work on 2.16 is already well underway. Some of the changes below have landed on main and are available in the nightlies; others are still in review, so details may change before the release.

Once a model's decode path no longer contains any MPSGraph ops, the GPU only starts on a token after the CPU has finished encoding all of its kernels. PyTorch 2.16 commits the command buffer every 16 kernels, so the GPU gets to work while the CPU is still encoding the rest. For compiled BF16 decoding at a 2048-token context:

Scaled dot-product attention is dropping MPSGraph completely: every shape will run on Metal kernels, with dedicated vector kernels for decoding and Metal Performance Primitives for half-precision prefill on newer macOS versions. The shapes that used to fall back to MPSGraph benefit the most. On an M5 Pro, decoding with grouped-query attention (32 query heads, 8 KV heads, head dim 80, 4K context) drops from 465 µs to 65 µs, and a 4K × 4K prefill with head dim 40 goes from 42 ms to 6 ms.

The move away from MPSGraph continues. Batch norm forward and backward are in progress, while MSE loss (up to 12× faster on small inputs), std_mean and var_mean (up to 4× faster) and bincount have already landed. bincount is the most dramatic: when most values fall into a single bin, counting 4 million integers used to take 6.8 seconds and now takes half a millisecond.

Bundled shaders will build for Metal 3.1 by default, with Metal 4 versions compiled only for the kernels that need them. That shrinks libtorch_cpu.dylib by about 25%, from 384 MiB to 287 MiB, and lays the groundwork for Metal 4.1 shaders with faster matmuls and native FP8 matrix multiplication.

PyTorch 2.15 brings FP8 to the Mac, faster LLM decoding for dense and MoE models, more linear algebra on the GPU and a long list of operations moved from MPSGraph to dedicated Metal kernels. Give the release candidate a try!

A big thank you to Nikita Shulga, Kurt Mohler and Aaron Gokaslan for reviewing much of this work, and to everyone who contributed to MPS in this release.

#9631. AnyLanguageModel 1.0: One Year of Local Models on Apple Platforms

Last November, we introduced AnyLanguageModel on this blog: a drop-in replacement for Apple's Foundation Models framework that lets you choose the model and provider your app uses. We heard from app developers who were curious about local models but weren't always sure how to get started. They also wanted to avoid the added complexity of supporting multiple inference providers. AnyLanguageModel grew out of that feedback.

Local and hosted inference each have their strengths, and both have a role in building this new generation of intelligent apps. A shared API makes it easier to choose the right model for each task.

A year and dozens of releases later, AnyLanguageModel 1.0 is out, along with swift-huggingface 1.0 and swift-xet 1.0.

The core idea of AnyLanguageModel remains the same: use the Foundation Models API with the model that fits your app. To get started, change your import statement:

The same session code then works with the system model, with open-weight models through llama.cpp, MLX, and Core ML, and with the hosted providers below.

Over the past year, we've added several major features:

On OS 27, AnyLanguageModel also works with any model that conforms to Foundation Models' LanguageModel protocol, including Core AI models.

Alongside AnyLanguageModel, we've built out swift-huggingface and swift-xet to bring accelerated model downloads from the Hub to Swift apps.

Support for hosted models expanded this year, too. AnyLanguageModel now supports:

With Inference Providers, you can use open-weight models that are too big to run on the device with the same session code:

Hosted providers get the same features as local models: guided generation, tool calling with streaming, and token usage on responses.

Reasoning is now part of the transcript too. When you switch providers, reasoning blocks are automatically omitted from requests if the new provider can't replay them.

API keys come from a closure instead of a string, so your app can fetch short-lived tokens from your own server. The README explains when to let people bring their own keys and when to route requests through a proxy.

AnyLanguageModel also runs on Linux, so the same code can work on a server.

While we've made local models easier to use, the models themselves have become more capable, making the small ones a good place to start. Here are some of the most downloaded models on the Hub right now:

The first two fit on an iPhone, and Qwen3.8 27B runs on a Mac with 32 GB of memory or more. Selecting the MLX model takes one line:

And if you have four maxed-out Mac Studios handy, GLM-5.3 from Z.ai takes about 1.5 TB in BF16. For the rest of us, it's available through Inference Providers.

If you're upgrading an existing app, see the migration guidance in the AnyLanguageModel, swift-huggingface, and swift-xet release notes for help updating your code.

Community feedback and contributions have shaped several of our major features. Thank you to everyone who contributed for helping make AnyLanguageModel more useful to app developers.

Language models have proven to be a powerful tool for building intelligence into products. They're also one of many kinds of models developers can put to work. We're excited to bring the same approach to more capabilities: familiar Swift APIs with a choice of models running on the device. Coming soon: models that decide, and models that listen.

#9630. GitHub Actions accepts invalid YAML

TL;DR: GitHub Actions accepts several invalid YAML productions, making it difficult (read: impossible) to parse some real-world action and workflow definitions with a properly conforming YAML parser.

This is related to zizmor#1116, which has been bugging me for a year and a half.

Last April, a user reported that zizmor was rejecting a workflow containing a step that looks like this:

Apart from the use of a multi-line flow-style string for the json: key, nothing particularly stands out about this step.

Except: it isn't valid YAML! YAML says this about flow-style nodes that are nested inside of a block-style parent collection (read: map or array):

Flow nodes must be indented by at least one more space than the parent block collection. Note that flow nodes may begin on a following line.

That means the correct syntax is instead:

YAML is a big and complicated spec, so it didn't even occur to me that this was invalid. Instead, I opened tree-sitter-yaml#36 to "fix" it. I've now opened tree-sitter-yaml#51 to revert that misbegotten fix.

On GitHub's side, I'm not sure if they have a clean path towards spec conformance here. Much of the code behind Actions is proprietary, but it seems likely that the underlying parser on their end is YamlDotNet.

Actions appears to use YamlDotNet 5.3.0, which was released in 2018. However, even upgrading to the newest version (18.1.0 as of writing) wouldn't fix this particular bug, since it's still present on that version (note the !isSingleQuoted guard).

My best guess is that a 2020 patch (YamlDotNet#467) only fixed the double-quoted form because YAML's official test suite only tests rule 8.2.3 with a double-quoted string, despite it applying to both forms.

InfoQ Homepage News Agoda Reduces API Code Review Time by 64% with Modular Architecture

Nov 23, 2026 2 min read

Agoda has introduced a modular monolith framework in its post-booking API to reduce code coupling and enforce domain boundaries without rewriting the existing service. The approach combines component-based code organization, automated architecture checks, and incremental migration. The team reported 64% shorter median code review time and 34% shorter time to initial substantive feedback for framework-backed changes compared with legacy code.

The change addresses growing maintenance challenges in BAPI, which coordinates cancellations, booking amendments, refunds, and customer communications. Agoda extracted the API from its aging core monolith in 2019 through a largely line-by-line migration. As development increased, merge requests more than quadrupled between 2022 and 2025, while some files exceeded 4,000 lines.

The team characterized the migration as a tactical design trade-off, drawing on John K. Ousterhout's A Philosophy of Software Design,

We had deliberately traded a strategic design approach for a tactical one to prioritize speed to market. This tactical mindset was exactly what the business needed at the time.

Rather than undertake a complete rewrite, the team introduced architectural boundaries incrementally.

The framework, called Platform, organizes code around business domains such as cancellations, rebooking, and payments rather than technical layers. Each component encapsulates its business logic and data access behind defined interfaces, with application, service, repository, and model layers contained within the component. This package-by-component approach aims to localize changes and reduce dependencies between business domains.

Platform framework boundaries inside a domain module (Source: Agoda Blog Post)

Agoda uses the Data Mapper pattern to keep repository-specific models, including database entities and API payloads, out of business logic. Typed builders centralize object creation and transformations, making it easier for developers to find where domain objects and service inputs are constructed.

The team also uses ArchUnit to encode architectural constraints as automated tests in continuous integration. For example, repository-specific models can only be accessed by their respective repositories. Violations fail the build rather than relying on code reviewers to identify unauthorized dependencies manually.

The team described these constraints as architectural fitness functions, a concept discussed by Neal Ford and Mark Richards in Software Architecture: The Hard Parts. One engineer explained:

By codifying our layer boundaries into an ArchUnit test suite, our CI pipeline serves as an automated guardrail, catching structural drift on every pull request before a human reviewer ever sees it.

Platform is now the default for new modules, while existing functionality is migrated incrementally when feature development provides an opportunity.

Agoda compared framework-backed and legacy merge requests in Q2 2026. Median review completion time was 1.08 hours for framework-backed changes, compared with 3.02 hours for legacy changes. Time to first substantive feedback was 10.34 hours versus 15.77 hours. Between June and August, framework-backed changes also used 29% fewer AI prompts per 100 changed lines, although median prompts per merge request were similar (20 vs. 22). Agoda cautioned that the AI findings were directional due to the short observation period. A related approach is Spring Modulith, which provides module verification and dependency-cycle checks for Spring Boot applications.

Presented by: Kiran Gangadharappa - Engineering Advisor at Harness, and Scott Davis - Senior Engineering Manager at Harness

#9628. Held together by spare time: Reviving wiki.alpinelinux.org during PHP2Shell

Reviving wiki.alpinelinux.org during PHP2Shell · November 21, 2026

It feels like this month (and last month..) has been nonstop chaos. PHP2Shell threw a nice little grenade into an already busy month, and while that was happening a GitLab RCE took down Alpine's GitLab instance. It was a whole thing, and as frustrating as it was, I'm kind of proud to say that I got to help respond to the event and write the incident announcement. Ikke did all of the real heavy lifting, but it takes a community to keep a distribution together. Everything, and I mean everything, is kept together by volunteers lending their time and talent with no expectation that there will be a reward for the effort.

We do it because we care for the work being done. Whether it's a critical service enabling a community of tens of thousands to distribute hundreds of petabytes of data that we call "Alpine", or simply enabling a small piece of software to work for personal desires. All of it happens because someone cares enough to do the work. I love this so much, frankly. It's absolutely flabbergasting what we as a community can do with our spare time.

I enjoy giving my time to Alpine Linux, because there's a community, and because we can have an outsized impact on the world by collaborating together. It's not perfect, but it's rewarding. I think I owe my career to it in a sense. I've learned so much by simply raising my hand and being willing to give my time and learn a few new things. But there's a limit to how far you get on donated time, both personally, and as a project.

Not in the sense that it wasn't used; it gets tons of traffic and contains a treasure trove of useful information that people depend on and are excited to contribute to. But between keeping the infrastructure afloat, migrating off of Equinix to new sponsored compute, and mitigating the constant wave of problems, from scale to RCE, that plague a small engineering team trying to serve a massive consumer base, well, it's no wonder that once alice was no longer contributing, the infrastructure languished a bit. This wasn't intentional, nor was it bad. There simply wasn't spare time to contribute to it.

So in November of last year ikke asked if anyone was interested in lending a bit of spare time to fixing that problem. Naturally, I raised my hand, happy to have an opportunity to do so.

2025-11-13 15:40:43 @ikke Anyone helping with infra that wants to help maintaining the wiki? 2025-11-13 15:57:01 durrendal ikke: I don't mind helping out, just let me know what you need done 2025-11-13 16:10:46 @ikke durrendal: the wiki is hosted in an LXC container 2025-11-13 16:18:11 durrendal that makes sense, it tracks how most everything else is deployed. It's mediawiki, so php + a db. Is it using postgres on the backend, and do you have it behind traefik or something else? 2025-11-13 16:22:07 @ikke It uses mariadb 2025-11-13 16:22:26 @ikke There is an nginx proxy in front 2025-11-13 16:22:51 @ikke The database is in a separate container 2025-11-13 16:26:56 durrendal That's not bad, seems like a straight forward setup at first glance. I use mariadb for my zabbix deployments so that's nice and familiar 2025-11-13 16:34:47 @ikke The current setup uses a combination of git submodules and composer from what I can tell (alice was the last one taking care of it)

All IRC timestamps in this post are in UTC.

This was essentially the sum of information I got about the wiki; it was all that was really documented. And despite my eagerness to jump in immediately and lift it up from whatever state it happened to be in, it took time to get access. We had a release to get out. We were fighting to get 3.23 finished and didn't even get it wrapped up until 12/3/25! So it's no wonder that it took until 1/16/26 before I got access to the server itself to start poking around and even begin to understand how the deployment was handled.

And as you can guess by the fact that I'm writing this post in October of 2026, I did not get in there and immediately upgrade it and move on.

And I think that's important. Even if I'm only giving away a limited amount of time, I hate to rush through things without fully understanding them. There's just no way I can improve something if I don't have a solid grounding. More importantly, I actually really love spelunking inside of old systems other sysadmins have set up. Everyone has a unique flair to how they deploy something. Enterprise admins end up deploying things in a real textbook manner, and when you deal with small businesses it's usually a hodgepodge of "just get it done". I haven't had a ton of opportunities to spelunk FOSS infrastructure though! What I found was interesting in its own right, mostly because I don't think I'd have deployed the service this way.

What ikke told me was spot on: MediaWiki was a git checkout with extensions and skins vendored as submodules inside the repo. You could slot in new modules using composer, and as long as you had an appropriate underlying PHP version to work with, you were golden. But that was then mixed with actual wiki data, like images, all of it lumped together in /var/www. Very simple, but not obvious if you'd not dealt with it before.

When I got into the server, MediaWiki 1.40.0 was running on PHP 8.2 on top of Alpine 3.20, but the LocalSettings.php that controlled the wiki was generated under 1.25.3. Just to give you a sense, 1.40.0 is from July 2023, and 1.25.3 is from October of 2015! It's really neat to get a sense for how long something was tended for. Of course, our friends at the Internet Archive have been archiving the Alpine Wiki since April of 2010, and based on the main page I can tell you we've been using MediaWiki for a solid 16 years now, if not longer. I'm positive it's not the same exact server, but probably the same-ish data. I made notes about all the little important bits I found, everything from extension inventories to known issues and interesting shell snippets I found in the server's history file. Anything can be, and is, helpful when you're spelunking. Truthfully, given the age of the deployment, the public facing nature of the server, and my relative newness to administering MediaWiki servers, I was approaching the problem with the utmost caution.

By the end of February I had MediaWiki figured out, but it wasn't committed until March. And not to bury the lede, but I mean that in the most me way possible. I went through the process of setting up a clone of the staging server in my homelab. From there I worked out how to package MediaWiki itself, and then break out all of the various extensions that comprise the core system into a proper APKBUILD. After packaging it, I was no longer surprised it hadn't been done before. The core extension list alone is absurdly long, and all told we use 36 different extensions for our wiki, so this isn't even a complete list.

And given the complexity, and that this was all production infrastructure, I tried to get it merged into the community repositories before making any sort of change to the production infrastructure. Anything less wasn't really right in my mind.

But it sat, not because it wasn't appreciated, but because we are woefully close to the absolute maximum storage we can host through our CDN. Not that we weren't working on that either; I started looking into our space limitations in earnest in March, when it was a potential blocker to our ability to release 3.24 in June. I knew the package was too big to go into community, but I also didn't think leaving it in testing made sense for production infrastructure. So I turned my focus to the clearer, bigger problem and started working with ikke and clandmeter to figure out a path to archive our older distributions.

By May that problem had turned into discussions with Jason at the Internet Archive, which, as this little aside suggests, was the least stressful component of any of this. Jason is an amazing archivist, and the work the Internet Archive is doing is a massive boon to FOSS projects.

And of course, dear reader, I bet you can guess what happened next. I packaged the ia tool, built a prototype to validate we could actually migrate things, and when a prototype wasn't enough, turned it into its own tool, arkivi, which can do partial migrations and reclaim space while it migrates data. None of that merged quickly either, because, well, we were out of space and had a release to cut. But once again, I had time to donate, and I wasn't going to provide half a solution to a problem I could solve.

This might seem like a bit of a detour, but I swear it's not! We are in fact still talking about upgrading the wiki! I couldn't get the core MediaWiki package merged into a stable repo, let alone any of the extensions, which means it can't be released on a stable branch. As much as I personally trust Alpine and think we do a good job keeping edge decently stable, the reality is that it's a testing area sometimes, and it makes very little sense to run production infrastructure off of it. Or if you are going to do that, you need to ensure you have the time to keep up with the constant churn. You can probably guess my concern here: I might not have that time to give.

There are so many disparate but interconnected problems going on in the background of most FOSS distributions that you just can't fathom until you live with them. And the wild part? Nothing I've described is unique. I work within a community of clever and dedicated people who turn this type of work around on the regular. But as you can imagine, I lost my momentum on actually reviving the wiki too. I got blocked by infrastructure constraints and couldn't complete the task in what I felt was a professional and sustainable manner, so I simply waited. My small problem didn't outweigh the needs of the distribution, and there were bigger problems to solve elsewhere. The wiki was stable, it was fine.

I'll get testing done tonight. Heading home from work now and should have time shortly after

PHP2Shell isn't the kind of thing you leave running on a public server, and the wiki was sitting on PHP 8.2 on a branch that was already out of support. So the wiki went dark. We were forced to throw up a maintenance page and block people's access to the wiki. And of course people asked why, and when to expect it back. Like I said earlier, a lot of people depend on this resource to use our distro!

Which of course kicked off a fever pitch of building, testing, and migrating. I wasn't ready for this! I was missing extensions, I hadn't fully tested the database upgrade process, it wasn't automated, and my packages weren't in a stable repo!

But I wasn't starting from zero either. The core package had been sitting in testing since March. I had a clone of stage in my homelab, and a README full of notes about every odd corner of the old install. The better part of a year that looked like stalling had at least given me some sense of how to proceed.

It would have been nice to take the easy out at this point, but it would have been the most temporary of bandaids:

So it was four upgrades at once: Alpine 3.20 to 3.24 (we're still working on 3.25 at the moment), PHP 8.2 to 8.3, MediaWiki 1.40 to 1.46.2, and the git submodule install to apk packages. Well, there really was no quick fix. Somewhere in that stack something would break, and it would keep creating problems down the line unless the work was done in a way that made it all easier to maintain long term.

Even if I wanted to take the quick path and just get the job done, that's the sort of logic that results in the same sort of languishing. Just run the old stuff, just upgrade the existing thing, keep it all similar, move onto the next thing. Sideload 1.46 the old way, get it up tonight, clean it up "later". I have so little time to give, and so many other important changes that need to be made. For anyone paying attention, that's only getting worse with the literal waterfall of RCEs being announced day after day after day, and we're expected to just keep up with it all. It's a lot, but it will only be worse if we cut corners and stop caring about doing it right. "Later" is exactly how the wiki got here in the first place.

Plus, that's not who I am. No, I'd rather dogfood a new tool I've been working on, finish the packaging work, and prove out that everything can and will work on a v3.24 mock and provide a good stable experience. Anything less would be unprofessional, an affront to the craft, or at the very least to my sense of pride.

Which leaves just one awkward bit. Despite all of my effort, the mediawiki packages are still making their way through testing. The work is never truly finished, there's always one more thing that needs to be done. But I'm confident once everything catches up the path forward is that much easier. Every mediawiki component and extension packaged provides a simpler maintenance path going forward. Nobody needs to remember anything I've described thus far. And anyone who wants to suggest an extension to make the wiki better can actively contribute to that process by packaging and testing it.

It turns out that emergencies are great times to stress test the library coverage of a configuration management tool, especially when you need to spin up a box, test a migration, and repeat it over and over. I could have done all of this with some shell scripts or with Salt, but it's a lot more fun to use scio and figure out how well the little Lua DSL I've put together maps onto things I'd either do by hand or know well enough another way. The reps are the point. Every time something broke, I fixed it in the state, threw the box away, and ran it again from nothing, until a fresh Alpine 3.24 container could become a working wiki without me touching it. If you're curious what that looks like, the full scio state is here.

If I as a contributor only have so much time to give, and my standard is that it's done well and to the best of my abilities, well, then I'll combine pleasure and work and solve two problems in one go. Servers get upgraded, I get a production grade test case for my configuration management system, and the entire thing is held together by spare time and tenacity!

I'll write more about scio in the near future. There's a lot to say, but now's not the time.

Did I mention I try to be meticulous? All of the preflight work isn't nearly enough when working with production infrastructure; I wanted to know exactly what I was touching. So naturally, I wrote a quick diff script to compare stage and prod, and the answer I got in the process was very reassuring. The two servers were nearly identical. The only real difference was prod's exposure layer, with go-away out front and nginx listening behind it. Then I wrote a backup script, because the existing backups weren't something I was willing to bet on. My process was obvious afterward: a throwaway incus container restored from a prod dump first, then stage, and only then prod.

Good thing, too. I could see every place I might trip, and I still managed to stumble.

First up was LocalSettings.php. Remember that file generated back in 2015 under 1.25.3? It had been carried forward through every upgrade since, collecting settings MediaWiki removed years ago ($wgScriptExtension, $wgDBmysql5, $wgUseTeX, $wgShowIPinHeader, $wgSquidServers) and path overrides pointing into a git tree that was about to stop existing. It fell over one dead path at a time. Fix a line, run the update, watch it die on the next one. Eventually I stopped playing whack-a-mole and just started over from scratch. A decade of "it still works, don't touch it", gone. I'll try my best to remember to leave a note for the next sysadmin who comes after me.

Even then, once I could actually open a page on the wiki, every image on it came back with "Error creating thumbnail: File missing." The old backups had never included uploads. The database was covered, but as far as the backups were concerned, every image anyone had ever uploaded to the wiki existed in exactly one place. Nobody was careless here. In the old install the uploads sat right alongside everything else in /var/www, and I hadn't understood where things lived well enough to notice they were missing from the backups. My mock tests never checked for them either. What an obvious and embarrassing look it would have been if I hadn't caught it on staging first!

But then I fucked up. On stage, I ran php maintenance/run.php install instead of update. It was late, it must have been nearing 1am or 2am at this point, and I wasn't fully paying attention. I should have stopped and rested, it could have waited another day, but I had committed to fixing this. If it's not obvious, install is for empty databases. Pointed at a real one, it overwrites an existing db with a fresh schema and admin account right on top of everything that's already there. Thank goodness I had a backup. I was able to easily restore the dump, put things back the way they were, start the whole thing over.

The rest were the kind of thing that just ate time, and they make for a pretty dull story. $wgMainCacheType = CACHE_ACCEL needs php83-pecl-apcu, and opcache doesn't count. The 3.24 mariadb client refuses non-TLS connections by default, so everything needed --skip-ssl initially. The packaged php-fpm listens on a unix socket rather than 127.0.0.1:9000, which I learned by way of 502s. Restored pages rendered stale, because their old page_touched values were older than the freshly built parser cache, which $wgCacheEpoch fixed. And AbuseFilter's grants were redacted in the capture I was working from, so I recovered them from the backup.

When it finally came together, the schema update on stage took 28 seconds. After all of that effort, 28 seconds.

That radio silence was the day job. PHP2Shell didn't just land on Alpine, it landed on everyone, and I spent my days scrambling over the same bug I was fixing for the wiki in the evenings.

By the time I sat down with prod, the hard part was over. It had become routine and easy because I put the learning up front where it belonged. Prod got a maintenance mode, a flag file that nginx checks on every request. Touch it and the world sees a maintenance notice, while requests from the box itself still reach the wiki, so I could test everything from localhost before anyone else could see it. 2026-10-24 02:40:57 durrendal ikke ncopa the production wiki is fully upgraded and back online! 2026-10-24 02:41:12 durrendal https://wiki.alpinelinux.org/wiki/Special:Version 2026-10-24 02:48:22 lotheac nice! 2026-10-24 02:57:20 durrendal thanks :) and it's using packages instead of the old git submodule install too so hopefully this shouldn't languish ever again 2026-10-24 02:57:57 durrendal I just need to open a few MRs now

The wiki is on Alpine 3.24, MediaWiki 1.46.2, and PHP 8.3, and every piece of it comes from apk. Which means the next time a PHP2Shell comes along, the fix is apk upgrade, run.php update, and a php-fpm restart. No submodules or composer, nobody needs to remember something special, all that's needed is a bit of Alpine specific systems administration knowledge and we're golden. This will get better as I finish documenting the new installation, so that when I inevitably run out of spare time, the next person to raise their hand can stand on my shoulders and reach a little higher.

Look, at the start of this I said there's a limit to how far you can get on donated time. I meant that, but not to signal some kind of fundamental flaw in the system. Alice tended to this before me, ikke kept it running alongside everything else, and when it needed someone, someone raised their hand. This time it was me. There are many, many people like me, what I've described is not unique. But look what it took, eleven months from "anyone want to help maintain the wiki?" to an actual upgrade, most of it spent trying to solve other problems around the one that was volunteered for. When the emergency came, it got fixed because someone was willing to pay down the technical debt all at once.

That's what spare time can carry, and it's a lot. It's also why it matters that Alpine is choosing to fund dedicated infrastructure engineering. Not because volunteers can't do the work, but because the work shouldn't depend on whether someone happens to have a free evening when the next CVE drops. Spare time built this wiki, and spare time will keep tending it. It just shouldn't have to hold it together alone.

As for me, I got what I always hope to get from raising my hand, an opportunity to learn. I walked in knowing very little about Mediawiki administration, and while I wouldn't call myself an expert from one small engagement, I'm happy to have come away with a few more packages, more confidence in scio, and a once more working wiki for Alpine. And a great reminder that part of giving your spare time is knowing when to stop, nobody will ever be mad that you ran out of spare time.

"Life is once, forever." — Henri Cartier-Bresson

#9627. Hugging Face ❤️ TorchTPU: TPUs, Natively

If you ever tried to run PyTorch on a TPU, you probably ported your code to torch_xla, or you ended up having to learn JAX. With TorchTPU, a native PyTorch backend, TPU is now just another device. It opens up native support of TPU in the Hugging Face ecosystem. Transformers, Diffusers and Kernels run natively on TPU. Pick a model from the Hub, send it to "tpu", and you're done.

TPU stands for Tensor Processing Unit. TPUs are Google's own AI accelerators. They are chips built for one job: the matrix math that neural networks spend most of their time on. Google has been designing them for about ten years, and uses them to train and serve its own models, including Gemini.

TPUs are available on Google Cloud, from a single chip up to pods of thousands of chips. They shine when you need a lot of compute, for training or for serving at scale.

The catch has always been software. The TPU stack grew up around TensorFlow and JAX, and PyTorch users had to work harder to get in.

Until now, running PyTorch on TPUs meant going through PyTorch/XLA (torch_xla). It worked, but it had its quirks. Tensors were lazy (the tensors, not you), so your code didn't always run when you thought it did. Small changes could trigger graph recompilations, and debugging was hard to reason about.

To make life easier, we built Optimum TPU. It gave Hugging Face models inference and training support on TPUs. Now that TorchTPU brings native support, Optimum TPU is not required anymore to run Hugging Face models with Transformers and Diffusers.

TorchTPU adds TPU as a new backend to PyTorch. You write regular PyTorch code. It comes with Pallas kernels tuned for TPUs, support for distributed training, and a torch.compile integration for when you want more speed. Installing it on a TPU VM takes one command:

The extra index gives you the CPU build of torch. Without it, pip pulls the much bigger CUDA build, which you don't need on a TPU.

Transformers v5 was built around one idea: be the source of truth for model definitions, so they can run anywhere. "Anywhere" now includes TPUs. To load a model on a TPU, pass device_map="tpu". That's it.

The model runs in eager mode by default. You can also use torch.compile for better performance, or run it in a distributed setup.

TPU is now a first-class device in Diffusers. For prototyping or debugging, eager mode only needs pipe.to("tpu"). For deployment, compiled mode adds one compile call. Your pipelines and code stay the same, and there's no TPU fork to maintain.

The first call compiles, and every call after that with the same image size reuses the graph.

Models too big for one chip? Pass a TensorParallelConfig to from_pretrained and the transformer is sharded across chips as it loads, so the full model never has to fit in one place. Many popular pipelines support it out of the box, and the ones that don't are just a tp_plan away. The Diffusers TPU guide has the full recipe.

Here are some examples run on a Cloud TPU v6e-4:

TP=4 (each model split across four chips) · bf16 · batch 1

The Kernels Hub has ready-to-use TPU kernels. Load one with the Kernels library and give your model a speed boost.

TPU kernels are written in Pallas, which gives you low-level control over the hardware. You can also bring in kernels from the Tokamax library. Here is a ragged-dot kernel from Tokamax plugged into a Mixture-of-Experts model:

The bigger the batch, the bigger the win. At batch size 64, decoding is 21.5× faster on Qwen3-30B-A3B and 12.8× faster on Gemma 4 26B-A4B.

Decode throughput on a TPU v6e-8, Hub kernel vs. the default implementation.

We're continuously improving TPU support in transformers by running the library test suite. We are working to add a nightly CI on TPU and make the results available in the (transformers dashboard)[https://huggingface.co/spaces/transformers-community/transformers-ci-dashboard].

The Transformers CI dashboard, with TPU results next to other accelerators. Work in progress!

It's not all green yet, and we're fine with that. Of the tests that run on TPU, 96.5% pass. Every failure we find becomes a small repro script and an issue on the TorchTPU repo. So far we have reported 34 issues, and 19 are already fixed. Running on TPU also caught a few bugs in Transformers itself, like in StaticCache and the Qwen3 tensor-parallel plans. We fixed those upstream.

If something breaks on TPU, we want to find out before you do.

TPUs are no longer a side quest for PyTorch users. Install TorchTPU, grab a model from the Hub, and send it to "tpu".

We can't wait to see what you build 🤗. If you hit a problem, open an issue and tell us about it.

#9626. Signal is Serious About Protecting Your Privacy

This means that we are restricting the latest AI agents built into mobile operating systems from potentially capturing and storing your Signal data.

We’ve already had to do this once with Windows. Last year, we used screenshot blocking to prevent Microsoft’s Recall AI from taking and storing screenshots of your Signal messages on Windows 11 operating systems by default.1 We will now be taking similar measures to restrict agentic systems built into iOS 27 and on Android versions where we can detect an AI assistant attempting to read your Signal screen.2

In order to gain access to information about you, these OS AI agents “scan” the information that’s on your screen. In doing so, your Signal data is captured, then made available to these agentic systems in order to allow them to answer your questions and do your bidding.

So, we are blocking such capture by preventing screenshots in the app on iOS 27 and when AI assistants attempt to capture screen data on Android.2

We also see a growing need for tools that can prevent third-party agents, like Meta’s Muse, from accessing application data using the deep permissions that users are encouraged to grant them during setup. In many cases these agents are leveraging accessibility settings that were meant to empower actual people to get the most out of their apps and services, not to act as a skeleton key that provides access to AI agents.

Microsoft Recall captures your screen every few seconds, extracts text from screenshots via optical character recognition, then populates a searchable on-device database with this personal data in order to allow the AI system to query it – potentially exposing and retaining your Signal data indefinitely, including disappearing messages. ↩

There are multiple versions of Android beyond the Google-provided distributions on Pixel devices. For many vendors, we don’t have a reliable way to detect when a screenshot was attempted if screenshots are already disabled. Rather than choose a poor user experience (where screenshots simply stop working, confusing users), we decided to instead focus on detecting when an AI assistant attempts to access the screen. We automatically enable the “Screen security” setting in Signal Android when this type of access is detected. ↩ ↩2

#9625. Profiling TorchNeuron (Part 1): System-level profiling on AWS Trainium.

Many ML practitioners have some intuition about how to make models run fast, but fewer know how to analyze why a model is slow. In Part 1 of this series, you will learn how to systematically analyze inference performance and identify where the time is spent.

This post starts from scratch and assumes no prior profiling experience. The walkthrough uses AWS Trainium, a purpose-built AI chip for deep learning training and inference workloads, and TorchNeuron, its open source native PyTorch backend. TorchNeuron supports standard PyTorch workflows on Trainium, including eager execution, torch.compile, and standard PyTorch APIs, with minimal code changes. Additionally, TorchNeuron integrates with Neuron Kernel Interface (NKI) to enable custom operators and performance optimization for Trainium hardware. By the end, you should know:

Before you profile a workload, it helps to understand how Neuron integrates with PyTorch.

The Neuron backend uses PyTorch's PrivateUse1 extension point. This mechanism lets an accelerator integrate with the framework without adding a dedicated dispatch key such as cuda. The torch_neuronx package works with upstream PyTorch to register Neuron as a native backend for PyTorch code. For details about this extension mechanism, see Facilitating New Backend Integration by PrivateUse1.

You use two objects to profile a Neuron workload:

The modes parameter selects the data streams to capture, such as device instructions and runtime traces. The capture_enabled_for_nc parameter selects the NeuronCores to trace. Setting correlate_device_time=True propagates device time from the trace into the key_averages() table, where you can compare CPU and Neuron device time. For the complete parameter reference and available ProfileMode values, see the NeuronConfig Profile Modes documentation.

Neuron Explorer is a browser-based viewer for the system trace, device timeline, and per-engine breakdown. You can access it through an SSH tunnel or the Visual Studio Code extension. In this post, you use Explorer to confirm what key_averages() reports numerically and inspect what happens between dispatches.

After profiling, the output directory contains the system trace and, when you capture device data, matched .neff and .ntff files. The Neuron Executable File Format (NEFF) contains the compiled Neuron executable, while the matching NTFF contains its hardware instruction trace. The files share a numeric hash that identifies them as a pair. To open the profile in Neuron Explorer, upload the complete output directory for a system or combined profile. For a device-only profile, upload the matching .neff and .ntff files individually. See Step 5: Upload your profile for the UI and command-line instructions.

For this first analysis, you profile RMSNorm, a small operation with a clear sequence of arithmetic and reduction operations.

You profile three implementations of the same operation:

The scripts use the same inputs, profiler configuration, and schedule so the results are directly comparable.

All scripts to reproduce this work are available in the torch-neuronx examples directory.

Start by writing RMSNorm with individual PyTorch operations. Each line maps to one or more ATen operations and can create intermediate tensors.

Call the profiler with two arguments required for the Neuron backend:

The schedule uses wait=2, warmup=1, and active=1 across four prof.step() calls. This records one warm iteration without including initial setup overhead.

Call torch.neuron.synchronize() inside the profiler loop. Without this synchronization, the profiler can export before the device finishes and leave the Neuron time column empty.

After profiling finishes, inspect the key_averages() table. Sort by self_privateuse1_time_total to place the operations with the highest device cost first. The table shown here is filtered to the RMSNorm operations that report Neuron device time. The full key_averages() output also includes CPU-side events such as allocations and host-to-device transfers.

The key averages table shows that three aten::mul calls account for the largest share of Neuron device time.

The table shows which ATen operations ran, how often they ran, and how much time they spent on the CPU and Neuron device. aten::mul has the highest total device time because the function performs three multiplications.

Each row maps directly to the function. aten::mul runs for x * x, x * rms, and the final multiplication by weight. aten::mean reduces the last dimension. aten::add adds the epsilon value and triggers a host-to-device copy because the scalar starts on the CPU. aten::rsqrt computes the reciprocal square root.

Neuron Explorer follows an aten::mul operation from framework dispatch through runtime scheduling to execution on the Neuron hardware lanes.

In Explorer, time flows from left to right and the event lifecycle flows from top to bottom. Each ATen operation follows the same pattern: creation in the framework lane, scheduling in the runtime lane as nrta_execute_schedule, and device execution in the hardware lane as nc_exec_running.

The system trace view organizes events into lanes. In the Default grouping mode, labels follow the pattern instance/PID/subsystem/identifier:

In eager mode, each operation runs independently. Use the dependency chain viewer to follow aten::mul.Tensor from the framework layer through runtime scheduling to device execution.

The dependency chain viewer highlights the lifecycle of one operation across the framework, runtime, and hardware lanes.

Replace the individual operations with PyTorch's built-in rms_norm function. Neuron lowers the operation to one fused kernel:

The fused RMSNorm appears as one device operation in the key averages table.

The fused RMSNorm follows one framework-to-hardware path instead of dispatching each arithmetic operation separately.

In the naive implementation, each operation crosses the dispatch boundary independently and follows its own framework-to-runtime-to-hardware path. In the fused implementation, one Python call covers the complete computation. The trace contains one dispatch and one hardware event, with no gaps between component operations.

For the final example, compile the original naive RMSNorm function with torch.compile.

With @torch.compile(backend="neuron"), TorchDynamo captures the Python bytecode as an FX graph and AOTAutograd lowers it to ATen operations. The Neuron backend receives the complete graph instead of dispatching each operation separately. It fuses the operations, optimizes memory access, and compiles the graph into a single NEFF artifact. The artifact runs as one hardware dispatch.

The compiled function appears as one Torch-Compiled Region in the key averages table.

The compiled graph follows one path through runtime scheduling and hardware execution.

The table shows one device execution, as in Profile 2, but the code takes a different path. Instead of calling a purpose-built fused operation, the compiler discovers the fusion from the original Python function. In this run, the Neuron time is comparable to torch.rms_norm, at 375 μs compared with 403 μs.

Both torch.rms_norm and torch.compile fuse RMSNorm into one kernel dispatch. In these runs, either approach takes about one-sixth of the naive implementation's device time. Fusion removes the gaps between hardware executions and avoids materializing intermediate values such as x_sq and mean_sq between separately dispatched operations.

key_averages() shows which operations consume device time, while its full output also reveals CPU-side setup and transfers. Explorer provides the corresponding visual trace. You can follow one operation from framework dispatch through runtime scheduling to hardware execution and see the gaps that fusion removes.

You can use the same workflow on larger models: find a hotspot in the table, verify it in the trace, and then determine whether a fused operation or torch.compile can reduce its cost.

In Part 2, we will move into the device-level profile. You open the NEFF, inspect the TensorEngine, VectorEngine, and direct memory access (DMA) breakdown, and place the kernel on the roofline to determine whether it is compute-bound or memory-bound.

Special thanks to Aritra Roy Gosthipaty for the inspiration to begin this series, and to my peers Pinak Panigrahi, Samir Araujo, Akhil Azhikodan, Esha Lakhotia and the rest for reviewing!

#9624. Second Norwegian Energy Company Breached in 2 Days

Breaking cybersecurity news, news analysis, commentary, and other content from around the world, with an initial focus on the Middle East & Africa, the Asia Pacific, Europe, and Latin America.

No specific link has been drawn between the two incidents, though they certainly sing the same notes.

Two Norwegian energy companies announced that they'd been breached on two consecutive days this week.

On the evening of Nov. 17, Equinor — one of the world's most economically and geopolitically significant oil and gas companies — announced that it had suffered a cyberattack. Hardly a day later, another billion-dollar Norwegian energy company called Skagerak Energi admitted to the same. The two companies' breach disclosures read remarkably similarly, though there is no evidence yet that the two attacks are connected.

Equinor did not respond to a request for comment on this story. Skagerak Energi declined to comment on specifics of the company's incident.

Equinor first publicly reported its cyberattack on the evening of Nov. 17, Central European Time (CET). Its initial investigation suggested that no data had been stolen, and that operations and production would remain uninterrupted. The issue seemed to be limited to internal IT systems. For instance, one employee told Reuters that the company's email system was down.

Related:Nok et norsk energiselskap har blitt utsatt for et datainnbrudd på to dager

The next morning, the company reported having gained "a clearer understanding of how the attack was carried out and which systems have been affected." Without sharing much, it alluded to the attack not being viral in nature, so there was "no risk" of it spreading. Besides that, it said there was no evidence employees, partners, or suppliers were impacted.

Despite all of the good signs in its first two updates, Equinor reported on the morning of Nov. 19 that it was still dealing with the attack, with no timetable for when the situation might resolve itself.

"This is yet another high-stakes cyberattack in what seems like weeks of relentless firefighting throughout Europe," says Anders Storbråten, cybersecurity expert at IDEX Biometrics. "Equinor says there is no indication that data has been stolen, but I wouldn't breathe a sigh of relief just yet. They wouldn't be the first company to offer early reassurances, only to have to backtrack once details become clearer."

Even if the breach does turn out to have been limited, he adds, "Energy companies depend on business systems to organize staff, maintenance and supplies. If those stay unavailable, keeping operations running safely gets harder. Production is unaffected, but nobody should need to see the gas stop flowing before taking this seriously."

Also in its most recent update, Equinor noted that its attack "does not appear to be specifically targeting Equinor." This was especially notable seeing as, between its Wednesday and Thursday updates, nearby Skagerak Energi disclosed that it too had fallen victim to a cyberattack.

Related:Philippine Migrant Worker Data Likely Leaked in 69GB Government Breach

In many ways, the Eastern Norwegian renewable energy and power utility company's press releases mirrored Equinor's. First, on Nov. 18, it reported an attack affecting its IT systems, which didn't impact operations or production. It added that there was no indication that any data had been lost. The next day it reported having obtained a better view of the situation, but provided no additional details.

Though the two companies' breaches remain separate incidents based on public reporting, other Norwegian energy sector companies have been put on high alert. A representative of oil and gas giant Aker BP told the press on Wednesday that it has mobilized its emergency preparedness and strengthened its monitoring, and the hydropower company Statkraft said it's also closely monitoring the situation.

"Every other energy company should be asking: Are we exposed to the same thing?" Storbråten advises. "The danger is treating this as Equinor’s problem until it becomes your own."

Three weeks before these incidents became public, Norway's National Security Authority (NSM) published an unprecedented warning. For the first time in its history, it declassified its national cyber-risk assessment, warning that Norway faced a "high" cybersecurity risk to businesses. NSM's director stated that it was time to finally share its assessment with the public, "because it is absolutely necessary to strengthen both resilience and the ability to handle cyber operations in Norwegian companies."

Related:State Bank of India Suffers a Customer PII Data Leak

Storbråten says that since the warning, "NSM and DSB [The Norwegian Directorate for Civil Protection] have urged households to prepare for power, water, and communications outages, and, earlier this month, the government called for every municipality to stress-test its security. But people still remain paralyzed and unsure what to do. The guidance is just that: guidance. It's not clear instruction, and thus businesses and civilians alike are in a sort of limbo."

Amid all this, less than one week before the incidents became public, Norway's Police Security Service (PST) published its own warning regarding the threat of cyber sabotage in Norway. Besides the defense industry and its suppliers, the press release highlighted that "Critical infrastructure can also be affected, for example, objects within the energy sector."

The country's energy sector has been trying to match its government's action. Earlier this autumn, representatives of Equinor and Aker BP, among other organizations, took part in "Grey Dawn Petroleum" — an oil and gas-themed tabletop exercise jointly arranged by the Norwegian Ocean Industry Authority (Havtil) and KraftCERT, a sector-specific combination Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT), Information Sharing and Analysis Center (ISAC), and Incident Response Team (IRT).

Per Atle Vagle, Equinor's head of cyber defense, characterized the exercise as "good training," which provided him with "new perspectives that we can bring back to our own business."

Nate Nelson is a journalist and award-winning scriptwriter. In addition to Dark Reading he writes for Darknet Diaries, the most popular show in cybersecurity across all media.

He began his career as a freelancer, ghostwriting Forbes and CNBC op-eds for executives in tech and finance. Then he transitioned to journalism at Threatpost, where he covered cybersecurity news and trends. Throughout those years he co-created a cybersecurity podcast, Malicious Life, which in its day climbed into the Top 20 technology podcasts charts on Apple Podcasts and Spotify.

He holds degrees from New York University and Bard College. As a born and bred New Yorker, he enjoys a superiority complex, but is polite enough to keep it to himself.
